items.en: DNA and vehicle-tracking help French investigators recover stolen Renoirs

NANTERRE, France — DNA left on a protective painting cover helped investigators recover two stolen Renoirs and uncover what they suspected were preparations for another art heist, a French prosecutor said Monday.

Four men were given preliminary charges in the investigation into the Sept. 8 theft from the small Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera. The charges include organized theft and criminal association, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said.

One painting, "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano," suffered a tear. The other, "Young Woman at the Well," had slight damage to its frame, Bessone said. He estimated their combined value at 4.2 million euros ($4.7 million).

The thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence, entered the museum through the ground floor and cut clips securing the frames of four paintings. An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that "apparently caused the perpetrators to panic," Bessone said.
"As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve," he said.
The DNA found on the abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old already under investigation in a drug trafficking case in which police were tracking his vehicle, Bessone said.
Vehicle-tracking data showed that the suspect, accompanied by a 41-year-old man, went to the home of a third man shortly after the theft, Bessone said.
Police surveillance also showed that the 29-year-old on Oct. 3 visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence — home to a large modern art collection.
The suspect then met with a fourth man known to police from art theft and forgery cases in 2001 and 2003.
Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the "very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent."

The two men suspected of carrying out the museum theft have been given preliminary charges of "theft committed by an organized gang" and "criminal association," among other counts. They were sent to prison pending further investigation. The have denied wrongdoing, Bessone said.

The third suspect acknowledged receiving the paintings at his home and hiding them behind a wall built beneath a staircase after the theft. Investigators recovered the Renoirs from the hiding place, Bessone said.

The fourth suspect acknowledged seeing photographs of the paintings but said he did not immediately recognize them. Both of those suspects were given preliminary charges of "concealment" of stolen paintings. They were released under judicial supervision and barred from leaving France.
Two additional people who had been arrested were released without charge.
The theft renews concerns about museum security

The Renoir Museum occupies the final home of the leading French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who lived there until his death in 1919. It is the best-known attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a Mediterranean coastal town between Cannes and Nice.

The theft revived painful memories of the spectacular theft of crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and renewed calls for better security and funding at the many cultural sites across France.

Christian Sainte, national director of judicial police, said Monday that the country "is repeatedly targeted by organized criminal groups that carry out theft operations targeting valuable objects that are part of our cultural heritage" in museums, castles, places of worship, private homes and art galleries.
French museums recorded 23 cases in 2025 and about 10 this year, he said.
Swansea soaring, Burnley get their first win and Tonda Eckert saga ends - Championship Catch-up

Swansea deservedly lead the way, Burnley get a win and Tonda Eckert saga finally ends as Southampton beat Portsmouth; Andy Hinchcliffe picks out the key stories in The Championship Catch-up; a Sky Sports column focusing on the second tier.
Welcome to The Championship Catch-up, a new Sky Sports column in which Andy Hinchcliffe rounds up some of the key stories from the second tier. This week:
Swansea City are deserved Championship leaders
Swansea have been stronger than we thought they'd be this season. It seems that less is more with them because last season Zan Vipotnik scored 23 goals and really carried the team.

This season, he's only scored a couple of goals and hasn't played that many games. They've shown now, again, that without a star striker they over-rely on for goals, they're more of a team, both defensively and importantly going forward as well.

You look at them from back to front, they've got one of the best goalkeepers in the division and one of the most stubborn, strongest defences in the division. If you're going to be successful, certainly in the Championship, that really does help.

They're not a defensive team, they're a team that defend well. They dominate the ball, they control games and they've got a variety of goalscorers now as well. They're not reliant on just that one centre-forward. Adam Idah's got four goals, so he's kind of the main threat, but it's still not just him and nobody else.

The way they play enables four, five or six players to get into goalscoring positions and score goals over the course of the season. You're better being that type of team than having that reliance on one central striker. If he gets injured or he's out of form, things can get really tricky.

They deserve to be where they are right now, and we're going to learn a lot more this week about whether they can stay the course. They head to Millwall on Tuesday night, then host West Ham on Saturday.

Coaches and clubs are looking at squad depth now. You can't just be reliant on a few players, even on six or seven players, and keep hoping game in and game out that those six or seven players produce and get the job done for you.
For Swansea, there are maybe five or six attacking players who can change the course of a game.

Every defence they play against isn't really sure how Swansea are going to line up. You probably know how they're going to play in terms of their set-up, energy, urgency, pressing game and passing game. But who's going to be in the team and who's going to impact the game? I'd much rather have one problem than four or five coming at me.
Vitor Matos has done a brilliant job. You listen to players playing under these coaches talk about them, and Ben Cabango was saying this team will run through brick walls for the gaffer.
I think that drives players on even more.
Burnley get off the mark with a thumping win at Watford

Looking at Burnley's overall performances, they weren't performing like a bottom-three team. They were probably around mid-table, but for the club Burnley are, what they're looking to achieve and the players they've got, mid-table performances in this league aren't really acceptable. They're much better than that.

They've had the big change since relegation. We thought Craig Bellamy was coming in, but that didn't happen, and Nicky Hayen came in. He and the players have got to get to an understanding, and that can take a little bit of time.

Playing Watford, you're never really sure what you're going to get. They're a struggling team at the moment, but they can suddenly produce. I never expected Burnley to win that game, so to win it so comfortably was impressive.

Looking at all the stats from the game, the expected goals, they thoroughly deserved to win. Their xG was three times higher than Watford's. It wasn't a case of scoring four goals from four shots and being lucky to win. It was a game they dominated.
You look at the personnel and the teamsheet and think that's a team that should win a lot of Championship games. Not necessarily 4-0, but they should be winning Championship games.

Now they've won a game, I guarantee the training ground will be a totally different place. Looking at the experience and quality they've got, I wouldn't be surprised if they started to put a bit of a run together.
Let's see how they back that up during midweek and in that big game against Wolves on Friday night.
Saints win derby against toothless Pompey - and draw line under Eckert saga

The situation rumbled on far too long with Tonda Eckert. I still have to say that I, and most people looking at the situation, were surprised there wasn't some kind of enforced lay-off when you consider the bans that are given out for other things.

I think the FA commission probably looked at it and thought they'd thrown Southampton out of the play-offs and imposed a points deduction. That is unprecedented and a massive punishment for the club and the coach. Maybe they thought piling more agony on Eckert's shoulders wasn't what was needed.
The decision drew a line under it, and then Southampton's performance against Portsmouth drew a second line under it completely.
Eckert showed in that game what a talented coach he is. How he managed it and how he coached his team through it.
We got back to talking about football and him as a coach, rather than someone who did something he has admitted was wrong and that shouldn't happen in the English game.

He showed why Southampton were so desperate to keep him. They know they've got a good guy and a good coach there. Why would you want to get rid of someone you know can do the job? His record and numbers are outstanding, as is the quality of football they play.
From a Portsmouth perspective, the goal they gave away was an absolute shocker. It was a dreadful goal to concede. Collectively and individually, it was so avoidable, yet they didn't defend properly.

They haven't conceded an awful lot of goals, with only 11 so far, but it's the kind of goals they're giving away. They're soft goals, and you can't afford to do that if you want to get anywhere in the Championship.

John Mousinho did his best, looking at how many attacking players he sent on to try to influence things and change the game for Portsmouth after the Southampton red card. Time and again, they got into promising positions, but absolutely nothing came from it.
The main criticism will be that they were toothless. How can they not have a shot on target when they have the extra man and all those attacking players on? It just didn't happen.

They also lost the game because of the goal they gave away, which should never have happened. Losing a big derby is horrendous anyway, but how they lost it will be so disappointing for Portsmouth when they sit down, watch the game and have a debrief.
Rugby League World Cup: Harry Smith insists England have a winner's mentality despite underdog tag

England have three group games against Tonga, France and Papua New Guinea, with a place in the semi-finals up for grabs; they get their campaign under way against Tonga in Perth on October 17, before facing France and Papua New Guinea
England's Harry Smith knows his side head into the Rugby League World Cup as underdogs, but that is doing little to dampen their belief. England are in Australia with one goal; to win the tournament.
Smith was part of the England side that suffered a 3-0 Ashes series defeat to Australia, with the world's No 1 side proving too strong across all three Tests.

Since then, there has been a change in the England setup, with Shaun Wane making way for Brian McDermott. The former Leeds Rhinos head coach has arrived with a clear belief that England can find a style of play capable of troubling - and ultimately beating - the likes of Australia.

With that in mind, he believes it was the game plan, rather than the playing group, that was the issue in The Ashes. Now, it is up to many of those same players, particularly in the spine, to play in a way McDermott believes can win them games, starting with their opening match against Tonga in Perth on October 17.
"It is a proud moment for myself and my family, a first World Cup so I am really looking forward to it," Smith told Sky Sports.
"It is my first time travelling abroad with my country so I am looking forward to it but us pale lads, like me and Zach Eckersley, we might be struggling so we will need plenty of sun cream.
"Speaking to Brian [McDermott] as a spine and also individually, he felt like we missed quite a few opportunities in The Ashes where we were too deep on the add line and not ready to play.

"He wants us to take every play as an opportunity to score so I feel like that is what he is going to push for, especially when you are playing against Australia and New Zealand, those really good defensive teams.
"You don't get many chances to score so when that arrives and opens up you have to take it."
After Tonga, England face France and Papua New Guinea as they look to progress through to the semi-finals.
Australia are the firm favourites for the tournament, but England begin with a familiar foe in Tonga in what is a crucial opening clash.
Smith played for England when they last beat Tonga and knows they will face plenty of size as they get their campaign off to a tough start.
Despite that, there is a belief within the England camp that they are good enough to go all the way and become world champions.
"There is a lot of big lads there, especially for people like me. It is exciting, you want to start the tournament well," Smith added.
"We start against a good team, we are looking forward to that challenge.
"I managed to play against them over here and it was really exciting, a really close game.
"Hopefully we can do the job again and get the win.
"Brian [McDermott] has pushed from the start that we are going out there to win the World Cup.
"From our first meeting he has said that we are here to win. That is the mentality you want and you need.
"Even though we are not the favourites, you need to go in with that mentality or there is no point showing up."
Josh Allen clinches first overtime win of NFL career as Buffalo Bills beat Los Angeles Rams in thriller

Josh Allen rushes for 121 yards, passes for 210 yards and accounts for two touchdowns as the Buffalo Bills beat the Los Angeles Rams in overtime; watch the Jacksonville Jaguars face the Houston Texans in the final NFL London game of the season at Wembley, live on Sky Sports from 2pm Sunday

Josh Allen racked up 331 total yards and two touchdowns, while Tyler Bass drilled a 45-yard field goal with 1:55 remaining in overtime after Greg Rousseau blocked a field goal attempt, lifting the Buffalo Bills to a thrilling 37-34 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers on Monday night.
Allen passed for 210 yards and rushed for 121 more for the Bills (4-1), who rallied to win a frantic game befitting the teams with the NFL's last two MVPs at quarterback.

The Bills appeared to be in trouble after James Cook fumbled early in OT, but Allen got another chance - and he finally won an overtime game for the first time in his career while besting Matthew Stafford, who passed for 383 yards and three touchdowns.

"That's the beautiful thing about football: You get another drive," Allen said. "You get another game. All you can do is keep moving forward. You're hoping someone on defense or special teams can make a play, and that's what happened. Greg Rousseau made a play."

Cook scored his second touchdown with 1:39 left in regulation for Buffalo, but Kyren Williams scored on a one-yard surge with four seconds left to force overtime. The Bills began by driving deep into Rams territory, but Aaron Donald recovered Cook's fumble after Nate Landman punched it out.
Stafford drove the Rams to the Buffalo 30, but Harrison Mevis missed his second field goal attempt of the night when Rousseau got a piece of it.
"The kicking game, with our PAT, field goal [unit] - not even close to good enough," Rams coach Sean McVay said. "It cost us the game tonight. I'm going to evaluate everything."

Allen then made scrambles of 19 and 13 yards before rookie Bills coach Joe Brady elected to try the field goal on second down with nearly two minutes still on the clock. Bass blasted his kick and ran away to celebrate before the officials signalled it good.
"The confidence I had in T-Bass was, 'Hey, 45 yards, he's going to make this kick,'" Brady said.
Allen got more than 100 of his yards rushing on scrambles, repeatedly escaping the pocket and rendering useless the Rams' tenacious secondary coverage.

"When it's there, it's there," Allen said. "I don't want to make a living on that, I understand that, but I do know how much of a backbreaker that can be on a defense when you think you're in pretty good coverage. I felt like there was some room to manoeuvre there and keep the chains moving."
Cook rushed for 111 yards before a costly fumble added to the Bills' recent ball-security concerns. Buffalo improved to 4-1, marking its sixth 4-1 start in the past eight seasons.
Puka Nacua hauled in a career-high 17 receptions for 138 yards and a touchdown for the Rams (2-3), who have started below 500 after five games for the fourth time in five seasons.

Rams head coach Sean McVay was furious with another special-teams collapse and also questioned his own decision to call a conservative play on third-and-5 before Harrison Mevis missed a long field-goal attempt in overtime.

"I wish I would have had a better play call and gone for it, got it tighter," McVay said. "I'm sick right now with myself, and I'm so proud of that group. This is the tough part of sports, but I'm proud of that team. I'm proud of the way we battled, and I'm sick that we came up short."

Buffalo's superior special-teams play and Josh Allen's relentless effort proved decisive as the Bills edged the Rams in another high-scoring shootout. Their previous meeting in December 2024 also produced a classic, with the teams combining for 902 total yards in Los Angeles' 44-42 victory.

After Davante Adams hauled in his second touchdown catch with 7:14 remaining, capping a game that featured six consecutive lead changes, Allen led Buffalo on a 71-yard drive, using two scrambles to exploit the Rams' defence.

James Cook then scored the go-ahead touchdown. Matthew Stafford responded by completing six of seven passes to move Los Angeles to the Buffalo 1-yard line, where the Rams opted against using a timeout before Kyren Williams punched in the tying score.

Adams' second touchdown also brought him level with Larry Fitzgerald for the sixth-most touchdown receptions in NFL history, with 121. Blake Corum added a rushing touchdown, while tight end Tyler Higbee caught five passes for 83 yards.
For Buffalo, Keon Coleman caught Allen's only touchdown pass of the night.

From above, the mere appearance of a curious geologic feature in Western Australia is enough to cause a fright. The aptly named Spider Crater, the product of a meteorite impact followed by hundreds of millions of years of erosion, sprawls across the landscape in the country’s Kimberley region.

The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured this image of the crater on September 20, 2026. The full impact structure has an oval shape measuring about 13 kilometers by 11 kilometers (8 miles by 7 miles), with the spiderlike central portion measuring about 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) across.

Geologists believe the unusual arachnoid pattern is the remnant of a central uplift, the raised portion of the crater floor that formed in the rebound of the initial impact shock. The light-colored “legs” are sandstone ridges that have endured while other rock layers in the impact zone have eroded away.

For decades after the feature’s discovery, scientists struggled to weave a tale about its formation. Some proposed it had a volcanic past. But with some legwork in the field, geologists identified telltale signs of a past impact: fan-shaped fractures called shatter cones. These fractures form only when intense shock waves travel through rock, and they are ubiquitous in Spider Crater’s central dome.

Scientists have subsequently performed lab analyses of shocked quartz and zircon crystals from the sandstone, which can help them reconstruct the angle of the meteorite’s impact. The date of the impact is uncertain, but estimates based on rocks in the region place it between about 900 million and 600 million years ago—making Spider Crater a creature of the late Precambrian.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has moved a step closer to launching its second-ever interplanetary mission — an ambitious, eight-year exploration of seven asteroids between Mars and Jupiter that will culminate with a landing on the mysteriously red asteroid 269 Justitia.

The mission team unveiled a half-scale model of the homegrown probe that will make that landing during an Oct. 1 press conference in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE. The autonomous craft will ride attached to the main spacecraft MBR Explorer, named after Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid al-Maktoum, the ruler of Dubai and the UAE's prime minister.

The flight-ready lander is being kept pristine in a vacuum chamber in the capital before being transported to Colorado by Etihad Airways, officials said, where it will be integrated with the main spacecraft, which was developed by the UAE Space Agency.

If all goes to plan, the mission will lift off from Japan in March 2028, kicking off the Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt (EMA). The project is an ambitious follow-up to the UAE Space Agency's Hope Mars orbiter, which has been studying the Red Planet since 2021.
"It's a proud moment for us here at the UAE," said Faisal al-Bannai, the secretary general of the Advanced Technology Research Council in Abu Dhabi.
'We don't know what we're going to find'

EMA will conduct high-speed flybys of six asteroids before reaching and orbiting 269 Justitia. It will travel a total of about 3 billion miles (5 billion kilometers), which is equivalent to circling Earth roughly 125,000 times, said Najwa Aaraj, the CEO of the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, which designed, built and tested the mission's lander.

Along the way, the MBR Explorer will utilize gravity assists from Venus and then Earth to swing deeper into space, zipping past its first three asteroid targets: 10253 Westerwald, 623 Chimaera and 13294 Rockox. A subsequent gravity assist from Mars will fling the spacecraft even farther out, guiding it past three more space rocks: 88055 Ghaf, 23871 Ousha and 59980 Moza.

By 2036, the spacecraft is scheduled to rendezvous with its final and most intriguing target, 269 Justitia. A roughly 30-mile-wide (50 km) object in the middle of the asteroid belt, 269 Justitia is unusual for its remarkably crimson hue.

Its distinct color more closely resembles icy objects in the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune than its immediate main-belt neighbors. This unique trait has led planetary scientists to hypothesize that the asteroid formed in the frigid outer solar system and migrated inward early in the solar system's history. If true, visiting 269 Justitia would offer a rare, close-up look at pristine material from the distant outer solar system via a much shorter journey.

Scientists are particularly excited that the asteroid may still hold water-related minerals and organic compounds preserved from its origins. Studying its surface could therefore offer clues to how water and organic material were distributed as planets began to form, Elias Tsoutsanis, a chief researcher at TII's propulsion and space research center, said during the press briefing.
"We don't know what we're going to find — that's exploration," Tsoutsanis told reporters. "We're really excited."

According to the mission plan, the MBR Explorer will spend roughly seven months studying 269 Justitia from orbit. Beginning at an altitude of 155 miles (250 km), the spacecraft will gradually lower its path before releasing the lander. The smaller probe will then head toward the asteroid's surface, a descent that should take two to three hours depending on 269 Justitia's precise gravity, which remains unknown.

Although TII describes the mission ending with a landing on the surface of 269 Justitia, the engineering details suggest a more violent endgame. Cruising toward the asteroid's surface at 15 to 27 meters per second (34 to 60 mph) with no meaningful way to slow down, the probe will function less like a traditional lander and more like a planned impactor.
"We don't expect that the probe will survive the touchdown," said Mariam Alhammadi, a researcher in TII leading the mission's electric propulsion.

To ensure its two onboard cameras capture essential imagery during the descent, the probe will rely on an attitude-control system to counteract any post-separation spin, Alhammadi said. Should the probe unexpectedly survive the hard landing, she added, its battery is built to last 20 to 50 minutes, providing a narrow but crucial window for it to beam close-ups of the asteroid's surface back to Earth.

The high-velocity impact is also expected to dig a small crater on 269 Justitia, possibly exposing pristine subsurface material. Because this material cannot be imaged from orbit, the team expects the probe's final images to be among the most valuable of the entire mission.
Back on Earth, the team faces an unforgiving timeline. To execute the planned flybys, the mission must launch during a narrow three-week window that opens in early March 2028.

"God forbid we miss that — we basically don't have a mission," Mohsen al-Awadhi, the mission director at the UAE Space Agency, told reporters at the press conference. The orbital mechanics are so rigid that another comparable opportunity will not arise for at least 100 years, prompting al-Awadhi to add that he is devoting no time and energy to a backup plan.

Meeting the launch window is just the first hurdle, however. Once deployed in deep space, the lander must operate with absolute autonomy, receiving no commands from Earth or the main MBR Explorer spacecraft, the team says.
"In these eight years, I have no control to call it back — so nothing can go wrong," said Aaraj.

The team is confident that rigorous engineering and testing have produced a probe that can essentially "think for itself." Equipped with AI, it is designed to decide on its own when to capture images and how to filter and rank the most valuable data. Rather than waiting until it reaches its destination, the lander will take images throughout its eight-year cruise and send the best ones back to Earth roughly every six months, according to a TII statement.

Officials declined to disclose the mission's overall cost or say whether it has stayed on budget. The United States' ongoing war in Iran has sparked missile and drone attacks across the UAE, but the mission team has persevered: WIRED reported that they pressed on even as missiles were intercepted overhead.
Beyond the immediate scientific return, officials said a central pillar of this mission is accelerating the UAE's sovereign deep-space capabilities and fostering its domestic space economy.

The UAE Space Agency, established in 2014, has steadily expanded its portfolio from satellite launches to a Martian orbiter and sending two astronauts to the International Space Station. The EMA probe represents a developmental leap, designed and built in just under two years by a team of roughly 50 local engineers and scientists, many of whom began their careers as entry-level technicians on the Hope Mars mission.
"I don't want to call them my kids — there's a lot of them — but that's how attached I feel to them," al-Awadhi said during the briefing.

The UAE aims to position itself among the world's 10 largest space economies by 2031, targeting a massive expansion of a sector currently valued at about $12 billion. According to al-Bannai, the EMA project is designed to be one of many programs to come. By the time the lander impacts 269 Justitia in 2036, the technology matured during this journey will already be driving the next generation of Emirati spacecraft, he said.

On. Oct. 11, 1968, Apollo 7 launched into space with NASA astronauts Wally Schirra, Donn Eisele and Walter Cunningham. This was the first mission of the Apollo program that carried a crew into space.
Apollo 7 rebooted the Apollo program after a fire killed three astronauts during a launch rehearsal 20 months earlier.

NASA needed to prove that their Apollo spacecraft worked with this mission, which was really more of a test flight. Though the spacecraft seemed to work alright, the crew got a little snippy during their 11 days in space. First they suffered from motion sickness after launch, then Schirra came down with a cold, and the crew was constantly arguing with mission control and each other. None of the Apollo 7 astronauts went back to space after that.

Had Apollo 7 not succeeded, the chances of NASA being able to fulfill President John F. Kennedy's 1961 goal, "before this decade is out, of landing a man on the moon and returning him safely to the Earth" would be called into question — not just because the clock was ticking down, but because of increasing political pressure to shut down the expensive moon program.

In the wake of the January 1967 Apollo 1 fire, NASA and North American Aviation, the prime contractor for the Apollo command module, needed to overhaul the spacecraft to make it safe for crews to fly in space. Apollo 7 provided a "shakedown cruise" for the vehicle, to confirm the fixes worked and that the command module was space worthy.

"In its day, the Apollo command module was the most complex machine ever built by man to be operated by man," said Walt Cunningham, Apollo 7 pilot, on the 40th anniversary of the flight in 2008. "We launched on the longest and most ambitious engineering test flight in history, testing the spacecraft systems, verifying the operating procedures, checking out the worldwide tracking network, and that's not to mention testing our crew."
Apollo 7 was deemed by NASA to a 101% success, setting up the first lunar landing in July 1969.
"All of us in the flights that followed were dependent on the Apollo 7 crew doing their job," said Neil Armstrong, Apollo 11 commander. "So thanks Walt and Wally and Donn."

We’ve had a lot of good Alien video games in recent years, but nothing has quite matched the highs and authenticity of 2014’s Alien: Isolation. It took a decade of players clamouring for a sequel, but in late 2024, our prayers were answered when developer Creative Assembly dropped a trailer announcing Alien: Isolation 2.

Now, we’re slowly learning about what developer Creative Assembly has in store for us. Scary teasers and comments from creative director Al Hope suggest we're looking at a bigger, more ambitious survival horror game beyond an obvious visual glow-up. Our hands-on preview at Gamescom 2026 also confirmed the protagonist isn’t Amanda Ripley, which instantly raises a number of questions.

Ahead of Alien: Isolation 2’s arrival, there are plenty of Alien movies and games to go through – plus Alien: Earth’s stellar first season. Now's also a great time to play through the original Alien: Isolation again, to prepare yourself for the horrors that await us with the sequel.
Now, enough yacking. It's time to get on the express elevator to hell and find out everything that we know about Alien: Isolation 2 so far.
Alien: Isolation 2 doesn't have a confirmed release window yet.

Despite the impressive in-game teaser and gameplay demos, Sega and Creative Assembly still haven’t talked about a potential release window. Though many outlets are running with a 2027 target as possible, the truth is the powers that be aren’t ready to commit yet.
What platforms will Alien: Isolation 2 be on?
Alien: Isolation 2 is launching on PC (Steam), PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and Nintendo Switch 2.
Though it’s unclear if the game will release before next-gen consoles arrive, the current plan is to target current-gen machines and, of course, PC through Steam.

Given the high-fidelity visuals, a Nintendo Switch 2 version might come as a shock, but looking at the excellent third-party ports the hybrid handheld has received so far, we’re confident the developers can deliver a thrilling experience on it as well.
After the aforementioned teasers, Sega and Creative Assembly finally unveiled Alien: Isolation 2 with the first-ever in-game footage in summer 2026. Watch its ‘Last Chance’ reveal trailer below:
When does Alien: Isolation 2 take place in the timeline?

Alien: Isolation 2 is confirmed to happen a few months after the events of the first game. Amanda Ripley’s battle against a Xenomorph infestation aboard the Sevastopol Station took place roughly 15 years after the events of the original 1979 movie, which places both games closer to Alien: Romulus in the canon timeline.
This time around, however, there are two big differences: Amanda Ripley isn’t the protagonist anymore, and, instead of a space station, we’ll have to survive on a rainy colony planet.

Deeper plot details are a secret for now, but we know the planet’s name is LV-921. There, a Weyland-Yutani employee named Blake and her colleagues come across a crashed part of the doomed Sevastopol station, which was destroyed by Ripley in an attempt to exterminate the aliens at the end of the first game.

The prologue demo we played at Gamescom didn’t offer much more context, but Blake is an administrative employee who’s just arrived at the colony and wants to prove she fits her new role. As you can imagine, that quickly gets her in trouble. A Xenomorph had crash-landed on the planet already, so maybe it’s up to her to finish the job that the previous Alien: Isolation protagonist started...
What type of game is Alien: Isolation 2?
Like its predecessor, Alien: Isolation 2 is a single-player, first-person survival horror game.

The gameplay loop of the original is preserved. This means you'll have limited access to weaponry and survival tools, and you'll face sneaky (and relentless) Xenomorphs that dynamically adapt to player progress and movement through each level. You’re not meant to kill the aliens, but rather to avoid and escape them.

Through patience, stealth, and smart use of supplies for crafting, survival is achievable, but this isn’t a bug hunt with the Colonial Marines. To quote Ash in the original movie, “I can’t lie to you about your chances, but you have my sympathies.”
Does Alien: Isolation 2 have a multiplayer mode?
Alien: Isolation 2 is a single-player survival horror game like the original. At the time of writing, no plans for a co-op or multiplayer mode of any kind have been shared.

At this point, it’s unclear what the whole Alien: Isolation 2 package will look like — and we wouldn’t rule out an extra, mission-based Survivor Mode like the original’s — but it seems Creative Assembly isn’t chasing co-op trends with the sequel in any way. This is a cinematic, high-intensity solo adventure.
Is there a public Alien: Isolation 2 demo?
Though attendees had access to the second Alien: Isolation 2 demo at Gamescom, no wider public demo has been released.

This could change in the future and as the game nears release, but without a launch window in sight, don’t hold your breath. It’ll be a while before most players can get their hands on the long-awaited sci-fi survival horror sequel.

NASA spots a giant patch of Moon-like rock on Earth

- An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed a remarkable formation in Madagascar that looks surprisingly similar to the Moonâs bright highlands. Made of anorthosite, a rock abundant on the lunar surface, the formation dates back at least 600 million years and bears the scars of ancient continental collisions.
An ancient formation of bright anorthosite, a rock commonly found on the Moon, stands out among the heavily deformed rocks of southern Madagascar.

A bright, unusual patch of rock in southern Madagascar has a surprising connection to the Moon. Seen from space, the formation stands out against the surrounding dry landscape. Although it may look unusual on Earth, the same type of rock is widespread across the lunar surface.

The rock, called anorthosite, is an igneous material that makes up much of the Moon's bright, reflective highlands. These light-colored regions are visible to the naked eye when looking at the Moon from Earth.

Anorthosite is not exclusive to the Moon. Large deposits also occur in several regions of Earth, including eastern Canada, Scandinavia, southern India, and Madagascar. In southern Madagascar, one particularly striking deposit forms a roughly circular feature that is easily distinguishable from the surrounding terrain.
NASA Astronaut Photographs Ancient Rock Formation
On August 28, 2026, an astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed the Saririaky anorthosite massif, a large body of rock exposed at Earth's surface.

Anorthosite is classified as an intrusive igneous rock, meaning it forms when molten material cools and solidifies beneath Earth's surface. Because this cooling process takes place underground, the minerals have time to develop into relatively large crystals.

Geological research suggests that the Saririaky formation originated during the late Precambrian, at least 600 million years ago. Today, the exposed rock covers approximately 100 square kilometers (40 square miles).

Although the formation is remarkable on its own, the surrounding landscape tells an equally fascinating story. The neighboring rocks preserve evidence of enormous forces that reshaped the region hundreds of millions of years ago.
Ancient Continental Collisions Reshaped Madagascar
The Saririaky massif lies within what geologists call a ductile shear zone. In these regions, rocks undergo intense deformation as powerful geological forces act on them deep within Earth's crust.

Under sufficiently high temperatures and pressures, solid rock can gradually bend, stretch, and change its structure rather than simply breaking apart. This process can also transform the minerals and textures within the rock, a phenomenon known as metamorphism.

Studies of the region have identified long, roughly parallel geological features extending from north to south. These patterns record the powerful deformation that affected the rocks surrounding Saririaky.

Scientists believe much of this transformation occurred as ancient landmasses collided during the formation of Gondwana, a vast supercontinent that eventually included parts of present-day Africa, India, Madagascar, Australia, and Antarctica.
As these continental fragments came together, immense pressure and heat reshaped large sections of Earth's crust.
Some researchers have suggested that a second anorthosite massif, located approximately 60 kilometers (40 miles) north of Saririaky within the same shear zone, was once connected to it.

According to this interpretation, the original rock body was stretched and separated by tectonic forces. The resulting structure is known as boudinage, a geological process in which a relatively strong layer or body of rock is pulled into separate segments as the surrounding material deforms.
If this explanation is correct, the two formations preserve evidence of the tremendous forces involved in assembling one of Earth's ancient supercontinents.
How Earth's Moon-Like Rocks Reveal Lunar History
The scientific importance of anorthosite extends far beyond Earth's geological history. Similar rocks provide an important opportunity to investigate how the Moon formed and evolved.

The Moon's anorthosite-rich highlands are more than 4 billion years old. Scientists believe these rocks formed early in lunar history, when much of the young Moon was covered by an enormous ocean of molten rock.

As this magma ocean gradually cooled, certain minerals crystallized and accumulated near the surface, helping form the Moon's early outer crust. The anorthosite produced by this process remains a major component of the bright lunar highlands visible today.

Apollo astronauts returned samples of lunar anorthosite to Earth, giving researchers valuable material for studying the Moon's distant past. However, the quantity of available lunar rock is limited, making similar geological formations on Earth especially useful for comparison.
One particularly close match occurs in Montana's Beartooth Mountains, where anorthosite deposits have a composition that closely resembles their lunar counterparts.

By examining these terrestrial rocks, scientists can investigate geological processes associated with the formation and evolution of anorthosite, helping them interpret the much older material found on the Moon.

The Saririaky formation offers another striking example of the geological similarities between Earth and its nearest celestial neighbor. Its bright appearance and dramatic surroundings also reveal how hundreds of millions of years of tectonic activity can transform ancient rock into a distinctive landscape visible from orbit.

New injection makes fat cells self-destruct
A promising new injection destroys fat cells, reduces dangerous belly fat, and could help keep lost weight from coming back.
- European Association for the Study of Diabetes

- Scientists have developed an experimental injection that destroys fat cells and significantly reduces dangerous belly fat, potentially opening a new path to treating obesity. Early research also suggests it could help prevent the weight regain that often follows stopping popular weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy.

An experimental injection that causes fat cells to destroy themselves has shown promising results in early human trials, significantly reducing dangerous fat hidden deep inside the abdomen. Researchers believe the treatment could eventually offer a new way to combat obesity and potentially help people maintain weight loss after stopping popular weight loss medications.

The drug, known as CBL-514, was highlighted at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy. Research indicates that it can reduce both subcutaneous fat, which sits directly beneath the skin, and visceral fat, which surrounds internal organs.

Dr. W. Timothy Garvey of the University of Alabama at Birmingham says the findings also raise the possibility that CBL-514 could reduce weight regain after patients discontinue GLP-1 receptor agonist medications (GLP1-RAs) like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound. However, this potential benefit has so far been demonstrated in animal studies and still needs to be confirmed in humans.
A New Injection That Makes Fat Cells Self-Destruct

What makes CBL-514 unusual is how it works. Rather than simply reducing the amount of fat stored inside existing cells, the drug triggers apoptosis (self-destruction), a natural biological process that causes cells to break down and die. CBL-514 is designed to target adipocytes, the body's fat-storing cells, while leaving other types of cells unaffected.
In phase 2 clinical trials, researchers observed substantial reductions in subcutaneous fat. This is the soft layer of fat immediately below the skin that can be "pinched."
At the eight-week follow-up, 69.6% of participants treated with CBL-514 had lost at least 150 mL of subcutaneous fat volume. None of the participants who received a placebo reached that threshold.

Animal experiments provided additional evidence that the treatment could affect more than just visible body fat. In preclinical studies (animal models), CBL-514 reduced body weight as well as subcutaneous and visceral abdominal tissue (VAT).

Visceral fat is especially important from a medical perspective. Unlike fat that accumulates directly beneath the skin, visceral fat lies deep within the abdominal cavity, surrounding organs such as the liver and intestines.

This hidden fat is biologically active and can interfere with the body's ability to regulate blood sugar and metabolism. Excess visceral fat is a major contributor to insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and cardiometabolic conditions, including heart attacks and strokes.
Could the Drug Help Prevent Weight Regain?
One of the most intriguing possibilities involves combining CBL-514 with existing weight loss medications.

GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs have transformed obesity treatment by helping patients lose substantial amounts of weight. However, maintaining those results can be challenging. Many people regain weight after discontinuing treatment.
Researchers investigated whether destroying fat cells could help address this problem.
In animal studies, combining CBL-514 with tirzepatide, a medication used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, produced greater weight loss than treatment with tirzepatide alone.
The researchers also examined what happened after tirzepatide was discontinued. Rats that had received both medications regained less weight than rats treated only with tirzepatide.

One possible explanation is that eliminating fat cells reduces the body's capacity to store fat again. With fewer fat cells available, the researchers hypothesize that fat may accumulate more slowly after weight loss.

Professor Garvey believes this approach could eventually help patients preserve the health improvements associated with losing weight, including better blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels.

However, whether CBL-514 can reliably prevent weight regain in people remains an open question. Additional clinical research will be needed to determine if the effects observed in animals also occur in humans.
Human Trials Reveal a Reduction in Dangerous Visceral Fat

To investigate the drug's effects on visceral fat in people, Professor Garvey and Yu-Fang Ling of Caliway Biopharmaceuticals, the drug's developer based in New Taipei City, Taiwan, analyzed data from two phase 2 clinical trials (CBL-0204 and CBL-0205).
The analysis focused on participants who had undergone magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, allowing researchers to measure changes in fat deep inside the abdomen.

Participants (BMI 22-30 kg/m2) received injections into the lower abdomen every three weeks for up to 12 weeks. The treatment involved doses of up to 600 mg of CBL-514 (n=23) or placebo (n=17), with participants ranging in average age from 36.4 years to 42.4 years across the groups.

The number of injections depended on how much abdominal fat each participant had. As the fat layer became thinner, fewer injections were administered. Treatment ended once the fat thickness fell below a specified threshold.

MRI scans were performed before treatment and again four weeks and eight to 12 weeks after the final injection. These scans allowed the researchers to compare changes in visceral fat volume between the treatment and placebo groups.

The original subgroup included 41 participants, with 23 assigned to CBL-514 and 18 to placebo. Of those receiving the experimental drug, 17 were women (74%), and six were men (26%). The placebo group included 10 women (56%) and eight men (44.4%).
At the later follow-up, data were available for 40 participants, including all 23 CBL-514 recipients and 17 placebo recipients.
Before treatment, average visceral fat volume was 563.85 mL in the CBL-514 group and 659.81 mL in the placebo group.

Over the following weeks, the two groups showed distinctly different patterns. Visceral fat decreased among participants receiving the experimental injection but increased among those given the placebo.
Four weeks after the final injection, participants treated with CBL-514 had experienced an average 12.01% reduction in visceral fat volume compared with their starting measurements.
In contrast, the placebo group showed an average increase of 5.68%. This represented a 17.69 percentage point difference between the groups.
The results remained encouraging at the later follow-up, conducted eight weeks after the final treatment in CBL-0205 and 12 weeks after treatment in CBL-0204.
By that point, average visceral fat volume in the CBL-514 group was still 10.45% below baseline. Meanwhile, the placebo group had experienced an average increase of 11.76%.
That produced a difference of 22.21 percentage points between the two groups, suggesting that the injection's effects persisted for several weeks after treatment ended.

The researchers concluded that CBL-514 significantly reduced visceral abdominal fat compared with placebo. Combined with the earlier findings on subcutaneous fat, the results suggest that the treatment can target both fat beneath the skin and fat surrounding internal organs.

The drug was also generally well tolerated during the trials. Most reported side effects involved temporary reactions around the injection site, including pain, swelling, and redness. These reactions were generally mild to moderate, and no serious adverse events were reported.
Beyond a Flatter Stomach: Potential Health Benefits
Although reducing visible belly fat may appeal to patients for cosmetic reasons, researchers emphasize that the potential medical benefits could be more important.

Professor Garvey says: "We expect that patients will be pleased by the cosmetic effects, such as the flatter stomach that can come with subcutaneous fat loss. But it is the reduction in body weight, loss of visceral fat and the improvements in blood pressure, cholesterol and the like that should be associated with this that will be important for health."
Because visceral fat is closely linked to metabolic disease, reducing it could potentially provide benefits beyond changes in appearance.

The researchers also point out that existing surgical approaches, including liposuction and abdominoplasty, primarily remove or reshape subcutaneous fat. These procedures are more invasive and do not directly address the deeper visceral fat surrounding abdominal organs.
CBL-514 could potentially offer a nonsurgical alternative that targets both types of abdominal fat.
"This is a highly innovative approach to obesity pharmacotherapy that has produced some remarkable results in early human trials," says Professor Garvey.
Larger Clinical Trials Will Test the Treatment
Despite the promising findings, CBL-514 remains an experimental treatment, and larger studies are needed to establish its effectiveness and safety.

Recruitment for the first of two phase 3 clinical trials was underway at the time of the announcement. Both studies are designed as randomized, placebo-controlled trials that will investigate whether CBL-514 can safely and effectively reduce abdominal fat without surgery.
The announcement indicated that initial results were expected at the end of the following year.
These larger trials will be important for determining whether the encouraging reductions in abdominal fat observed in early studies can be reproduced in broader patient populations.

Researchers will also need to establish whether reducing fat cell numbers produces lasting improvements in weight management and metabolic health, particularly after patients stop taking GLP-1 medications.
If the findings hold up, CBL-514 could represent a different strategy for obesity treatment, one focused on eliminating fat cells rather than simply reducing the amount of fat they contain.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday defended India as a "mother of democracy," as protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter fraud are intensifying.

"A wide range of issues are debated openly, and diverse perspectives are discussed by the people," Modi said, speaking at a Bloomberg New Economy event. His comments coincide with a severe crackdown by authorities against protestors demanding electoral reforms.
Earlier today, a key members of the viral pseudo-political movement, Cockroach Janta Party, were detained for protesting without permission.

CJP, whose leaders were detained by authorities over the weekend as well, had sought permission from Delhi Police on Monday to launch fresh protests at the Jantar Mantar grounds in the capital. However, the government then barred the use of the site for protests.

On Monday, thousands of people reportedly joined leaders of Indian opposition parties in their march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to file a petition against revisions made to the voter list by the Election Commission.

Names of 130 million people have been struck off from the voter list after the commission began conducting "special intensive revisions" (SIR) to update voter lists across the country last year, as per several local media reports.
Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India, said the huge crowds were a sign that people were not going to be "intimidated" by the government.

"There are no parallel protests. It's one protest, and it's a protest where everybody is standing together," Gandhi said, dismissing concerns over the absence of members of the Cockroach Janta Party who had called for protests over the weekend.

"Delhi is once again flooded with people standing up to save democracy," Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the viral pseudo-political movement, CJP, said in a post, reacting to the crowd amassed for the march led by Gandhi.

Over the weekend, Indian security forces reportedly clamped down on protests in the capital city, detaining young people, several opposition party politicians, YouTubers, lawyers and a few journalists.
The Delhi police, which is under the control of the Indian home ministry, did not respond to an email seeking comments.
Experts told CNBC that while the scale of the protests does not pose a threat to the stability of India at present, crackdowns could broaden the unrest.

"If security forces keep taking heavy-handed approaches, this will create a more volatile environment that could make protestors angrier and galvanize even larger groups of marchers," Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council told CNBC.

He added that at present the scale of the protests was not significant enough to impact "capital flow and investor behavior" but warned that "heavy-handed tactics that generate violence and volatility" by the state could change it.

The United Nations Human Rights Office on Saturday raised concerns over mass detentions and called on Indian authorities "to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled."

On Sunday, India's Ministry of External Affairs responded to the UNHR's comments, calling them "unwarranted" and claiming they constituted an "unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of India."

The crackdown during the latest protest has been "significant and massive" compared to earlier reactions to farmers' protests or uniform civil code protests, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at Teneo, told CNBC. He added that there is a higher chance that the broad-based retaliation to the police crackdown could lead to more demonstrations.

The CJP had first called for a nationwide protest on Oct. 2, seeking the removal of the election chief after an investigative report by the Indian Express showed discrepancies in the functioning of the Election Commission and reports of deletion of millions of voters.

On Sept. 26, following reports of the voter deletion, the Election Commission of India launched a special drive across India to enroll voters who have been left out of the rolls. It has downplayed discrepancies as highlighted in the Indian Express report and maintains it is "committed to ensuring that no eligible voter is left out of the voter list."

However, Modi's ruling party, the Bharatiya Janata Party, has defended the Election Commission and said the deletions were made on account of 28 million people who died, 68 million who relocated, 10 million with duplicate entries and 30 million absent or non-traceable voters.

The sweeping revisions of the electoral roll have raised serious constitutional and legal questions, Milan Vaishnav, director and senior fellow of the South Asia Program at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told CNBC.
The core demand of the movement is for Kumar to resign and for the commission to "seriously modify the so-called 'Special Intensive Revision' of the electoral rolls," he said.
BEIJING — U.S. credit card giant Visa announced Tuesday it had received approval from the People's Bank of China for setting up a bank card clearing business in the country.
The news comes as the U.S. and Chinese presidents plan for their third meeting this year.
"This marks an important milestone toward the company serving China's domestic payments market," Visa said in a statement.

"For more than 40 years, Visa has been an active contributor to China's dynamic payments landscape," Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said. "We look forward to taking the necessary steps in the process, pursuant to the PBOC's regulations, to begin operating domestically in China."

McInerney joined U.S. President Donald Trump's business delegation to Beijing in May and subsequently became chair of the U.S.-China Business Council in June. The Visa CEO also led a trip to Beijing in early September.
"The timing is notable," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice, The Asia Group.

"Beijing chose to approve visa's license just ahead of the APEC Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen next month, where Xi [Jinping] and Trump are expected to meet again," he said. "The move suggests that Beijing is keen to demonstrate tangible progress for American businesses before Trump's next visit to China."

Trump told Fox News after his Beijing trip in May that he brought up Visa's request to gain China market access. After the summit in September, China said it would approve applications from all foreign financial institutions to operate in the country.
Mainland China has kept a tight grip on its financial sector, favoring domestic players and restricting cross-border capital flows.
Visa previously said it had applied with the PBOC in May 2020 to operate a bank card clearing institution.

The company has worked with Chinese banks for dual-branded cards, for which China's UnionPay processes transactions domestically and Visa processes overseas payments. In January, Visa said the mainland China-issued cards could be linked to Apple Pay for use overseas.
Rival Mastercard's joint venture in China said it started processing payments in 2024 after getting the PBOC's approval to begin bank card clearing preparations in February 2020.
American Express was the first, receiving its processing license in June 2020 after getting the PBOC nod back in 2018.
Mobile pay dominates daily consumer transactions in China, primarily facilitated by Tencent's WeChat and Alibaba-affiliate Ant's Alipay.
BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down.

"People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future."

Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work.

What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said.

That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said.

The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces.

World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them.

The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away."

The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said.

Banga, however, is less pessimistic about the disruption to the job market from AI. "Large language models are estimated probably to create some degree of disruption in jobs in the developed world," he said. "But by the time you get to middle-income countries and lower-middle-income countries, actually, the opportunity from small AI to build jobs and build productivity is enormous," he told CNBC on Tuesday.

AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said.

"Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva.

Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it."
AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

Of all the contradictions that make up Mike Tyson‘s public persona, none causes me to scratch my head as much as this: Tyson‘s entire ethos could be boiled down to not caring what “people” — the mainstream in general, but the media in particular — think of him, but no figure of his stature has put in the conspicuous and shameless effort to make sure that anybody whose residency is not beneath a rock has heard Tyson’s version of who he is.

He has been the focal point of an Animal Planet documentary about himself and his love of pigeons (Taking on Tyson) and the centerpiece of an Adult Swim animated series about himself and, well, his love of pigeons (Mike Tyson Mysteries). He had a long-running one-man show about his life (I assume pigeons were involved, but I don’t remember). Even when Hulu made a limited series about his life — 2022’s Mike, which couldn’t have made less of a cultural footprint — and Tyson threw a tantrum comparing Hulu to a slave master, that unauthorized version of Tyson’s story was completely interchangeable with the authorized version he has told so many times.

I suspect this simultaneous desire to be represented and professed antipathy at being represented isn’t an unreasonable facet of the celebrity condition, and that if somebody were to ask him why he can’t stop telling his own story, one viable answer would be “money” — which is probably reasonable as well.

I assume Tyson wasn’t paid for his central role in Floyd Russ’ Netflix docuseries Tyson, and he isn’t even an executive producer on the four-parter. But it’s only ever the version of Mike Tyson’s story that he wants it to be — candid and emotionally raw one moment, stubbornly and annoyingly evasive the next.

Russ never directly asks Tyson what he hopes to get out of appearing in the project, which makes it clear that for all the objectionable and illegal behavior that have been part of Tyson’s life, he has never been “cancelled,” so to speak. He was out of the public eye for a couple of years when he was serving prison time for rape, and the tone of the conversation may have briefly darkened in the few months after he repeatedly bit Evander Holyfield in the ring, but Tyson has retained his position in mainstream culture better than nearly any figure with a comparable rap sheet.

That, ultimately, is what Russ’ docuseries is about. If you were already fascinated by Mike Tyson, Tyson is four hours of storytelling so aesthetically formulaic that it borders on parody, and I don’t think it will provide much new information or even fresh perspective, since Tyson has already given his perspective endlessly. Yet Tyson’s vulnerable volatility is hard to look away from, and Tyson is as well — especially since most people who are grossed out by the excessive platforming of this severely damaged pugilist probably won’t watch anyway.

A plot summary for curious viewers thinking, “Finally, this will be my opportunity to learn something about that guy from The Hangover“: Russ traces the established facts of Tyson’s life from his rough-and-tumble youth in Brooklyn to his juvenile run-ins with the law to the youth facility where he discovered boxing and which, in turn, connected him to legendary trainer Cus D’Amato.

I’m a big enough boxing fan that I have to admit I’ve watched videos of most of Tyson’s fights, some many times (you could watch his knockout of Michael Spinks nearly 40 times per hour if you chose to); I know it’s hard to look away from the run of vicious stoppages that led to his becoming the youngest heavyweight champion ever.

Russ follows the rise and fall and rise and fall of Tyson’s boxing career to a certain point, interspersing the rape trial, the misadventures of Tyson’s Holyfield fights, the tragic death of his daughter, his drug addiction and recovery and relapses and more. Nothing is exactly off-limits, but most things are governed by when Tyson wants to be forthcoming and when he threateningly looks at the director and urges him to find another line of questioning, which he does a number of times. He’ll talk about his ill-fated marriage to Robin Givens, acknowledging some levels of abuse while avoiding confirmation of others, but when it comes to the Indianapolis rape accusation, one-sentence denials are all you’ll get. Since Givens and Desiree Washington either declined to appear or didn’t respond to requests to appear, what Tyson says goes.

Tyson is at once scary, funny, personable, distasteful, introspective, superficial, articulate and incoherent. He cackles at things a decent person absolutely shouldn’t be cackling at and he’s reduced to conveying wordless sorrow multiple times per episode. I suppose if you’ve never watched any of Tyson’s exercises in self-portraiture, you might find his open-wound quality to be revelatory. Yes, Tyson seems to be comfortable talking to Russ, but I’m not sure that Tyson wouldn’t have been equally unfettered in conversation with a bowl of potato salad. Russ leaves in all those scenes of Tyson telling him to change the subject just to show where his limits are.

The documentary isn’t exclusively a conversation with Tyson. Russ has a solid roster of people from different stretches of Tyson’s life, from childhood friends to gym partners to follow boxers to family members to several of the women who didn’t divorce him or accuse him of rape.

There are insightful conversations with the likes of Lennox Lewis and James “Buster” Douglas, whose attempts to explain what it meant for him to beat Tyson just weeks after losing his mother yielded my only emotional response to the docuseries. There are painful and real interviews with Tyson’s children, who highlight the positives and negatives of having Mike Tyson for a father. While many of the more contentious and controversial aspects of his life are presented in one-sided fashion, friend and former manager Rory Holloway’s still-raw sense of betrayal at Tyson firing his entire team is evoked with vivid irritation.

Russ keeps the storytelling very straightforward and very much in keeping with the style that ESPN and HBO sports documentaries have codified over the years. That means that it’s strictly chronological, except for a few times he “hits rewind” and goes back a few days or even hours, usually to no particular advantage. The editing is rudimentary throughout, whether it’s the myriad scenes intercut with footage of fluttering pigeons or the predictable rhythms of stock footage and inserts. There’s a real opportunity in the fourth episode to do something fun, or at least interesting, when Tyson convinces Russ to join him in smoking hallucinatory toad venom, but no flair or flourishes emerge.

Every once in a while an outside observer, almost always journalist and commentator Van Lathan, will say something that could open the door for Tyson to situate its subject as a product of a specific historical moment or in terms of race in America. Tyson, a student of boxing history, surely would have appreciated a deeper discussion of the role of the Black heavyweight champion in culture. R.J. Mitte‘s Breaking Bad co-stars are paying tribute to the actor after he died at age 34.

Mitte, who was diagnosed with cerebral palsy as a child and later became a disability rights advocate, died Monday in Brownsville, Texas, his reps previously shared. No cause of death was revealed, but TMZ reported that he died by suicide.

One of his most notable roles was playing Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston and Anna Gunn’s characters, Walter and Skyler White, on Vince Gilligan’s Breaking Bad. The Emmy-winning series ran for five seasons, from 2008 to 2013.

Earlier this month, Mitte made an appearance on The Joe Vulpis Podcast, where he praised working with Cranston and Gunn on the crime drama. “Bryan and Anna, they have such a wealth of knowledge and have been working in the industry for many years at the time and even more now,” he recalled. “And so every day, as far as it being a dark show having heavy themes, everything was very light-hearted, even in between takes.”
Following the news of Mitte’s death, Cranston, Aaron Paul and Dean Norris are among those remembering the actor.

“I’m in deep despair as I write this tonight,” Cranston shared in a lengthy post on Instagram “RJ Mitte, my sweet son on Breaking Bad has died. I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm. Born with Cerebral Palsy, he never – ever – allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination. Always listening to the advice that his TV parents (Anna Gunn and myself) gave him – but being a teenager, sometimes mischievously ignoring the counsel in order to learn the hard way… He was one of the stars of a hit TV show – but still a kid.”

He continued, “That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor. He parlayed his experience on the show to be a vocal advocate for performers with disabilities, and was the head of a philanthropic organization with a focus on helping the disabled community. All that promise and potential now is such a loss. It is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life. Why? We were texting each other just a few weeks ago – figuring out when we could meet for lunch. I don’t know if that lunch would have changed his future… But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed… I’ll miss you, son.”

“I can’t stop there without imploring anyone who is contemplating suicide to please call for the support you need at 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (https://988lifeline.org/). There is hope,” Cranston concluded.

Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman, also wrote in a statement shared with The Hollywood Reporter, “I am at a loss. I am heartbroken over this news. RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed. And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that.”

Norris, who played Hank Schrader, the uncle to Walt Jr., shared, “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and his family.”
