Journalists, entrepreneurs, and even some public relations professionals will tell you that the PR process is broken (buy me a drink sometime, and I’ll give you my rant). But could AI actually make things better?

Honeyjar, which will be attending this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt as part of the Startup Battlefield 200, wants to use AI to make the expertise and judgment of the best PR pros available to everyone, including founders who have no idea where to start.

The startup’s founders, CEO Michelle Masek and CCO Nadia Jamshidi, certainly fit the bill when it comes to PR expertise. They’ve both spent decades in the field, doing in-house communications and working at agencies. Masek recently served as senior vice president of marketing and communications for Ev Williams’ venture firm, Obvious Ventures.

As Masek described the challenges involved in “helping with the why and when of comms and marketing for 110 portfolio companies” (the startups her firm had invested in), I flashed back to my own brief stint leading marketing at an early-stage VC firm, where founders were constantly asking for help getting into TechCrunch. So I wasn’t surprised that Masek found herself asking, “Is there a way to scale the senior-level expertise into AI [in a way] that actually helps users do the work of comms in the proactive and skilled way that we do?”

Honeyjar is her answer to that question. It automates processes like writing announcements, finding the best journalists to pitch, and identifying the most promising speaking opportunities. But Jamshidi told me in a follow-up email that Honeyjar’s vision goes beyond getting press coverage and beyond specific AI tools.

“Honeyjar can find reporters, build media lists, scan news and social, track coverage, and surface opportunities,” she said. “Those capabilities are important, but they’re just one piece of what we’re building. The bigger idea is bringing the whole communications workflow together: signals, context, strategy, judgment, timing, and execution.”
And it’s not just for founders. Masek said she’s come to realize there are “millions and millions of unassigned communicators responsible for the work of comms.”

“They don’t have the title of comms, but they’re marketers, investors, authors, creators, school superintendents, sports team leaders,” she added. “It’s incredibly horizontal, this need to nail strategic communications. It’s always passed around, but the problems are very often not solved.”

Nor is Honeyjar trying to replace PR professionals. Masek said she and Jamshidi built the tool they wanted to use themselves. She argued that Honeyjar can make PR firms and in-house comms teams more effective, while allowing individual PR practitioners to “take on that third client without any scaling cost.”

When Honeyjar opened its waitlist, it received 10,000 signups in the first 24 hours, said Masek. Beta testers include Nextdoor, tech startup Coco Robotics, investor Bloomberg Beta, and agencies Mission North and Full Picture.

That sounds promising for companies looking to get more attention, but it could be a nightmare for journalists. We receive more pitches than we can respond to, many of them already written by AI chatbots.

When I raised my fears about getting inundated with even more PR slop, Masek noted that while Honeyjar can draft a pitch email or a social media post in the customer’s voice, the customer actually has to hit send or publish.
“We never want a world where the human is removed from the loop,” she said.

And that’s also where judgment is key. Masek said she and Jamshidi tried to “infuse and encode Honeyjar with our wisdom.” Through a broader initiative called the Comms Lab, they’re now training the product on the judgment of other PR pros as well.

“For us, judgment is knowing what to do, what not to do, when to act, and how to adapt to the situation,” Jamshidi added. “That comes from understanding a company’s goals and priorities, what’s happening inside and outside the organization, and knowing what to say, to whom, where, and when.”
In some cases, Masek said Honeyjar might even tell a founder that they’re simply not ready for coverage.

“We hear from reporters all the time who want better pitches, who want to hear from experts directly,” she said. “We actually see a future where there are more credible pitches in your inbox from sources who you actually want to hear from.”

When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says.

The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs.

SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales.

And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”

Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined.

Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code.

That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups.

Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use.

There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales.

While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.

He has an all-American handsomeness that makes you want to cast him in a denim campaign. (His debut studio album is called Boy in Jeans.) But he is not a public guy. For most of our interview, he is coy and circumspect, instinctively hesitant to reveal too much about his life. “I don’t know why it’s so hard for me to answer these simple personal questions,” he says.

His latest album, Sweet Fortune, is about the private universes you can share with another person. “Did you hear what my words couldn’t tell?” he croons in his single “Secret Language,” a sweet love ballad to his boyfriend. Sweet Fortune has a vintage sound indebted to ’60s and ’70s singer-songwriters like Harry Nilsson, James Taylor, and Joni Mitchell — a far cry from the pop-R&B he made when he first started out as a “straight” teen heartthrob on Radio Disney. “I feel like I was giving everything I could when I was 15,” he says. “I think I was scarred a little bit by that. Then, when I was around 19 or 20, I really asked myself, Do I even want to be an artist? What does this all mean to me?”

In the years since, he has come out as gay and carved a path for himself as not just a singer but a songwriter — most notably co-writing four songs on Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter, which won the 2024 Grammy for Album of the Year. “Having someone like that believe in you is incredible,” he says. He has also collaborated with Clairo, Jack Antonoff, and Tyler, the Creator. He’s still working on talking about himself, though: “I think permission to go there is a new and rare thing for me. I’m so sick of gripping everything so tightly.”
RIYL: Your boyfriend’s worn-out sweaters, folk singer-songwriters, Clairo’s Charm, cross-country road trips, love letters, lounging in bed.
Song you should start with: “Secret Language”
Top artist: “Joni Mitchell. I was listening to For the Roses a lot while making Calico.”

On his biggest pinch-me moment: There are a lot of artists I admire who I never thought would even know my name or hear my music. Obviously, Beyoncé and I working together is very public. The work ethic at that level is Olympic. Every time I look at the Grammy at my house, I still sit in awe of the fact that it’s a real thing.

On his fear of sharing too much: In my personal life and with the people who are close to me, I feel like I’m a very open, free person. But when it comes to giving my vulnerability to the world, I’m really fragile and sensitive.

I really looked up to Frank Ocean, and I admired the way he went about things and how private he was. Now I’m willing to open up a little more, and I’m actively trying to do that. Even onstage, I’ll say out loud, “I’m realizing I don’t know how to speak in front of you all.” [Laughs.] But I think acknowledging that takes some of the weight off for me.

On writing about his relationship: Approaching it was kind of scary. The material was there; it was more about figuring out how to approach it in a way that felt safe — not safe exactly, but that kept it safe for me — while also being honest in the music. Naming Massachusetts in it felt like I was really giving people a place to put this.

It was also about giving myself permission to write a love song. When I first started teasing this record, a lot of the comments were like, “Oh my God, just when I got to an emotionally safe place. I’m not ready for this.” It was funny for me because the whole time I was thinking, Ooh, this one’s kind of joyous and happy.

On his big breakthrough on the album: “Phantom” immediately went to a different place. It felt a little more theatrical than I’d ever gone. The year before, I’d listened to a lot of Harry Nilsson. “Without You” weirdly made its way into the DNA of that song. There’s something so arms wide open and emotional about it. The writing is also ultimately about my relationship to being an artist in some ways, and that’s something I hadn’t talked about in my music before. It’s about everything you can sacrifice for this thing that you love.

On the colors of the album: “Tulane green” is obviously a reference to the college, but it’s also about my boyfriend’s old college memorabilia. He would give it to me, and I would steal it and wear it. I love those little details.

On the music that influenced Sweet Fortune: I kept thinking of Jim Henson’s “Rainbow Connection.” There’s a purity in it that feels like more of a universal love song. I was listening to a lot of Bread, and I think they have some really beautiful love songs. “Baby I’m-a Want You” is such an amazing love song. Honesty and simplicity, I think, are what make a good love song.

Favorite moment from Drag Race: There are too many. I’ll never forget watching Sasha Velour take her wig off and reveal the rose petals in season nine. I was actually at Flaming Saddles in West Hollywood, which is now closed, watching that finale. Full-body chills. Alyssa Edwards is probably one of my favorite queens, so anything she says or does, I kind of worship.
I’d love to guest judge someday. Putting that out into the world.

Most important qualities in a drag queen: For me, a good lip-sync. A good lip-sync is more than just a girl who can buck. If I can feel like they feel the song in their bones, they could stand and park and bark — “park and bark” is when a queen just stands and sells the song without really moving. But if it’s coming from the heart and coming from the bones, that’s it for me.

I also think a good queen has to be a little bit delusional. They have to fully believe their own fantasy. They could be wearing literally a trash bag, but if they believe it’s the most glamorous thing in the world, then I believe it, too.

On his favorite Housewives franchise: I’m rewatching Atlanta right now. I was watching it a lot during the making of Calico. Anytime I rewatch it now, I have strong memories of being at Shangri-La after a session. I literally wrote “Versus Off the Beach,” then went back to my room and watched season four of Atlanta. I’m excited for the new season of Salt Lake. I feel like because I grew up around women, I have some kind of understanding of these women. There’s another layer of connection there. New York, I feel like season six, seven, eight, maybe, was the golden era of New York. I could talk about this all day.

The Housewives cast member he most wants to meet: It needs to be the O.G. RHONY cast. I want to get drunk with Luann. I want her to be chain-smoking cigarettes all night. But then there’s doing the chalet with the Salt Lake girls. I just feel like drama in ski gear is a lot of fun. [Laughs.] I always love seeing that. Sharing a Diet Coke with Lisa Barlow would be fun.

Across the country, in the reddest of red states and districts, Republicans — clinging to what were once thought to be safe seats with a Blue Wave breaking — have a plan to eke out a victory in November: Avoid Donald Trump.

In Florida — Trump’s adopted state, and one he has won three times — gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds has scrubbed references to the president, including a photo of the two of them, from his website. Representative María Elvira Salazar, who represents a district Trump won by 15 points in 2024, recently cut an ad attacking Trump over his immigration policies. In Kansas, a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932, Senator Roger Marshall posted on social media that he had gone to the White House directly to air his complaints to Trump about the president threatening to ban the sale of Canadian-made Bombardier jets in the United States. As Trump and JD Vance have held rallies from Iowa to Texas, Republicans are suddenly finding their campaign schedules filled with conflicts that keep them away from any camera capturing them with a president who has record-low approval ratings.

Despite the national landscape, Trump is finding a warmer reception in the unlikeliest of locales: his one-time home state of New York. On Friday, Trump held a rally in Syracuse with Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive running an uphill race against incumbent governor Kathy Hochul. “I’m asking you to do me a favor,” the president said, “just pretend I’m on the ballot.” The association does not seem to be hurting Blakeman. The gubernatorial race isn’t as uphill as it should be. New York is nearly as Democratic a state as it gets, a place where Republicans haven’t won statewide office since 2002 and a Republican presidential candidate hasn’t won since 1984. Democrats outnumber Republicans by more than two to one. But in a national political environment that pollsters say boosts Democrats by eight percentage points, Blakeman is down only 11 points to Hochul; not close enough to win, but close enough to make congenitally fretful Democrats fret a little more.

And it is not just in statewide races. Democrats are scarcely contesting two congressional seats out on the eastern half of Long Island that were in Democratic hands for much of the Obama administration. Republicans have poured more than $11 million into an effort to unseat Tom Suozzi, a longtime fixture in Nassau County. In New York City, polls show Nicole Malliotakis, who represents a district that covers Staten Island and a slice of Brooklyn, cruising to victory in a district that, according to one Democratic official who has seen the polling data, is one of the few in the state where Trump has a net-positive approval rating.

Republicans say that their resilience is due to Democratic mismanagement. They point to high taxes, disorder on the streets, a punitive business climate and a Democratic Party in thrall to Democratic Socialism as the reason for their gains. “Democrats have a good shot at taking the House back, but the path isn’t going to go through New York,” said Chapin Fay, a longtime GOP strategist currently working on a Blakeman SuperPAC. “This is a big complicated state, and it’s fun as a Republican to see it causing Democrats fits.”

Talk to a dozen Democrats and you get two dozen theories about why Republicans aren’t being dragged by Trump as much as in other states. Some say having a New York City Democratic Socialist as the biggest star in the state frightens moderates. Others complain the New York Post feeds suburban readers stories about crime and chaos on city streets. Andrew Grossman, a senior advisor to Battleground New York which helps run a number of House races in New York this cycle, says the fact that the state has been so uncontested for so long at the presidential and statewide levels has allowed muscles to atrophy. “New York typically doesn’t see any action in the primary or the general election in presidential years, and so we don’t have the kind of four-year organizing that occurs in states that are presidential swing states or even senatorial swing states,” he said.

Another theory goes that while voters in the heartland are whipsawed by Trump’s tariffs, the price of diesel, and the ongoing conflict in Iran, New Yorkers are largely shielded from the downdrafts of the Trump economy. Even tentative MAGA voters in Rockland County have watched their stock portfolios grow. They haven’t had to witness the crops on their farm wilt on the vine because of migrant-labor shortages or because of Trump’s trade wars. Instead, Republicans in New York remain animated by DEI, Trump’s so-called war on woke and immigration, all areas where the president has delivered, and don’t have to question that their devotion to the cause is hurting their 401k’s.

The current state of play in New York mirrors what happened in the state during the last midterms. 2022 was a good year for Democrats nationally. The party gained a seat in the Senate and narrowly lost the House. But New York ran counter to those trends, as a sharp rightward turn in the electorate resulted in four lost House seats on the Democratic side while Hochul squeaked by with a modest six-point victory over Lee Zeldin. (To put that number in perspective, going back to 2006 Democrats have won the governor’s races in New York by an average of 27 points.)

The transformation of New York can be witnessed in the career of Mike Lawler, a congressman from the suburbs just north of New York City. Democrats have been angling to defeat Lawler ever since he unseated Sean Patrick Maloney, a powerful Democratic lawmaker in 2022. Lawler was a State Assemblyman and a well-regarded political consultant and had been a delegate for Trump in 2016. But after he won, Lawler became a Trump skeptic. He said that Joe Biden was the rightful victor of the 2020 election and suggested that Trump should not be the nominee in 2024. Lawler became a regular on cable news and on the Sunday shows, slotted in as the sensible Yankee Republican who could deliver the party’s message while criticizing its extreme elements. He castigated Trump when the then-former president said he wanted a “termination” of the Constitution, joined Biden when the president held an event in his district, became a member of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus, and praised Kevin McCarthy for negotiating a debt-ceiling deal with his Democratic counterparts. It was enough to give Lawler a comfortable six-point victory in 2024 even as Kamala Harris narrowly won his district.

But now, facing another fierce reelection, and despite a national environment leaning toward Democrats, Lawler is finally finding his inner MAGA. At a time when most endangered Republicans found reasons to avoid Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas, Lawler not only appeared but spoke from the stage. In May, he held a rally with Trump in the heart of his district, declaring, “I am proud to be here today for President Donald Trump.” Lawler not only backed Trump’s unpopular “One Big Beautiful Bill,” he is running ads touting his support for it.

It is an audacious gamble. Lawler thinks Republicans in New York are insulated from the Trump economy enough to let their MAGA flag fly without concern that it will mean the end of abortion rights (a number of elected Republicans in the state are pro-choice) or large cuts to the social safety net (which city and state governments in New York have tried to repair in the face of Trump’s cuts). The hope is that MAGA in New York will feel energized enough in an off-year election to counter Democratic desire to give Donald Trump a crushing defeat.
With only three weeks to go, it seems to be working so far, as polls show a margin-of-error race.
Beyond a black hole's event horizon, information as we know it meets a mysterious fate.

There, in one of the most extreme environments in the Universe, quantum information is thought to become scrambled almost beyond recognition, dispersed into a bewildering tangle of quantum interactions.
Connect two such monsters to each other via an umbilical wormhole, however, and something incredible becomes possible.
Under just the right conditions, information swallowed by one black hole could emerge from the other.

This idea is still very much ensconced in the realm of theory – but it has inspired a particular approach to quantum teleportation that, researchers have now discovered, doesn't actually require one of quantum computing's more powerful resources to work remarkably well.

That resource is quantum magic – and by showing that a black hole-inspired teleportation protocol can achieve high fidelity without it, physicists Sudhanva Joshi and Sunil Kumar Mishra of the Indian Institute of Technology (Banaras Hindu University) have opened a new window into understanding this very peculiar, but very real phenomenon.
Quantum teleportation doesn't work quite like the teleportation of science fiction.

No physical matter is moved, nor is the process instantaneous. Instead, the quantum state of one particle is transferred to another, using a connection between them known as quantum entanglement, as well as classical communication.

Entanglement is one of the strangest consequences of quantum mechanics – where the properties of two objects become so deeply correlated that they can no longer be fully described independently. This link cannot be explained using classical physics.

The process doesn't allow information to travel faster than light, and the original quantum state is destroyed in the process. But still, the result is almost magical: a quantum state can be reconstructed across large distances, and no one has to go anywhere.
In quantum mechanics, though, "magic" has another, more precise meaning.
In quantum computing, magic is a property that allows certain quantum operations to go beyond what can be efficiently simulated by an ordinary computer.
Think of it like freight. A truck and a plane can both transport cargo between two cities, and for some journeys, either will do the job.
But a plane has capabilities that a truck cannot efficiently reproduce, such as crossing an ocean in a matter of hours.

Quantum magic is a little like that additional capability. It allows quantum computers to perform certain calculations that ordinary computers cannot efficiently replicate – but not every quantum task requires it.
Now we need to go back to the black holes.

These ultradense objects are thought to be the fastest scramblers of quantum information in the Universe. What falls in becomes so hopelessly tangled up with everything else that's in there that recovering the original information would be extraordinarily difficult – even setting aside the small problem of the event horizon.

But according to quantum mechanics, the Universe can't just destroy quantum information. It's one of the rules. And, at least in theory, if two black holes are connected in just the right way, information that gets scrambled by one can be retrieved by the other.
Physicists have developed quantum teleportation protocols inspired by this theory, using quantum circuits to mimic the scrambling process rather than actual black holes (can you imagine, though).
And this raises an intriguing question. How much quantum computational power does that scrambling really need?
That's what Joshi and Mishra set out to investigate.
To find out, the researchers mathematically investigated two different ways to scramble quantum information in a black hole-inspired teleportation protocol.

One involved a class of quantum operations known as Clifford circuits. These can generate entanglement and manipulate quantum information, but they don't require quantum magic, and their behavior can be efficiently simulated by an ordinary computer.
The other involved more general, randomly selected quantum operations, known as Haar-random scramblers, which typically possess substantial quantum magic.

The researchers crunched the numbers for both approaches, then compared how faithfully each could teleport quantum information – basically, how closely the recovered quantum state matched the original information.
And the results contained a big surprise.
On average, both approaches achieved exactly the same teleportation fidelity, even though one used quantum magic and the other didn't.
But an average is only part of the story of a dataset.

Say you have two sets of five numbers, and the average of both sets is 10. For one set, every one of the five numbers is exactly 10. The five numbers in the other set are -1,000, 0.5, 4, 45.5, and 1,000 – add them together and divide by five, and you still wind up with 10.
Something similar emerged with the two teleportation protocols. Although the average scores were the same, the Haar approach was dramatically more consistent than the Clifford approach.

In one numerical comparison involving eight quantum bits, or qubits, the variance in teleportation fidelity in the Clifford approach was around 40,000 times greater – far more spread out around its average performance.

This suggests that although quantum magic isn't necessary to achieve excellent average teleportation fidelity in this model, the choice of scrambling operations can make a rather significant difference to how consistently that fidelity is achieved.
But there was another interesting result.

The researchers also found that, as the modeled quantum systems grew larger, the Clifford approach became increasingly successful, with its teleportation fidelity approaching perfection – despite the scrambling operations generating no quantum magic at all.
Its results also became more consistent as the systems grew larger, although the Haar approach remained substantially more reliable.

The researchers also found that adding quantum magic wasn't enough on its own to improve the teleportation results. The way the scrambled information was decoded was crucial – the decoding process had to be matched to the way the information was scrambled in the first place.

Now, this doesn't mean physicists have figured out how to teleport information through actual black holes. The study is theoretical, based on mathematical models of quantum systems under idealized conditions, the kind of foundational work that could guide future attempts to reproduce and test the protocols on real quantum hardware.

Whether the findings hold in more realistic scenarios remains to be seen. But the results suggest that the ability to scramble and recover quantum information isn't necessarily dependent on the computational sophistication of the scrambling process.

That could help physicists better understand not just the wild behavior of quantum information, but a small – very small – part of what it might take to recover information from some of the most mysterious objects in the Universe.
The research, which is yet to be peer-reviewed, is available on preprint server arXiv.
The Space Force has finished transferring the last of the Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard members covered by the Personnel Management Act that created a hybrid full-time/part-time force.

The last cohort of transfers—Air Force Reservists transitioning to part-time jobs in the Space Force—swore in to their new service on Oct. 1. The main transfer ceremony took place at Los Angeles Air Force Base, Calif., with some service members joining via video teleconference, according to a service release.

Over the past two and a half years, hundreds of Reservists and Guardsmen have transferred into the Space Force as part of the groundbreaking effort to consolidate space-focused units and personnel and create a force with no components that will allow Guardians to transition between full-time and part-time positions with fewer bureaucratic hurdles.

The Space Force Personnel Management Act, passed in late 2023 as part of the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act, laid out the process for those transfers to take place, starting with the Air Force Reserve. A year later, lawmakers voted that space missions in the Air National Guard would also be absorbed by the Space Force instead of creating a separate Space National Guard.
Officials said implementing the Personnel Management Act, or PMA, would be a yearslong process.

In May 2024—before the transfer of Air National Guard space mission into the Space Force was finalized—USSF announced a six-month window for members of the Air Force Reserve to apply to transfer into the new service on a full-time basis. Officials then conducted a series of boards, eventually selecting 380 Reservists for transfer by April 2025.
Then, in August 2025, USSF started accepting applications from Air National Guardsmen to transfer on a full-time basis. Another board selected 99 Guard members in early 2026 for transfer.

Separately, in September 2025, the Space Force announced it was accepting applications for Air Force Reservists to transfer in for part-time positions. In April, the service said it selected 247 individuals to do so, and the first part-time Guardians came aboard in July.
The Oct. 1 transfer ceremony was for the last of the part-time cohort. Guard and Reserve members can still join the Space Force through the prior service program, but the main movement is complete.

“The recently completed transfer cohort represented the final PMA-directed movement of [Air Reserve Component] members in the designated space-mission population,” a Space Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
As part of the transition, the Space Force started assuming the Air National Guard’s space missions on Oct. 1, 2025.

The Space Force never opened a window for Air National Guardsmen to transfer into part-time work roles. The spokesperson noted that USSF “will continue to evaluate manpower requirements and the potential need for subsequent transfer windows as part of the overall growth model.”

The new members serving in a part-time capacity are called Guardians “Not on Sustained Duty.” They will be required to serve the equivalent of at least 36 days—48 four-hour Inactive Duty Training periods and 12 Annual Training days—per year to have a “good year” toward retirement.

The former Reservists and Guardsmen joining the Space Force bring deep experience to the service at a time when it is looking to grow dramatically—that’s important, officials say, to match the coming surge of brand-new Guardians.

Too many new Guardians with little experience entering at the lowest ranks could wreak havoc on the service’s grade structure, Deputy Chief of Space Operations for personnel Katharine Kelley said last month at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.

“We’re trying to balance not having all of our accessions be brand new in terms of experience,” she said. “We’re looking for ways to make sure that we can kind of balance this as a sourcing model and a sustainment model for people.”
A heavy-duty quadcopter carrying Sig Sauer’s new M250 light machine gun has completed a test requiring it to identify and engage targets from the air, the company announced Tuesday.

Sig Sauer completed the test in concert with Israel Aerospace Industries, maker of the Fire Storm 250, a reusable drone that can stay airborne for two hours and is designed with a stabilized machine-gun mount.

According to a Tuesday announcement from the companies, the test required the system to hover over a simulated battlefield, ID targets with an onboard camera and fire on them using both single-shot and semi-automatic firing modes “from varying distances and altitudes.”

It’s a fast development timeline for the drone, which was first unveiled last October. The defense publication Janes reported in February that flight tests for the system were scheduled for summer 2026. The system, as Janes reported, incorporates Sig’s micro-remote-controlled weapon system along with the M250, a version of which is set to replace the Army’s M249 squad automatic weapon as part of the service’s Next-Generation Squad Weapon program.

According to Tuesday’s announcement, the system can carry 200 rounds of ammunition and the 53-pound RCWS. It can take off and land vertically, lending itself to operation in austere forward locations.

“Sensor information and fire-control data are combined into a unified targeting solution, giving the operator a continuous operational picture and supporting a rapid sensor-to-shooter cycle,” the companies said.

An internal combustion engine can accept a variety of jet fuels, allowing the drone to be reused in the field, per the Janes report. It’s designed, according to the company, to accompany tactical units “with limited manpower and support requirements.”

While it’s previously been reported that the system incorporates artificial intelligence to automate components of tracking and detection, the companies emphasized its human-in-the-loop fire control system, allowing human operators to make engagement and fire decisions while receiving imagery and tracking data from the Fire Storm 250’s onboard sensors.

“FIRE STORM 250 brings together the most advanced technologies in the world,” Sali Okanin, Israel General Manager for SIG SAUER, said in an announcement. “We’re proud of the new SIG SAUER M250, which is combat-proven technology. It is a belt-fed platform with greater range than legacy systems and weight savings that not only provide squad-level benefits but also make drone capabilities possible.”

Sig Sauer executives told Military Times earlier this month that fielding for the M250 is expected to begin in the first half of next year. While the Army’s version of the weapon is chambered in Sig Sauer’s internally developed 6.8X51mm ammo, the Israel Defense Forces began using a 7.62X51mm variant in 2025. The Fire Storm 250 reportedly can carry either.

Just two weeks after it was launched, the Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite returned its first images and measurements from two of its key instruments – a major milestone that confirms the satellite is working well and on the road to monitoring the health of Earth’s oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.

This first set of images includes stunning views of Italy, the Arctic and the Caribbean from the satellite’s ocean and land colour instrument, as well as measurements of the height of the Greenland ice sheet and sea surface from its synthetic aperture radar altimeter.
Sentinel-3C is the third satellite in the Sentinel-3 series and will continue the mission’s long-term task of delivering environmental data that are essential for a wide range of applications.
As the workhorse mission for Copernicus, the Sentinel-3 satellites carry the same suite of instruments to measure systematically Earth’s oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.

Over oceans, Sentinel-3 measures the temperature, colour and height of the sea surface as well as the thickness of sea ice to support, for example, the monitoring of marine pollution and marine heatwaves.

Over land, this innovative mission monitors drought and wildfires, maps the way land is used, checks vegetation health, and measures the height of rivers, lakes, and polar ice sheets as shown in the animation of Greenland below.
Sentinel-3's observations are also particularly valuable for providing near-realtime parameters for weather forecasting and for monitoring long-term changes associated with climate change.

The European Space Agency is still in the process of commissioning Sentinel-3C for service, an important and intricate task that will take another five months, but after only two weeks in orbit, the satellite’s initial images already showcase that it is on the road to excellence.

The first image, captured by the ocean and land colour instrument on 30 September, is a striking natural-colour view that reveals Italy in beautiful detail, stretching from southern Germany in the north to Sicily and the southern Mediterranean.

Just above the centre of the image, the broad, flat expanse of the Po Valley – Italy’s agricultural heartland – stands out in shades of brown and green. Just to the north, the snow-capped Alps form a dramatic contrast with the lowlands, their bright peaks clearly visible against the surrounding landscape. Across the rest of Italy, variations in green and brown reflect differences in vegetation, agriculture and other types of land cover.

To the east, the deep blue waters of the Adriatic Sea separate Italy from the Balkan Peninsula, which is partially visible in the image. Noticeable variations in sea colour can be seen along Italy’s eastern coastline, where lighter blue waters hug the shore. These brighter tones are likely caused by sediment carried into the sea by rivers and transported along the coast.

On Italy’s western side, the dark waters of the Tyrrhenian Sea surround the islands of Sardinia and Sicily, which are clearly visible, while Corsica is largely obscured by cloud. Together, the contrasting colours of the land, snow-covered mountains and surrounding seas provide a vivid view of Italy’s diverse landscape from space.

The second image, also captured by the ocean and land colour instrument on 30 September, features part of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, to the west of Greenland. Snow- and ice-covered islands dominate the scene, with rugged coastlines, deep fjords and exposed rock creating intricate patterns. At this time of the year sea ice is at a minimum but some fractured floes are visible on the dark open water.

The Arctic is warming much faster than the global average, causing rapid melting of ice on land and ice in the sea, which leads to further warming through feedback loops. Sentinel-3’s different instruments measure ice in different ways – all contributing to a better understanding of the vulnerable polar regions.

The third image captured on 29 September, also by the ocean and land colour instrument, is a spectacular view of part of the Caribbean, with Cuba to the south and the Bahamas towards the top of the image. Shallow waters around the islands appear in a beautiful turquoise set against the darker deeper waters of the open sea.

Low-lying islands and coastal regions around the world are at risk of sea-level rise. Sentinel-3’s synthetic aperture radar altimeter measures changes in the height of the sea surface to help monitor rising seas and contribute to action on climate change and mitigation strategies.

The map above shows measurements of sea-surface height across the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea from Sentinel-3C’s synthetic aperture radar altimeter, compared to the Copernicus Marine Service multimission sea-level anomaly. These new data demonstrate that the altimeter is performing well and comparable to current measurements. Once commissioned, the altimeter will contribute to monitoring changes in sea-surface height around the world, complementing long-term records from missions such as Copernicus Sentinel-6 and Jason.
High-precision satellite altimetry has enabled scientists to establish the rate of global sea-level rise, which has averaged 3.64 mm per year since 1999, with the rate of rise accelerating.
The altimeter will also measure changes in the height of lakes, rivers, sea ice and land ice, also complementing the upcoming Copernicus CRISTAL mission.

The animation above shows measurements of the height of the Greenland Ice Sheet acquired by Sentinel-3C between 30 September and 4 October. The measurements also demonstrate that the altimeter is performing well, with all of the measurement tracks closely matching the reference digital elevation model.

Monitoring changes in the height of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets is essential for understanding the impacts of climate change and, importantly, for improving predictions of future sea-level rise. Ice loss from the sheets is a major contributor to sea-level rise, and satellite altimetry provides a valuable way of tracking changes in their surface elevation over time.

All in all, these first acquisitions from Sentinel-3C’s ocean and land colour instrument and from its synthetic aperture radar altimeter provide early confirmation of the satellite’s performance and mark an important step towards full operational service following the completion of the commissioning phase.
Coming soon: the first observations from Sentinel-3C’s sea and land surface temperature radiometer – stay tuned.

Sentinel-3 is part of Copernicus – the Earth observation component of the EU’s Space programme. For the Sentinel-3 satellites, ESA is responsible for the development and implementation of the satellites as well as the operations up to the completion of commissioning. After the commissioning phase, the Sentinel-3 mission is jointly managed by ESA and Eumetsat, where Eumetsat is responsible for routine satellite operations and the delivery of marine and atmospheric data, while ESA delivers land, cryosphere, inland water and offline atmospheric products. Together, the two agencies provide mission data for the Copernicus services and users worldwide.

NASA is working with Boeing to launch an unpiloted Starliner capsule in the December-January time frame to test upgrades and improvements ordered in the wake of a 2024 mission that suffered multiple propulsion system failures, stranding two astronauts on the space station for more than nine months.

If the unpiloted test flight goes well, NASA and Boeing hope to launch a piloted Starliner flight in mid 2028, officials said Monday, incorporating redesigned propulsion system valves, more robust subsystems and other modifications expected to prevent the sort of failures that occurred in 2024.
Veteran astronaut Warren “Woody” Hoburg will command the mission, joined by other crew members to be named later.

SpaceX’s Crew Dragon capsule is the only currently operational U.S. astronaut ferry ship. NASA wants to bring Boeing back into the mix as soon as possible to ensure a sustained U.S. capability to carry astronauts and researchers to the International Space Station through its planned retirement in 2030.

Equally important, NASA managers want to make sure an American spacecraft will be available to support flights to commercial space stations later in the 2030s, after SpaceX phases out its Falcon 9 rockets and Crew Dragon spacecraft.

“It’s always been the Commercial Crew Program’s goal to have two crew transportation providers to ensure commercial access to low Earth orbit,” said Dana Weigel, manager of NASA’s low-Earth orbit operations.

“As SpaceX has publicly stated, the Dragon and the Falcon won’t be around forever. Certifying Boeing’s Starliner is important for both supporting ISS and also for follow-on future commercial destinations.”

Said Boeing in a post on the social media platform X: “Together with @NASA, we’re making Starliner hardware enhancements and adding resources for human spaceflight certification. These changes support the spacecraft as a long-term provider of crewed missions to low Earth orbit.”

Astronauts Barry “Butch” Wilmore and Sunita Williams, both now retired from NASA, blasted off aboard a Starliner on June 5, 2024, for what was billed as a 10-day test flight to the International Space Station. It was the first piloted launch of a Starliner after two uncrewed test flights, both of which had problems.

During their rendezvous with the space station, Wilmore and Williams ran into multiple propulsion system helium leaks and thruster failures. They were able to dock, but their return to Earth was repeatedly delayed while NASA and Boeing worked to resolve the technical issues.
An independent review board later classified the propulsion mishaps as a “close call” that put the astronauts in jeopardy.

When all was said and done, the Starliner returned to Earth without its crew three months after launch. Wilmore and Williams stayed an additional six months aboard the station in order to hitch a ride home aboard a Crew Dragon on March 18, 2025. All told, the 10-day flight they expected ended up lasting 286 days.
An independent review board identified three major problems with the Starliner, along with a host of less severe shortcomings that had to be addressed.

During the rendezvous with the space station, five thrusters in the capsule’s service module failed, resulting in a temporary loss of full maneuverability. The failures were blamed on trouble with Teflon “poppets” extruding in propellant valves that restricted flow.

A thruster in the Starliner crew module failed during the ship’s unpiloted descent to Earth, leaving the ship without redundancy in a critical system. The third major issue involved helium leaks in the propulsion system pressurization plumbing.
In addition, the board concluded, the Starliner design did not have the required redundancy in the system responsible for the rocket firing needed to drop the spacecraft out of orbit.
Boeing said all of those issues are being addressed, along with operational changes intended to further reduce unexpected heating that contributed to the thruster problems.

The company is replacing the valves in all 12 crew module maneuvering thrusters, along with implementing measures to prevent erosion. The service module thruster poppets are being redesigned. A faster flight data recorder is being added to more precisely measure thruster performance, along with upgraded batteries and improved parachutes.

NASA and Boeing now plan to launch an unpiloted mission — Starliner 1 — in December or January that will rendezvous and dock with the space station. Along the way, flight controllers will thoroughly exercise the thrusters and their pressurization systems, putting the fixes to the test.

“Our goal is to fly Starliner One as soon as the vehicle and the team is ready,” Weigel said. “We really need to see how those thermal modifications perform on the spacecraft, and we intend to put the propulsion system through its paces.

“We’ll do a series of on-orbit demonstrations and tests, stress the thrusters, and we’ll take that set of data coming out of the mission combined with redesign, and that’s what will inform the final crewed vehicle certification. We will fly the Starliner One mission with stricter performance parameters in place when we’re flying closer to space station.
“Long term, we are committed to Starliner certification and ensuring commercial crew access to low Earth orbit.”

The Starliner has relied on United Launch Alliance’s Atlas 5 rockets for the ride to space, but only a half dozen of the venerable boosters remain in ULA’s inventory. As a result, NASA plans to help get ULA’s new Vulcan rocket certified to carry astronauts aboard Starliner capsules.

For its part, ULA said in a post on X that “we are already working towards the Starliner-1 mission and look forward to our continued work with @BoeingSpace and @NASA to integrate and certify our #VulcanRocket for human spaceflight.
“We are committed to being a long-term launch provider of human spaceflight capability to low Earth orbit.”

Seasonal changes redistribute enough water around Earth to shift the planet’s center of mass back and forth by fractions of an inch relative to its geometric center. NASA scientists are on the case, tracking the oscillations because Earth’s center of mass is a crucial reference point for satellite navigation and elevation measurements.

A team, led by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, has proposed a way to calculate the seasonal swings with extreme precision. The technique and findings are detailed in a new study published in Geophysical Journal International. The authors paint a vivid picture of springtime thaws, churning oceans, and dense winter air shifting massive surface loads from season to season.

The study isn’t the first attempt to pin down Earth’s center of mass. Scientists over the decades have pioneered several space-based techniques to define and locate it. But it’s a moving goalpost. If Earth were a hard blue marble, its center of mass would simply overlap its geometric center. In reality, the planet is sloshing and sagging under the weight of water, ice, and air. Because of this, Earth’s center of mass continually swivels around its geometric center by as much as several millimeters.

How accurate are existing methods to measure the size of the swivel? The last two international estimates, made in 2017 and 2023, differ by 0.27 inches (7 millimeters), about the height of three stacked nickels. The difference is almost as large as the motion itself.
To reduce uncertainty, JPL geoscientist Donald Argus led the development of a new technique based on ultraprecise satellite tracking.

Driven by gravity, satellites naturally orbit Earth’s center of mass, as if bound by invisible tethers. Tiny changes in the distance between satellites and ground stations reflect Earth’s shifting center of mass.

Using satellites to locate Earth’s center of mass is not a new idea. In fact, dense metal satellites, launched in 1976 and 1992, are dedicated exclusively to this purpose. Resembling 900-pound (408-kilogram) disco balls, both Laser Geodynamics Satellites (LAGEOS 1 and 2) are studded with reflective prisms and tracked with laser precision via ground stations globally distributed across more than 20 countries.

However, one limitation of satellite laser ranging is the uneven distribution of ground stations around Earth. The new technique improves accuracy in two ways: It adds GPS tracking into the mix along with orbital data from several satellites in low Earth orbit to provide a diverse array of targets. And it considers how the weight of water and ice deforms Earth’s crust, taking ground stations along for the ride.

The technique was developed by Argus along with researchers from JPL’s satellite orbit determination team, the University of Nevada, University of Montana, and the Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences in Germany.

“We’re now estimating the size of the movement of Earth’s mass center back and forth each year to be about half of what we believed it to be eight years ago,” said Argus. “Our findings suggest that the mass of Earth’s water and air moving between the hemisphere is smaller than previously thought.”

Felix Landerer, one of the study’s coauthors at JPL, noted that “while these movements might appear tiny, our modern world relies on extremely accurate positioning measurements. By unraveling and understanding the mechanisms that change reference systems, we can build better reference systems that ultimately benefit mapping and navigation — from global shipping logistics to precision agriculture.”

The study authors tracked Earth’s center of mass oscillating seasonally and attributed the cause to three categories: oceans, atmosphere, and continental water (made up of land ice, snow, lake and river water, soil moisture, and groundwater).

They found that snow accumulation in North America and Eurasia reaches a maximum in March and shifts Earth’s center of mass about 3 millimeters toward the North Pole. A month later, in April, rainwater in the Amazon River basin peaks at 2,400 gigatons, swinging Earth’s center of mass 2.2 millimeters toward South America. Monsoon water in southeast Asia attains a maximum of 600 gigatons six months later in November, adding slightly to the annual oscillation.
