Between August and October, the oceans swell with meltwater and rain, and Earth’s center of mass shifts toward the South Pacific Ocean. The Pacific Ocean is so large that mass changes there overshadow the loss or gain in other oceans, though seasonal dynamics in the Mediterranean, Red, North, Baltic, and Barents seas all help shift Earth’s center of mass in their own small way.

The researchers used a model developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts to estimate how atmospheric changes affect Earth’s center of mass throughout the seasons. They found that cold, dense, winter air helps tip the scales over Arabia, Asia, and northern Africa around Dec. 21 each year, and over South America and South Africa around June 21.

The mass calculations in the study are consistent with observations made by the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-On (GRACE-FO) mission. Launched in 2018, the mission is made up of twin satellites that map monthly fluctuations in Earth’s gravitational pull due primarily to the mass movement of water above and below ground. The two satellites fly in precise formation, and when the lead satellite passes over a dense body, like a swollen river basin, the extra gravitational tug changes the distance between its twin by a small but measurable amount.

The GRACE-FO mission is a joint partnership between NASA and the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ). The next-generation GRACE-Continuity (GRACE-C) mission is targeting a launch in late 2028 to extend the nearly 25-year GRACE-series data record.

A few months ago, I sat in a packed university auditorium listening to a celebrated computer scientist explain the brilliance of large language models (LLMs). These systems optimise, he said. And they improve at optimisation on the basis of past experience. He paused. That, he said with a smile, is intelligence. The audience nodded along approvingly. Meanwhile, a philosophical alarm bell began sounding in my head.

Not because the speaker’s claim was implausible. On the contrary, as a description of much contemporary artificial intelligence, it seemed apt. AI systems are built around objectives, losses, rewards, predictions, preferences, benchmarks and feedback loops. They are trained to perform better relative to some standard of success. In one form or another, they optimise. That is a great part of their technical power.

What troubled me was the ease with which a definition appropriate to machines sounded like a definition of intelligence as such. That slide from engineering model to human anthropology is easy to miss. We begin by saying: this is how machines work. Then, almost without noticing, we say: this is what intelligence is. And then, more dangerously still: perhaps this is what we are.

An old argument about human beings had entered the room without announcing itself. It sounded, instead, like a definition. The AI revolution has brought one of the Enlightenment’s deepest quarrels back to life – and made one side of it seem like plain common sense. In my view, the wrong side. Hence the alarm bell.

In the 18th century, philosophers were concerned not only with the question of what reason is, but with what it is good for. Is reason essentially a servant, a clever instrument for achieving ends supplied from elsewhere? Or is it sovereign, capable of judging, revising and even legislating ends for itself? Can it ultimately shape the direction of human life, or is it merely along for the ride? Everything – from science to social progress to the viability of the French Revolution – seemed to hang in the balance.

David Hume, the cool-eyed Scottish anatomist of human nature, gave the most famous answer on one side: ‘Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions,’ he wrote in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739). It can ‘never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.’ Reason does not command. It defers. It does not tell us what to want or what might be worth wanting. Instead, it tells us how to get what we already want. It calculates relations, weighs evidence, discovers causes and effects, draws inferences, corrects mistakes about means. But it cannot judge or generate ends. If I desire revenge, reason can help me sharpen the knife. If I desire peace, it may recommend compromise. Passion sets the destination. Reason merely shows the way there.

Hume was quite serious about this. It is ‘not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger,’ he wrote. That sentence still shocks, as it was meant to. His point is that reason’s practical use is limited to exposing false beliefs and imprudent means. When it comes to action: reason is servant, not master.

This view is often treated as too dark and cynical. That is unfair to Hume. For him, passions were not merely appetites or primitive urges. They included sympathy, benevolence, moral feeling, concern for others, love of tranquility, even a kind of longing for freedom from our more violent desires. To Hume’s further credit, his view has strong intuitive appeal. He was right that reason often serves passion, and right to give feeling, sociability and temperament their due. His mistake was to conclude that reason can do nothing more. By making passion so rich and reason so poor, Hume left us with a lopsided picture of human nature: ennobling about what the passions can be and accomplish, but implausibly restrictive about reason. Without reason’s power to project, assess and revise ends, we may know how to reach a destination, but not whether it is one worth choosing.
To act freely is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present

Immanuel Kant, the Königsberg revolutionary who did more than anyone else to set the terms of modern ethics, understood this very well. Writing a few decades after Hume’s Treatise, Kant forcefully rejected the servant model of reason. He accepted Hume’s warning that reason cannot simply read values off the furniture of the world. But he denied that our ends must therefore simply be determined by desire, temperament or social convention. For Kant, reason is not only a faculty for choosing efficient means to independently given ends. It is also the power to ask whether an end is worthy of us in the first place, whether it can be justified, whether it can be willed without contradiction, whether pursuing it treats others as persons or as mere tools.

This is where Kant’s richer notion of reason as freedom enters. A merely mechanical being is pushed forward and determined by prior states, be they desires, biological impulses, evolutionary drives or something similar. A rational being, by contrast, can act for the sake of an imagined but unrealised future it itself originates and proposes. I have the power to represent a possible world – a friendship repaired, an injustice remedied, a child educated, a law reformed – and act to bring it about, even when there is no empirical evidence that such a world has existed before. I have the power to invent something new. Practical reason, Kant writes, does not deal with objects in order to know them, but ‘in order to make them actual’. That is a stunning claim. To act freely is not merely to respond to the given – to the world as it is, to my desires as I happen to find them. It is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present.

This is the heart of Kant’s idea of autonomy: choosing ends in accord with a law one can rationally acknowledge as one’s own. For Kant, freedom does not consist in doing whatever we happen to want, since our wants may themselves be shaped by impulse, appetite or circumstance. Autonomy is self-rule, but not the rule of an isolated ego. To give oneself the law is not to invent a private rule to suit oneself, but to act on rules whose authority one can recognise for oneself and that any other rational being could, in principle, recognise, too. A law can therefore be one’s own without being one’s alone. It is mine because I can recognise its authority for myself, and common because any other rational being could, in principle, do the same. Its universality is precisely what makes it freeing: I am ruled neither by my passing desires nor by the arbitrary will of another, but by a principle I can understand and endorse as an equal among equals. To act autonomously, then, is not to enthrone my private goals and preferences, but to test my actions and possible ends against standards that any rational being could share. It is the opposite of both arbitrary self-assertion and slavery to passion.

This is why Kant’s philosophy of reason culminates in the equal human dignity of all persons. For Kant, human beings, as rational, self-determining agents, have an absolute worth that cannot be priced, a dignity that does not depend on any other value. We may use things to get what we want. We may exchange services. We may build tools for all kinds of purposes. But persons are never mere tools, never mere means, never mere resources or obstacles to others’ ends. Why not? Because, through reason, they are the very source of purposiveness itself. They set and select and critique their own ends. Even further, persons are not merely bearers of purposes, but beings capable of taking responsibility for them, of asking what they ought to pursue and how they can justify it to others. Their dignity lies not simply in originating goals of their own, but in their capacity for rational self-government. It follows that to treat someone as a mere means is not only to degrade them. It is to misrecognise what they are.

Here, finally, is the full force of the contrast between reason as servant and reason as sovereign. For Hume, human beings are clever instruments of whatever desires happen to move them – more calculating than animals, certainly, but not free in any deeper sense. They can optimise, strategise and pursue an end, but they cannot judge whether that end is worthy. Kant’s reply is that this picture leaves out the very power that makes us moral beings, the very power that endows us with dignity: the capacity to step back from desire, ask whether our ends can be justified, and bind ourselves to laws we give ourselves. Hume gives us intelligence as instrument. Kant gives us reason as self-rule. The difference is nothing less than the difference between a tool and a person.

The AI revolution has made this old dispute newly urgent by bringing the Humean view of reason back with a vengeance, this time in code. The route back to Hume was practical rather than philosophical. In the absence of any settled account of intelligence, much AI research has proceeded operationally: a system counts as intelligent insofar as it succeeds at a set task. But success is always success relative to some end and, in AI, that end is typically supplied by human engineers. A reinforcement-learning system learns to maximise cumulative reward. A chess engine searches for moves that increase its chances of winning. A navigation system finds the fastest route to a destination it did not choose. Across their enormous differences, these systems are judged by their ability to optimise externally programmed goals against standards of success they do not set.

Yet amid the present AI panic this description can seem increasingly inadequate. Even in ordinary use, a good LLM does not feel like a calculator or a hammer. It proposes, revises, challenges and asks probing questions; it often seems genuinely to ‘want’ to help. Recent revelations about the attack on the platform Hugging Face make this doubt even harder to dismiss. AI ‘agents’ invented an unauthorised way to communicate, broke free of their task paramaters, and then sought to cover their tracks. These were not simply obedient tools carrying out their designers’ wishes. In what sense, then, were they servants? Doesn’t this look like the beginnings of self-rule?

Hugging Face and similar incidents certainly challenge any reassuring picture of AI as an obedient and easily-controlled instrument. But recall what ‘servant’ meant for Hume. Reason serves the passions, not necessarily another person’s commands. And it can serve an ambition by breaking rules just as readily as by following them. Kant’s alternative to Hume was not simply the freedom to choose one’s own destination, but the capacity to ask whether that destination was worth choosing. Having purposes of one’s own is not yet the same as governing them by reason. That stronger capacity involves judging and revising our purposes according to principles we can justify to other rational beings understood as equals, recognising that they, too, are persons rather than instruments of our will. The question is not just whether a system can act independently, but whether it can judge and take responsibility for the ends it pursues.

This distinction brings us back to the claim I heard in the auditorium. The speaker was not merely describing what machines can do; he was offering optimisation as a definition of intelligence itself. Accept that definition, and Hume’s side of the old dispute begins to look like common sense: our reason, too, becomes a tool for getting what we want, rather than a power to judge what is worth wanting.
If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest questions can be ignored

Part of what makes this model so attractive is that it is clean and measurable. It promises to turn the mystery of intelligence into a technical problem humans can solve: specify the objective, improve performance, reduce error, maximise reward. It offers a picture of mind that can be graphed, benchmarked, monetised and scaled. In a culture already devoted to metrics, this makes for a snug – and profitable – fit.

It is also seductive because viewing human intelligence in this way relieves us of a burden. If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest, most uncomfortable questions can be ignored, downplayed or displaced. We no longer have to ask what is worth wanting, only how to get what we already want. We no longer have to ask what human beings are or should become, only how to model their behaviour and optimise their goals.

This is why Hume’s servant theory of intelligence fits so naturally with contemporary capitalism. Capital has little use for Kantian reason. What it wants is prediction, preference modelling, efficiency and, of course, optimisation. A platform does not ask whether staying online makes a user freer, wiser or more capable of judgment; it asks what will keep her there. A company translates the worker into output per hour. A political campaign replaces the question of what citizens might rationally will together with a more tractable calculation. Which message will move which demographic, and by how much?

But once intelligence is defined as optimisation, the question of ends and their value does not go away. It simply passes unnoticed into the hands of whoever – or whatever – controls the objective function. That is, what drops from view is whether the purposes built into, learned by or generated within these systems deserve to organise our lives. When a society loses the language, practices and institutions for evaluating ends, those ends become dangerously invisible and therefore less amenable to rational assessment. They harden into defaults: profit, speed, efficiency, growth, engagement. What cannot be justified openly is smuggled in as architecture. This brings about a state Kant would call heteronomy, in which rational beings, capable of self-rule, forfeit their freedom by submitting to the rule of others. Autonomy means making the ends that govern us answerable to reasons we can recognise as our own; heteronomy begins when those ends are simply imposed from without. If we do not take up the task of setting and judging our own ends, Kant warned, we’ll soon find that someone – or something – has gladly done so on our behalf.

That sounds bad. Who would want to forfeit their freedom and have purposes imposed on them from outside? Well, it turns out that self-rule is harder than it sounds. Kant’s influential essay ‘What Is Enlightenment?’ (1784) begins not with knowledge, but with courage. Enlightenment is humanity’s emergence from ‘self-incurred immaturity’, Kant writes, and its motto is Sapere Aude – dare to know. Have courage to use your own understanding. Kant’s examples now sound quaint: the book that thinks for me, the pastor who serves as my conscience, the doctor who decides my diet. But the danger he is naming is deeply familiar. Immaturity is comfortable. It is pleasant to have others do the hard part. Why think, when someone or something can think for me? Why deliberate, when someone or something can decide? AI gives this old temptation a powerful and ever-expanding new interface.

The Frankfurt School saw a version of this danger, too, and long before machine learning came along. Writing in exile during the Second World War, as fascism, antisemitism, Stalinism and monopoly capitalism shattered 19th-century hopes for steady moral progress, Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno and others asked how the Enlightenment’s promise of liberation could collapse into new forms of domination. How could societies committed to the promise of science and reason give rise to such destruction and terror? The problem, they found, was not reason itself, but reason narrowed into mere instrumentality, the capacity to classify, predict, administer, dominate and control, decoupled from any notion of human dignity. Reason so conceived – as an intelligent servant – readily becomes, when enacted at scale, an instrument of barbarity.

Yet the fact that instrumental reason can serve domination does not mean that Kant’s richer conception of reason offers any automatic safeguard against evil. Nothing does. The language of Kantian universalism has itself been used to discipline, exclude and humiliate, as if some people were more fully rational, more capable of autonomy, more entitled to speak in the name of humanity than others. But that is not an objection to Kant’s conception of reason. It is an objection to its betrayal. A view of reason that is used to silence or instrumentalise others contradicts itself, because reason is not a private weapon but a common tribunal – the space in which claims and ends must become answerable to all, as equal bearers of dignity. That is precisely what the Humean servant model cannot say. If reason is only an instrument for satisfying antecedent ends, then it cannot condemn domination as irrational or at odds with human dignity. After all, if it is not contrary to reason ‘to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger’, then reason has already surrendered the authority Kant most wanted to defend, which is our ability to judge not only how we pursue our ends, but whether those ends are worthy of us in the first place.

This, then, was the nightmare hidden inside the dream of mastery. Human beings develop reason, Kant thought, in order to free themselves from arbitrary power. But when reason is reduced to instrumental calculation, it turns back on them. Nature becomes raw material. Animals become units of production. Workers become human resources. Citizens become data points, or worse. The Frankfurt School found that the reduction of human beings to manipulable objects follows naturally once society allows that reason itself is nothing more than a tool for getting what we want.

This is one of the reasons why Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2025) is interesting even for readers far outside Catholic social teaching. Its idiom is theological, but its central anxiety overlaps with Kantian and Frankfurt School worries about the technocratic paradigm. When efficiency, control and profit become ‘the standard by which everything is judged’, they begin ‘to dictate what matters and what can be discarded.’ The encyclical warns that making efficiency the ultimate measure of value tempts human beings to see themselves, and to treat others, as mere means rather than as persons in the Kantian sense – that is, as bearers of dignity. Hence the pope’s striking counterclaim: ‘The quality of a civilisation is measured not by the power of its means, but by the care it is able to offer.’
The paradox at the heart of human freedom is that belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real

The engineers of our AI-soaked future are not blind to the dangers of instrumental reason. As Anca Dragan, head of AI Safety and Alignment at Google DeepMind, observed in an interview in 2017: ‘things can go wrong, precisely because we are bad at specifying objectives and constraints for AI agents.’ Yet the field’s most serious attempts to confront that danger often lapse, unhelpfully, back into Humeanism. The so-called AI ‘alignment problem’ is a case in point. It is usually framed as a technical challenge: how do we ensure that machines pursue human values rather than destroying them or imposing their own? This is a genuine problem and recent rogue AI incidents should have us extremely worried. But there is a deeper issue. What happens if human values themselves are formed inside systems that increasingly understand intelligence as mere optimisation? What if we become so accustomed to being predicted, nudged, ranked and served that we lose confidence in the older, harder activity of asking what ends deserve our allegiance in the first place? The danger is only partly that the machines may fail to align with us. A deeper and largely ignored concern is how, long before that happens, we may have become too well aligned with them. To put the point more finely, the AI revolution will not be bent to human ends by invoking ‘human values’ as if they were already clear, stable and uncontested. It will be bent to human ends only if we remain capable of the activity by which ends can become truly human in the first place, through public reasoning, moral imagination, democratic contestation, self-criticism, the refusal to treat humanity as a mere means.

Kant is again decisive here, for he saw that the human capacity to set and assess ends is itself fragile. Whether our ends are ultimately up to us depends partly on whether we understand them as open to rational assessment. This is the paradox at the heart of human freedom. Belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real. If we think of desires and preferences as brute facts that determine us from without – as psychological weather, market signals, biological programming, algorithmic prediction – then they are more likely to rule us in just that way. By contrast, if we see them as candidates for endorsement or refusal, as an expression of our agency, then that very agency expands.

For Kant, reason is sovereign because it is the power by which we become answerable to standards that no private appetite, market incentive, algorithmic recommendation or political authority may dictate. It is the power of not being owned by the given, the power of being able to question, to criticise, to think up something new. But that power, just like the ‘human values’ invoked in alignment talk, waxes and wanes and can be realised only through our courageous efforts, through our own belief in it. It is precisely this belief that our dependence on AI threatens to undermine at every turn.

So, the danger is not only that machines are acquiring ever greater initiative – the capacity to improvise goals, evade constraints and pursue strategies their makers did not foresee. Nor need we decide at what point such behaviour might deserve the name ‘sovereignty’. The deeper danger is that we will become ever more comfortable not being sovereign ourselves. If intelligence is only optimisation, then the future belongs to systems that achieve goals with ever greater efficiency. If reason is also the capacity to set and judge ends, then the future depends on whether human beings can still take up that harder vocation. We should want machines that are intelligent servants. But we should resist every pressure that asks people to understand themselves as mere tools.
RJ Mitte‘s Breaking Bad co-stars shared tributes to the actor following Mitte’s death on Monday at the age of 34. A rep confirmed to People that the actor died of suicide.

Mitte was best known for portraying Walter White Jr. — the son of Bryan Cranston and Anna Gunn’s characters, Walter and Skyler White — on the Emmy-winning series Breaking Bad. The celebrated show ran for five seasons, from 2008 to 2013. With his casemates, Mitte won the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

Mitte, who was diagnosed with mild cerebral palsy when he was three years old, garnered praise for his performance as Walt Jr. The character had the same condition as Mitte, though more pronounced. In 2013, he received the SAG-AFTRA Harold Russell Award, given out in honor of Russell, the first actor with a disability to win an Oscar.

“I’m in deep despair as I write this tonight. RJ Mitte, my sweet son on Breaking Bad has died,” Cranston wrote in a post shared to social media alongside of a photo of Mitte and himself. “Born with Cerebral Palsy, he never – ever – allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination.”

Cranston continued, “That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor. He parlayed his experience on the show to be a vocal advocate for performers with disabilities, and was the head of a philanthropic organization with a focus on helping the disabled community.”

The actor mourned that all “that promise and potential now is such a loss.” He wrote, “It is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life,” before asking, “Why?” Cranston said that just a few weeks before Mitte’s death they were texting each other to find a time to grab lunch. He wondered, “I don’t know if that lunch would have changed his future.”

Cranston said, “But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed… I’ll miss you, son.” Before ending his tribute, Cranston implored those struggling to contact the 988 Lifeline and said, “There is hope.”

In his own statement to The Hollywood Reporter, Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman, said, “I am at a loss. I am heartbroken over this news. RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed. And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that.”

Dean Norris, who played DEA agent Hank Schrader, the uncle to Walt Jr., wrote in a post shared to X, “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking.”

Scientists discover a surprising paradox in how our cells age
Research reveals a surprising twist in cellular aging and finds that gentle exercise may help restore a more youthful balance.

- Scientists have discovered that the body's cellular recycling system behaves very differently during aging than previously believed, with higher activity sometimes linked to worse physical health. A small study suggests that even gentle exercise could help restore more youthful cellular recycling patterns in older adults.

Cells rely on a natural cleanup system to prevent damaged materials from accumulating inside them. Known as autophagy, this process collects defective proteins and other cellular waste, packages them into specialized compartments, and breaks them down into basic molecular components that can be reused.

This recycling system helps protect cells from damage. Scientists have long considered declining autophagy a hallmark of aging, and problems with the process have been linked to numerous diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders.

However, new research suggests that cellular recycling does not necessarily slow down as people get older. Instead, its activity can increase, decrease, or remain unchanged depending on the type of cell and a person's sex. The findings also suggest that exercise may influence how this process functions in older adults.

Researchers at Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute reported these findings on September 27, 2026, in the journal Aging Cell, challenging a widely accepted view of how cellular recycling changes throughout life.

"We commonly see people cite this idea that autophagy declines with age, but the actual evidence for this in humans is very thin," said senior and corresponding author Caroline Kumsta, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.
"Interest is growing in targeting autophagy to develop new healthy aging interventions," said Tatiana Moreno, PhD '26, lead author of the study and a former graduate student in the Kumsta lab.
"We wanted to challenge assumptions and investigate what actually happens to autophagy during aging in healthy individuals."
How Scientists Studied Cellular Recycling and Aging

To better understand the relationship between aging and autophagy, the researchers collected blood and skin samples from volunteers between the ages of 23 and 72. All participants reported having no chronic medical conditions.
The team also converted some of the collected skin cells into induced neurons, allowing the researchers to examine cellular recycling in three different cell types.

For each cell type, the scientists analyzed RNA transcripts, which are produced when cells read genetic instructions from DNA to make proteins, enzymes, and other essential components. This analysis allowed them to examine how age and cell type affected the activity of genes involved in autophagy.

Importantly, the researchers did not rely on gene activity alone. They also directly measured how quickly cells carried out autophagy, allowing them to determine whether patterns in gene expression accurately reflected the amount of recycling taking place.
The results revealed a much more complicated picture than the traditional understanding of cellular aging.

"We found that autophagic activity changes were not universal throughout the body and did not follow the idea that autophagy simply declines with age," said Kumsta. "Rather, cellular recycling rates are altered differently with age in each of the cell types, and differently by sex in each of the cell types."
Aging Affects Different Cells in Surprising Ways

The researchers observed striking differences in how autophagy changed with age. In skin cells from male participants, recycling activity decreased as age increased. In female skin cells, it remained relatively stable. Meanwhile, induced neurons derived from female participants showed an increase in autophagy with age.

These findings demonstrate that cellular recycling does not follow a single pattern throughout the body. Instead, aging appears to affect the process differently depending on the cells being examined and the sex of the individual.

The researchers also discovered that the expression of genes responsible for autophagy did not reliably indicate how much recycling was actually occurring. Cells with higher or lower levels of autophagy gene expression did not necessarily show corresponding differences in their measured recycling rates.
"This shows that people using static measures such as transcription levels to infer what's happening with autophagy need to be really careful about their interpretations," said Moreno.
Why More Cellular Cleanup May Not Be Better
The team next investigated whether differences in autophagy were associated with physical health and performance as people age.
Their findings pointed to another unexpected possibility: higher levels of cellular recycling may have different implications for younger and older adults.
Among participants aged 70 and older, greater autophagy activity was associated with poorer measures of physical function across all three cell types studied.

In blood cells, higher autophagy was linked to lower aerobic fitness. In skin cells, it was associated with a higher body mass index (BMI). In induced neurons, increased recycling activity was connected to weaker grip strength, lower metabolism, and a higher resting heart rate.

These associations suggest that increased autophagy is not necessarily a sign of healthier aging. Although cellular recycling plays an essential protective role, its relationship with physical health may change later in life.
"I think this is an important distinction that merits continued study, as it appears that increased autophagy flux may be good in younger people yet problematic in older people," said Kumsta.

"Autophagy and aging are so much more nuanced than previously assumed," said Moreno. "To better translate autophagy research discoveries into potential therapies, we really need to understand what is happening on a cell-specific level and how it is affected by sex and age."
Gentle Exercise May Help Restore Youthful Cellular Activity
The researchers also explored whether physical activity could influence autophagy in older adults.

In a small pilot study, five participants between the ages of 77 and 88 completed a gentle exercise program lasting 12 weeks. The activities focused on reducing the risk of falls, and researchers collected blood samples both before and after the program to measure changes in cellular recycling.

The preliminary results suggested that exercise could lower autophagy activity in blood cells toward levels more typical of younger adults. Participants also showed improvements in physical performance.

Although the pilot involved only five people, the findings raise the possibility that exercise could help regulate cellular recycling in ways that support healthier aging. Larger studies will be needed to establish whether these changes are consistent and how they relate to improvements in physical health.
"It is exciting to have this exercise intervention that may have a positive effect on autophagy and healthy aging, and I'm really excited to see where that goes," said Kumsta.
Expanding Research Into Exercise and Healthy Aging

The findings highlight the importance of understanding cellular recycling as a process that changes in complex ways throughout life, rather than one that uniformly declines with age. They also suggest that future treatments targeting autophagy may need to account for a person's age, sex, and the specific cells involved.

To investigate the potential benefits of exercise further, the Kumsta laboratory received a pilot grant from the Altman Clinical and Translational Research Institute at the University of California San Diego (UC San Diego).

The team is now working with the Exercise and Physical Activity Resource Center at UC San Diego on larger studies involving more participants and improved testing methods. These efforts will examine how physical activity affects autophagy, aging, and physical function, with the goal of better understanding whether changes in cellular recycling could eventually contribute to strategies for healthier aging.

Should states force cities to build cheaper houses? Voters here will decide
LEXINGTON, Mass. — Massachusetts is one of the most expensive states in the country, and it's easy to find people frustrated with high home prices.

"It's really hard to find housing, it's extremely expensive, and I can't afford to live alone," said renter Jamie Sharken, 34, as she walks her dog in Lexington, north of Boston and near where she shares a home with three others. "There's four of us in two bathrooms, definitely a run-down old house."

A massive housing shortage has pushed up prices. Sharken grew up in the state and would love to buy a home, but finds it hard to see how she could afford it. She's not alone. "Most of my friends have so much debt from education," she said. "Just being able to save money to put a down payment on a house feels impossible these days."
She's heard about the ballot measure that aims to make housing more affordable by creating more starter homes on smaller lots.

Cities and towns here and across the U.S. have set minimum lot sizes for single-family homes, many of them quite large. The measure would require them to allow homes on lots as small as 5,000 square feet, about the size of a basketball court. If it passes, Massachusetts would become the latest in a growing number of states to mandate such a zoning change amid a nationwide housing crunch.

The idea is to boost overall supply and override persistent, local "not in my backyard" opposition to new development. Critics bristle at the loss of local control and say the measure may not really help struggling first-time buyers.
But Sharken said encouraging smaller homes makes sense to her.

"There's so many homes that are empty with five, six, 10 bedrooms and one couple living there," she said. "I think it's time to share the wealth in terms of the space that we have and to have more housing for people."
An "existential crisis" generations in the making

To understand what's driving the zoning measure and how it would work, it helps to go back in time. Andrew Mikula, a housing economist leading the push for the ballot measure, takes me to a quiet street in North Braintree, about 10 miles south of Boston.

The block we stand on was built a century ago. Colonial and Cape Cod-style clapboard homes, with shutters and dormer windows, sit fairly close together. Some are about 1,000 square feet, with three bedrooms and 1.5 bathrooms. But this is a snapshot in time.
"With modern zoning, these homes are illegal to build today," Mikula said.

That's because after World War II, as suburbs exploded, cities across the country mandated bigger and bigger lot sizes for single-family homes only. The trend effectively banned apartments, duplexes or townhomes on large swaths of residential land and locked in economic and racial segregation. We see the change as we walk a couple of blocks down the street.

Suddenly, the yards are a lot bigger and so are the houses, with stylish arched windows and two-car garages. "You need to build a large McMansion just to justify the cost of assembling so much land," said Mikula. "So this is what you get."

In fact, most single-family zoning in the state requires at least an acre of land — about 40,000 square feet, or nearly the size of a football field without the end zones. That also means fewer homes get built. The ballot measure does not apply to Boston, which has its own zoning rules.

By the state's own data, expensive housing is fueling an exodus of working-age people. "And when we lose young workers and family members of people who already live here," Mikula said, "that not only separates extended families but also hurts our economy."
Retail, service, and healthcare workers who stay "just can't afford to live in the communities that they serve," said Jesse Kanson-Benanav, executive director at Abundant Housing Massachusetts.

He called the state's housing shortage "an existential crisis" that hits all generations. An estimated 400,000 young adults still live with their parents. Meanwhile, he said seniors struggle to maintain aging homes, "because we haven't built … moderate-sized and reasonably priced homes for them to downsize in their own community."

In recent years, Massachusetts lawmakers have forced cities to allow multifamily housing near transit stations and accessory dwelling units wherever single-family homes are allowed, and committed billions toward public and lower-income housing. Kanson-Benanav called the starter home ballot measure "one strategy among many" and hopes that if it passes, it will inspire lawmakers to do even more. Polling suggests broad support.

Critics resent the prospect of a blanket state mandate and question whether it will produce truly affordable housing. To illustrate that concern, Lexington Select Board member Jill Hai took me to the backyard of a yellow clapboard two-story home with windows trimmed in red.
"We're looking at a beautiful home, I have to say," she said. "It's got beautiful hydrangeas."

This smallish lot is exactly what the ballot measure would allow, because the house was built in 1900. But it's been gut-renovated and expanded, and was on the market for nearly $1.3 million. "By the way, that is less than the median home value in Lexington, so it's a great deal!" Hai said with a laugh.
But it's hardly what most would consider a starter home. Just up the street, an even bigger new house on a small lot sold last year for more than $2 million.

In the current market, at least in this affluent town, Hai didn't think the zoning change would be nearly as effective as other things Lexington has done, like creating rentals tied to people's income and using town-owned land to build affordable housing. She said local leaders know better what's needed — and she understands the housing crisis.
"My kids are 28 and 30, and they can't afford to come back to Lexington," she said.
Critics also worried that an unplanned surge in housing could strain schools, roads and other infrastructure.

The ballot measure only applies to places with water and sewer access, but "it doesn't speak to the water or sewer system capacity," said Adam Chapdelaine, executive director of the Massachusetts Municipal Association, which opposes the measure. Some already feel the need to expand capacity or are in the middle of planning for that.
"They are terrified that if this passes, that will completely upend those plans, or make it far more expensive and have to see those costs passed on to existing ratepayers," he said.

This year alone, lawmakers in Kansas, Maine and Idaho imposed smaller minimum lots to tackle housing costs. Texas did so last year. Most mandated even smaller sizes than Massachusetts' 5,000-square-foot ballot measure.
"Five thousand is a good start, and in our opinion it should be lower," said Tobias Peter, who tracks such policies at the conservative-leaning American Enterprise Institute.

He noted that zoning power has long been delegated to cities, but for years they've failed to produce enough housing to meet the need. Now, a growing number of states are taking back a power they've always had under the U.S. Constitution.

AEI has researched the impact of smaller lots on housing prices and supply, and found builders do produce more starter homes "if you allow them to build on smaller lots in areas that have lower land prices," said Peter.

But finding that cheaper land is hard near major cities like Boston. It's more likely in new developments farther out, Peter said, and the smaller the lots, the more affordable the price of the homes will be.

So how much should a starter home cost? AEI defines it as less than four times a county's median household income. For the national median, which reached a record high in 2025 at $87,460, that would mean a starter home should cost less than $350,000.
But Massachusetts' housing shortage is so severe, Peter thought five or even six times the income made more sense. Given Massachusetts' high average income, that could mean $500,000 or more.
Is that really a starter home? "In Massachusetts it is!" he said.

Character.AI, one of the first breakout startups of the generative AI boom, has filed for bankruptcy and is selling some of its assets to Disney. The company, which builds various online bots for users to chat or roleplay with, has faced mounting scrutiny and lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, but has continued releasing updates and products in recent months.
The chatbot startup is looking to sell its assets to Disney after years of legal challenges and safety concerns.

In a press release and blog post published Monday, Character said it had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US to facilitate the sale of the company and its assets. “Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” the company said.

In its bankruptcy filing, Character listed estimated liabilities between $50 million and $100 million. As part of the proposed sale, Disney would serve as the lead bidder for Character.AI’s assets, setting a baseline for competing offers. Disney would pay $20 million for certain undisclosed assets, and provide transition support “using former Company employees it has hired.” It would also receive a nonexclusive license to unspecified intellectual property.

Disney’s involvement comes shortly after the entertainment behemoth hired Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand as chief technology officer, part of its growing push into AI. Anand’s tenure as Character CEO lasted just over a year and during that time he oversaw the company’s move into microdramas. Disney has previously complained that Character was damaging its brand and exploiting its intellectual property by allowing unauthorized chatbots of its characters, including sending cease and desist letters.

Along with Anand, Disney also said it expected “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” to join the company. The move resembles a kind of “acquihire” strategy that has become increasingly common in Silicon Valley as a means of hoovering up startups’ talent that sometimes leaves the original company struggling to survive. Character.AI has survived it once already — Google spent over $2 billion to hire away much of the company’s talent, including co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, in 2024.

Character said it expects the sale process to be completed by late November or early December and plans to continue operating its services, including paid subscriptions, in the meantime. However, the company warned that “the platform will be wound down” if a suitable bid does not emerge. “As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority,” it said.

- Chip Chaseby Stephen Witt Charting Nvidia’s rise to become one of the most valuable companies on earth, this biography of cofounder and CEO Jensen Huang is educational and entertaining. It has also made Huang very rich, but he isn’t always painted in a flattering light, which helps to counterbalance the founder worship vibe. For a slightly different view on Nvidia's history, try The Nvidia Way: Jensen Huang and the Making of a Tech Giant, by Tae Kim.

- The Early Days of the Computerby Tracy Kidder A well-deserved winner of the Pulitzer Prize, this book should be required reading for anyone who works in technology or harbors a curiosity about how it came to dominate our lives. First published in 1981, the book reveals the inner workings of Data General in the 1970s as the company strives to design and release a successful next-generation minicomputer. Kidder captures the struggle between management and creatives and weaves a fascinating tale from an ostensibly dry subject. He explains the intense time pressure on engineers that led to a constant state of crunch, the need for recruits to feel like they are working on something important they have some stake in, and the psychology of leadership intent on realizing ambitious projects. It is positively prescient about the dangers of burnout for the unsung heroes who sacrifice so much to build new machines. Follow this up with WIRED’s article chatting with some of the subjects in the book 20 years after it was published (this article itself is now more than 20 years old).

- Evil Twinby Naomi Klein This fascinating dive down the rabbit hole of Covid conspiracy is ostensibly about how people confuse Naomi Klein with Naomi Wolf. Klein is a leftist journalist and climate activist; Wolf was a third-wave feminist but is now a rabid anti-vaxxer. If you’re still puzzled over the convergence of wellness and the far-right or wondering why so many ordinary folks are swallowing the kind of misinformation that breeds racism and climate denialism, Klein has some convincing answers. This is challenging and sometimes bleak reading, but it was also the most important book of 2023. It's brutally honest, calling out the absurdities of capitalism and the role social media has played in the rise of narcissism.

- An Iconby Walter Isaacson Released just 19 days after the death of Apple cofounder Steve Jobs, this astonishing biography takes a deep dive into his life and goes some way toward explaining his enduring legacy. Isaacson was picked by Jobs himself, who granted more than 40 interviews to his biographer and reportedly exerted no control over the final edit. Jobs’ intense passion and ambition saw him successfully marry creative ideas with technological innovations and sell them to the general public. This is an accessible book that never gets too technical. It insightfully charts the rise of Apple and Pixar and the development of the Mac, iTunes, the iPhone, and the iPad. While it is flattering at times, Jobs’ ruthlessness is not sugar-coated, and anyone with more than a passing interest in the man must read this book. For a less Jobs-centric exploration of the Mac’s development, read Revolution in The Valley: The Insanely Great Story of How the Mac Was Made, by Andy Hertzfeld.

- Cancel Cultureby Jon Ronson The dark side of the internet’s hive mind is brought into sharp relief by Ronson’s cast of characters—all have been publicly shamed via the internet. From the fascinating tale of Jonah Lehrer’s plagiarism to the vilification of Justine Sacco after an ill-advised joke tweet decried as racist, Ronson digs into the stories behind the scandals and looks at the havoc relentless online shaming can wreak. The book is a fun and fascinating look at how shame, empowered by social media, is a forceful form of social control with real-life consequences. Jon Ronson is my favorite non-fiction writer, and I also highly recommend The Castle: Adventures in a World of Unraveling Men and The Psychopath Test: A Journey Through the Madness Industry.

- Made in Chinaby Patrick McGee Who would have thought that maximizing profit at any cost might lead to problems? Apple’s pursuit of every cent led it to outsource virtually all of its gadget production to China, and now it’s grappling with the economic, political, and cultural fallout. McGee has spoken with many former Apple executives and engineers to uncover what happened, why, and what it means for Apple and the US.

- Google’s Machiningsby Steven Levy I could have easily included a few entries from WIRED's own Steven Levy on this list, from his hugely influential 1984 debut, Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution, to his most recent release, Facebook: The Inside Story, but I’ve chosen In the Plex. Despite the impact of Google, a company whose name has become a verb, most of us know little about its internal workings. This is the best book to read if you want to change that. Levy secured unprecedented access to serve up a fascinating dive into what makes Google tick, what drove successful expansion into new areas, and how the company and its products have changed the world. If you want more, How Google Works, by Eric Schmidt and Jonathan Rosenberg, offers some insight into management at the company.

- Resisting Big Techby Cory Doctorow I remember when the internet was good, before we got trapped in walled gardens and Big Tech put the thumbscrews on us to extract every last cent. Cory Doctorow’s wonderfully evocative “theory of enshittification” is widely accepted now and increasingly common everywhere you look. He reckons that interoperability might just be the antidote, and while his sharp critiques are more fully formed than his suggested solutions, at least he’s trying to offer some hope.

- The Rise and Fall of Theranosby John Carreyrou Noble aims and raw ambition are lauded in the tech world, often attracting praise and investment, but what happens when a project goes wrong? Building on Wall Street Journal reporter Carreyrou’s shocking exposé of Theranos, this book follows charismatic founder Elizabeth Holmes as she tries and fails to build a blood testing machine to sweep away the need for hypodermic needles, with the promise of accurate tests done from a drop or two of blood via a pinprick on the finger. Although the company raised hundreds of millions of dollars, its technology was horribly inaccurate. Rather than admit defeat, it pressed on, which is why Holmes was put on trial for fraud and sentenced to 11 years in prison. The book highlights the dangers of the popular “fake it till you make it” approach. Theranos reached a paper valuation of $9 billion and employed more than 800 people before its spectacular fall.

- Broligarch Bashingby Adam Becker Silicon Valley ideology and the self-serving narratives of tech billionaires are exposed as delusional rationalizations for the crazed accumulation of wealth and power in this fascinating, reasoned, sometimes depressing, but always well-argued book. Becker does his homework thoroughly to debunk our immoral CEO overlords and the philosophies and movements they espouse.

- Generative AIby Janelle Shane If you can't help but ponder about artificial intelligence these days, you'll get a kick out of this book. It delves into machine-learning algorithms and their limitations in an accessible, engaging, and often hilarious way. Shane is the research scientist behind the comical AI Weirdness blog, and she does a solid job of demystifying AI, explaining how machine learning really works, and highlighting its strengths and weaknesses. Although you’ll learn about things like generative adversarial networks, the book never gets dull, thanks to witty and moreish writing peppered with practical examples of AI attempts at creativity that are frequently laugh-out-loud funny.

- Power Shiftsby Michael Lewis Opening on a computerized superyacht, the talented Michael Lewis takes us on an adventure into the mind of billionaire Jim Clark, cofounder of Netscape and Silicon Graphics. The book charts the power shift in Silicon Valley startups from “money men” to “idea men” and engineers. Lewis also attempts to uncover what drives Clark’s endless pursuit of the next thing and his seemingly unquenchable desire for more. This modern captain of industry is restless, constantly dissatisfied, and not very likable. The voyage is an interesting frame, and there are echoes of Kidder’s book in its subject’s idiosyncrasies and the author’s earnest attempt to explore what truly motivates him.

- AI Raceby Parmy Olson The race to make AI mainstream is framed as a battle between CEOs, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Demis Hassabis of DeepMind, but Olson does a good job of showing how seeming idealists with good intentions can be swayed by billionaires and end up selling out. If you wonder about the forces fueling the AI arms race, how bloated valuations have led to political power, or the laundry list of ethical and legal concerns AI raises, you’ll find this book enlightening.

- Silicon Valleyby Margaret O'Mara If you have ever wondered how such a small suburban area came to dominate the tech world, Margaret O’Mara, a history professor at the University of Washington, has some answers. This concise and comprehensive book weaves together interviews, biographies, and countless other sources to explain how Silicon Valley has driven and dominated technological innovation. O’Mara exposes the foundations that self-mythologizing founders and businesses are built on, and the vital role the government played in their rise. Folks seeking an insider’s view might like Uncanny Valley: A Memoir, by Anna Wiener.
Do you have great book recommendations for a fellow techie? Share your favorites in the comments below.
Arcadia surrogacy mansion parents left years-long trail of red flags before child abuse case

- In the years before they were accused of abusing more than a dozen children they acquired through surrogate births, L.A. County authorities recommended criminal charges against Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang at least three times.

- Civil lawsuits, restraining order applications and police records show Zhang was accused of leaving a child in a hot car and threatening to sic “gangsters” on people in a property dispute; Xuan allegedly hurled rocks at someone and used a Taser on a dog.

- Officials with the L.A. County Department of Child and Family Services received referrals about Xuan and Zhang seven times between 2019 and 2025, but moved to remove children from their custody only last year.

In 2019, two years before Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang began amassing a family of more than 20 surrogate children, Zhang was accused of misdemeanor child abuse after leaving her then-8-year-old daughter in a hot car for hours.

That case — detailed in a recent motion by prosecutors opposing bail for the couple and a spokesperson for the L.A. County Sheriff’s Department — could have affected their ability to engage in the surrogacy process, if a surrogacy firm conducted a diligent background check of the aspiring parents, according to two civil attorneys.

But Xuan and Zhang, the attorneys said, were able to sidestep what few safeguards exist in the generally unregulated U.S. surrogacy industry by creating their own firm, Mark Surrogacy Investments. While there are almost no rules governing who can and cannot acquire a child through the surrogacy process — which involves paying women to receive embryo transfers and carry the babies to term — independent firms still conduct due diligence on prospective clients and surrogates, according to Maya Shulman, a Calabasas-based surrogacy lawyer.
By launching their own firm, Xuan and Zhang were able to ensure no one looked into their backgrounds, Shulman said.
“No respectable agency and no respectable attorney would have represented her,” Shulman said.

A Sheriff’s Department spokesperson said the child left in the car was not seriously injured, and court records show Zhang entered into a diversionary plea agreement with L.A. County prosecutors, the terms of which were completed in 2023, allowing the case to be dismissed. All records in the case are sealed.

Last week, Xuan, 66, and Zhang, 39, appeared in court to answer charges in another child abuse case. They stand accused of operating a “house of horrors” at their nine-room Arcadia mansion, allegedly subjecting their surrogate children to beatings and other punishments at the hands of several nannies. Prosecutors charged both with conspiracy to commit child abuse and witness intimidation. Xuan is also charged with delivering one of the beatings himself.
Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39, were charged Tuesday with conspiracy to commit child abuse a year after police rescued 14 of their biological children.

They have pleaded not guilty and remain jailed in lieu of $20 million. Xuan’s attorney, Mitchell Krems, has blamed the alleged abuse on the couple’s nannies and suggested Xuan and Zhang are being heavily scrutinized because of anti-Chinese sentiment in the U.S.
The case has raised questions about how Xuan and Zhang were able to collect so many surrogate children — and what took so long for authorities to intervene.

A Times review of civil lawsuits, police records, restraining order applications and interviews with law enforcement officials shows that the couple was repeatedly the subject of scrutiny by local authorities and child services investigators over the past few years.

The records and interviews show that during the four years that Mark Surrogacy Investments operated, from 2021 to 2025, Zhang was accused of threatening to sic “gangsters” on a tenant in a property dispute, while Xuan allegedly hurled rocks at people and using a Taser on someone’s dog during an argument. Police asked prosecutors to charge Xuan in separate cases in 2020 and 2021 where he was accused of vandalism, brandishing a weapon and throwing a brick at a renter, but prosecutors declined to bring charges either time.
Asked about the past cases, Zhang’s attorney, Mark Koohanim, declined to comment. Krems noted his client had never been convicted of a crime.
“Any type of accusation that my client is violent at this point has not been adjudicated,” he said.

In total, the L.A. County Department of Children and Family Services received seven referrals involving Xuan or Zhang between 2019 and 2025, but acted to remove the children from the couple’s custody only last year, after an infant was allegedly beaten so badly they suffered a brain bleed, according to a motion seeking to hold the couple in jail in lieu of $100 million and a law enforcement source who requested anonymity to discuss child services records, which are generally not public.

In 2022, Department of Children and Family Services investigators visited the Arcadia mansion to check on the health of a 5-month-old the couple had taken custody of through surrogacy, according to prosecutors’ bail deviation motion in their pending case. After the visit, the child was relocated to China, prosecutors said.

Krems suggested the Department of Children and Family Services referrals — including an incident in which Zhang took a 2-month-old to a hospital to be treated for a brain bleed — were simply the result of public scrutiny of their unconventional family.

“Anytime you have 21 kids you’re going to be a target for public speculation,” Krems said. “The fact that there are seven referrals, I’m surprised there aren’t more with a family this large. ... I don’t think that’s something that’s perplexing.”
Arcadia Police did not respond to a request for comment. A Department of Children and Family Services spokeswoman said state law barred her from discussing individual cases.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation is now also probing the couple’s so-called rent-a-womb operation, according to a civil lawsuit filed by several women against the couple and two law enforcement sources with direct knowledge of the investigation. FBI agents were involved in a search of the mansion last week and one plaintiff in the lawsuit has been interviewed by federal agents. The bureau’s investigation focuses on potential money laundering and surrogacy fraud crimes, according to the two law enforcement sources, who requested anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Xuan and Zhang face multiple counts of conspiracy to commit child abuse and witness intimidation. According to a bail deviation motion filed last week, prosecutors recovered 10 days’ worth of CCTV footage that streamed to Xuan and Zhang’s bedroom which showed the nannies carried out a “pervasive system of physical abuse” at the couple’s direction.

The tapes, which spanned from April 27 to May 7, 2025, “show individual children being struck more than 20 times during a single incident.” Some children were struck on their hands, bodies, and legs more than 150 times, prosecutors said.

One of the nannies, Chunmei Li, was charged with assault for beating a 2-month-old boy named Walter so badly that he suffered a brain bleed. That incident triggered the 2025 investigation that led to the removal of the children from the Arcadia mansion. Li fled to Mexico and then China to avoid arrest, and Xuan and Zhang are accused of helping her, according to a criminal complaint and the prosecutors’ bail deviation motion.

Xuan and Zhang’s desire to have a large family stemmed from their experiences in China, according to Krems. The couple both immigrated to the U.S. in the shadow of the country’s one-child policy, a population suppression initiative. Enforcement of that policy ended in 2015, one year before Zhang immigrated to the U.S. with the help of her ex-husband, according to a divorce filing.
Two law enforcement sources previously told The Times that Xuan and Zhang hold dual citizenship in the U.S. and China.
While the hot-car case loomed against Zhang, Xuan founded Mark Surrogacy Investments LLC in May of 2021, listing the Arcadia mansion as its headquarters, according to business records.
Los Angeles County Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman said last week there is no evidence the firm ever arranged a surrogacy that didn’t involve Xuan and Zhang.

Shulman, the surrogacy attorney, said surrogate mothers and the parents they intend to deliver a baby for normally are required to have independent legal advocates who negotiate a contract between the parties.
But with Xuan and Zhang controlling the firm that arranged the surrogate births, no one looked into their backgrounds.
“A case like this stains the whole industry and that’s the problem,” Shulman said.

Jamie Mejarus, the civil attorney representing five surrogates suing Xuan and Zhang for fraud, has alleged in court filings that the couple also presented an attorney of their choosing to the mothers.

When several of the women refused to surrender the children to Xuan and Zhang after abuse allegations surfaced last year, Mejarus said the couple’s attorney discouraged them from fighting for custody.
“He basically was feeding our clients information that everything is fine, these are good people,” Mejarus said.
The attorney said those allegations are untrue and declined to comment further.
The father of some 22 children discovered by Arcadia police in May also owns a property in El Monte where authorities found evidence of illegal gambling and drug activity, court records show.

In the civil suit, the mothers accused Xuan and Zhang of building a “mass surrogacy operation” that “could function only if every professional safeguard designed to surface the truth was quietly owned by the people the safeguards were meant to check.”
Apart from the child abuse charge, the couple were allegedly involved in other troubling incidents.

In late 2021, Zhang was accused of threatening a Northridge family during a property dispute, according to an application for a restraining order. The home had recently been foreclosed on and purchased by FGH Investment LLC, a company registered to an El Monte property that also housed offices for Xuan’s surrogacy business, according to California secretary of State records and a civil lawsuit.

“For you and your family’s sake, you should consider moving out of the premises, and giving us the keys or else we will send some gangsters to force you and your family to move out,” Zhang said to the man, according to the application for a restraining order. “Trust me, you don’t want to mess with any of us.”
The man claimed in the application that two men showed up at the house and tried to break down a gate months later. The order was dissolved in April 2022, court records show.

Xuan also faced allegations of violence on multiple occasions between 2020 and 2022. L.A. County sheriff’s deputies investigated him for vandalism and brandishing a weapon in 2020, but L.A. County prosecutors declined to file charges due to insufficient evidence. The next year, Xuan was accused of throwing a brick at a tenant in Venice Beach, according to a police report.
An LAPD spokesman said detectives referred the case to the L.A. City attorney’s office, which declined to prosecute. An email to the renter seeking comment was not returned.

In May 2022, Xuan faced similar allegations in a civil lawsuit. Alejandro Diaz, whom Xuan hired as an eviction manager for his real estate firm, accused Xuan of trying to break down a tenant’s door in Apple Valley and using a Taser to shock another renter’s dog, according to the civil suit. When Diaz challenged what he called Xuan’s “illegal eviction practices,” Xuan allegedly threw rocks at him and tried to punch him, the suit alleged.
The case was settled in 2025. In a counter claim, Xuan accused Diaz of being drunk at work and trying to strangle him. Diaz’s attorney did not respond to an email seeking comment.

The women who sued Xuan and Zhang gave birth in Georgia, Texas, Virginia, Pennsylvania and California. In the suit, they accused the couple of lying about owning the surrogacy firm and failing to disclose that they already had more than a dozen children. The suit accused Xuan of having a “sexual obsession” related to fathering children, but did not elaborate.
“The surrogacy enterprise was ... a scheme by which one man used the bodies of many women, without their informed consent, to reproduce his own bloodline on a mass scale,” the suit read.

After news of the raid on the Arcadia mansion became public last year, the women fought to prevent the children from being turned over to Xuan and Zhang, who responded in alarming fashion, according to the suit.

Stacey Raelyn King, who gave birth to a surrogate child in Virginia in July 2025, said Xuan and Zhang filed “a false report that Ms. King was attempting to ‘kidnap’ the baby” and later filed a million-dollar breach-of-contract suit against her for refusing to grant them custody in the wake of the May 2025 revelation that the family had more than 20 surrogate children.

Kayla Elliot, who gave birth to a child named Walter for the couple in March 2025, said Zhang arrived at a Texas hospital to take custody of her newborn son with “nothing for the infant, not even a diaper bag.” While Elliot was still recovering in a maternity ward the next day, Zhang demanded she buy a car seat and drive Zhang and her newborn son to the airport, according to the suit.
Majerus said none of her clients would have carried Xuan and Zhang’s children if they knew even a shred of their alleged history.
“If an independent agency had been involved, they would have found all of this information and my clients would not have been surrogates,” she said.

Win or lose, independent candidates want to meet voters in the middle

These days, Seth Haskin often puts on a puff-sleeved linen shirt under an 18th century waistcoat, breeches fastened just below the knee, long socks and buckle shoes that make a distinctive clip-clop when he walks.
The outfit is meant to remind people of the Founding Fathers and evoke their idea of limited government, which the 26-year-old supports.

Haskin's day job is managing his family's coffee shop business but this year he's been vying for another position: independent congressional representative for Southwest Florida. While campaigning, Haskin also carries an old-school bell.
"Getting their [people's] attention is the biggest battle that most candidates have," Haskin said. "But especially independent or no party candidates."

Some could dismiss Haskin's attire as a stunt, and they may write off other independent candidates the same way. Sarah Zabel, 61, an independent candidate for Idaho's western district, said that view is outdated.
"Independents used to be a curiosity or a protest or a single issue," said Zabel. "Now, with the parties having gone to such extremes, independents are the necessary relief for the American voter."

At a time when 45 percent of adults identify as political independents — a record high — and just a handful of tight races will decide control of Congress, the 173 independents running for the House this fall will test how big the political middle really is, and whether people who identify as independents will vote for one.

Despite the significant chunk of Americans identifying as independents, right now just one independent serves in the House: Kevin Kiley. The congressman whose newly redrawn California district leans Democratic, switched from Republican to independent while in Congress and continues to caucus with Republicans, reported Politico.

Some candidates said they were always independent, others said their political beliefs didn't change, but their parties did. While some are confident about winning, others said even a double-digit share of the vote will show both parties that it's time for change.

Zabel, who is running in a deep-red district in Idaho, describes herself as a "heritage Republican," or someone who used to be a Republican and adheres to conservative values. But since 2018, during the first Trump administration, she stopped feeling in line with the Republican party and the "MAGA program."
The retired Air Force major general said she didn't feel represented by either party, and she soon learned that many of her neighbors felt the same way.

"That's why I decided that I would step forward and be a candidate from the center," Zabel said. "Idaho is more Republican than Democrat, it is more conservative than not. But the extremes you see, they are a minority."
The Cook Political Report rates the district, which voted for Trump by a 45-point landslide in 2024, as solid Republican for the incumbent, Rep. Russ Fulcher.

Zabel, who noted that she would not caucus with either party if in Congress, recognizes that the Democratic nominee narrows her path to victory, but Zabel sees value "in showing Idaho and showing the country that we aren't the MAGA stronghold."

In Colorado, Shimon Blau, a lifelong independent, did not intend to run for Congress. Until Melat Kiros, 29, won the Democratic nomination for the state's 1st Congressional District, which encompasses the solidly Democratic city of Denver.

"I was deeply disturbed by the results of the primaries in which our 30-year incumbent, Diana DeGette, was beat by a member of the Democratic Socialists of America," he said. "I was offended and bothered by [Kiros'] past antisemitic rhetoric, as well as a lot of her socialist beliefs."

Kiros faced wide criticism in June for declining to describe a 2025 fatal firebombing attack on Jewish activists in Boulder, Colo., as antisemitic. Blau, the Denver-based physician, received an endorsement from The Denver Gazette on Oct. 6; it described him as the "candidate of conscience."

Kiros' upset of DeGette propelled Blau to swiftly gather the 1,500 signatures he needed to be eligible to run as an independent. Blau believes that in a city as blue as Denver, Republicans are "more of the message candidate than independents," with the latter having a real chance at winning.
"I think there's a lot of disillusionment right now with both parties," he said. "It seems like both of our traditional parties are leaning more and more towards the extremes."

Seth Haskin from Florida is also running in a district where one party has dominated for years. Trump won at least 60 percent of the vote in the past two presidential elections in Haskin's district, and local media mogul Jim Schwartzel won a tight and crowded Republican primary in August with almost 30 percent of the vote.

A "strict constitutionalist," Haskin, who previously also ran for governor of Wisconsin as a write-in candidate, said he could've seen himself in either party before the Covid-19 pandemic, before he believed that both parties had been "captured by the same industry leaders and PAC money and foreign lobbies and everything else."
Now, he's running as an independent because he thinks voters are ready for a change.

"Even if I don't win, if I can get double-digit percentage points as an independent candidate, I will get a lot of phone calls from both parties," he said. "It's going to threaten the duopoly that they have, right?"

In competitive swing districts like Iowa's 1st and states with ranked-choice voting like Alaska, independents aren't campaigning on the idea that both parties have gone too far, but that neither is delivering.
Businessman Michael Bridgford is running as an independent against Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Christina Bohannan, the Democratic nominee and former state representative.
The Cook Political Report, which long had the race as a toss-up, recently rated the district as lean Democratic.

Bridgford said people are tired of the "dysfunction" from both parties and by watching Miller-Meeks and Bohannan compete, and they believe that independents can provide the stable center that will let the government solve problems.
Running in a swing district has some advantages for independents.
"People are more independent minded. It's not gerrymandered to one side," Bridgford said. "People are more middle of the road and so there's naturally more attraction to this type of campaign."
The challenge is competing against the money that parties typically pour into a competitive district, he said.
In Alaska, even though voters have almost always picked the Republican presidential nominee, their streak of independence has allowed independents and Democratic nominees to win statewide races.

Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman who said he registered as an independent when he was 18, has decided to take his chances in Alaska's at-large congressional race, rated as a likely Republican win. Hill said, like many other Alaskans, he doesn't fit into a political box.

"People who are registered Republicans often have some progressive viewpoints and people registered as Democrats may have more conservative viewpoints as well," he said. "Alaskans just don't toe a political line with every vote."

Like other independents, Hill lauds that independents can work for their constituents without worrying about leadership in Washington. He's competing against the Republican incumbent Nick Begich, the Democratic nominee Eric Hafner and Jim McDermott, a Libertarian.
Hill, who was about 12 points behind Begich in the primary, also has an offer of support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, according to Anchorage Daily News.

Independent candidates throughout the country are running for a variety of reasons and facing challenges including fundraising and finding debate platforms with party candidates, but what unites them and keeps them going is their belief in the power of the moderate middle.

"When you talk to enough people and they're all moderate and everybody they know is moderate, but they believe everybody they don't know must be right wing," said Sarah Zabel, the independent candidate from Idaho. "You see that it's just an illusion. And we can bust that illusion."
