The line-up across the main categories includes:
- Top Apprentice: Level 2 and Level 3 learners facing practical workshop tasks set by head judge Colin Denton to test real-world mechanical, electrical, and diagnostic skills.
- Top Technician: Five finalists tackling 50-minute live diagnostic challenges covering EV platforms, modern diesels, and complex network faults.
- Top Garage: Finalists evaluated on operational excellence, customer care, and sustainable business strategy by an independent judging panel under head judge Ian Gilgrass.
Accolades will also be presented for the Service Advisor Award and the Ben Workplace Health & Wellbeing Award.

Daytime access to the live finals and technology showcases at Delphi Academy is free to trade visitors. The event will culminate that evening at the Top Awards Dinner at the DoubleTree by Hilton in Coventry, where the 2026 champions will be crowned. Tickets are available from the Top Awards website.

Returning to the finals after competing in 2025, Katie Bowes says the experience has helped build her confidence and challenge perceptions surrounding apprentices: “I had doubts in my head, but competing reassured me and proved that I can do it. People often think apprentice means sweeping floors and making tea; this shows you are capable of so much more.”

“Seeing the calibre of this year’s finalists shows just how high the bar has been raised,” said Ian Gilgrass, head judge, Top Awards. “Reaching the finals of the Top Awards is a massive achievement, because you have to step up and prove your capability.

“What makes this series so special is the community and the standard it sets. Everyone comes in nervous, but they leave better at what they do. Technicians, apprentices, and garage owners use this as a benchmark to find their weak spots, learn, and push the entire industry forward.”

“Every single finalist has proven their calibre through a demanding, multi-stage process,” said Ryan Fuller, managing director of Top Awards. “We invite the entire trade to join us at Delphi Academy on 14 November to see the standards, meet the partners, and experience what makes our aftermarket community so exceptional.”

Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is an embedding model. We turned it into a speech-to-text model: an hour of audio in about 13 seconds on a base MacBook Air, entirely on device.
Can an embedding model transcribe speech?
EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model: text, images, audio and video in one shared space. Say a word out loud and its audio lands close to the written word.
So we tried reading words straight out of that space.
- EmbeddingGemma 2's audio encoder stays exactly as it is.
- A small reader moves each short slice of audio into the model's text space.
- The closest of ~229,000 English words wins, and the slices become a transcript.
- A tiny extra model adds punctuation and capitals.
Only the reader is trained: under two hours on 8×H100, on openly licensed English speech. The base model was never trained for speech-to-text.

× real time: seconds of audio per second of processing. Rows 1–2: our tests on the same base M3 MacBook Air. Rows 3–5: FluidAudio's published benchmarks on larger, newer Macs and different audio. A rough guide, not a like-for-like ranking.
Its word error rate is about 5% right now, against 2–3% for leading speech models. We believe a better-trained reader can close that gap; that's the next iteration.
Drop in an audio file, or hold Right Option, speak and release to dictate into any app. It runs on the Mac's Neural Engine; your audio never leaves the machine.
The U.S. Air Force will buy data collected by WindBorne Systems‘ fleet of autonomous weather balloons under a new contract that could be worth nearly $50 million to the startup.

WindBorne currently has about 700 weather balloons flying around the globe, collecting atmospheric sensor readings that the company sells to customers and also feeds into its own AI weather forecasting model. WindBorne, founded in 2015 and based in Redwood City, California, is one of the first organizations to directly feed empirical data into a deep-learning weather model.

The company has worked closely with the U.S. government, particularly the National Weather Service and the U.S. Air Force and Navy, but this is the single-largest contract the company has participated in. The contract is worth up to $49 million, but the Air Force pays only as it needs data. It can place orders for specific regions at specific times. So far, it has ordered $1.7 million worth, and executives expect more orders to follow.

“This is largely a vehicle through which continued growth of the constellation can be supported, as well as some work on research and development to continue to improve the hardware and performance of the balloons,” WindBorne co-founder and CTO Andrey Sushko told TechCrunch. He added that the contract, which was awarded without competitive bidding, is “a determination by the government that for this capability of collecting global data, we were the only company able to provide it in the way that met their needs for these operations.”

WindBorne CEO John Dean told TechCrunch in August that the company had raised a $37 million Series B round to continue scaling its business. Earlier this summer, the company released the latest version of its forecasting model, WeatherMesh 6, which it says provides more accurate forecasts than the traditional model run by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which simulates the atmosphere using the laws of physics.

Since the arrival of transformer model architectures and the ECMWF’s release of a massive weather dataset a few years ago, AI weather forecasting has become one of the more productive uses of deep-learning technology. Meteorologists previously relied on expensive supercomputers running detailed equations that approximate how the atmosphere behaves. Now, end-to-end learning can ingest decades of weather data and issue predictions more quickly.

Models built by frontier labs and government agencies are proving more accurate than traditional forecasts, although it is still a jagged frontier, with both types of forecasts required to enable useful understanding of the weather. Google DeepMind’s latest weather model offers important new capabilities, and its cyclone forecasting tools are becoming increasingly central to how the U.S. government responds to hurricane season.

In August WindBorne became the first organization to send an unpowered flight system — one with no engine — to collect data in the eye of a typhoon. The company maneuvers its balloons by adjusting their altitude, bleeding air, or dropping sand carried as ballast, to send the vehicles into winds that take them where they need to go.

“That’s a pretty novel step, and the two ingredients for that are one, having good wind and weather models, and knowing how to navigate them; and two, having a large enough constellation that you have balloons in the right places,” Sushko said. “It’s one of the first times that a deep-learning model was used for actual operational decisions.”

Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.

These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.

“I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.

There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.

Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.

Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so.

If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications.

Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure.

But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.”

Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it.

Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience.

But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models.

“I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.”
Are open models riskier than closed ones?

The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic, several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude.

So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model.

There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid.

Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands.

But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them).

In fact, some experts who spoke with MIT Technology Review argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code.

Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown how this can work for closed models with its Project Glasswing initiative, which enables some trusted companies to use its most capable models for cyber defense. But plenty of other companies were left to fend for themselves.

Open models, however, can be used much more widely. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters.

Nevertheless, many experts still perceive open models as riskier than closed models. The time-tested open-source security logic doesn’t necessarily hold up when dealing with tools as powerful as today’s—and tomorrow’s—models. “Where it gets complicated is when you start taking seriously the one-off instances of particularly catastrophic incidents that might be lower probability, but if they happen would be disastrous,” says Seger. If a wildly powerful open hacking model were dropped into the world today, for example, a bad actor could devastate our technological infrastructure before anyone had a chance to shore up their defenses. An event like that could be impossible to recover from.

The risks can look even more dramatic when you consider what models might do of their own accord. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If open models did decide to misbehave, it might be difficult to detect what was happening because they are so decentralized. For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models.
Can we make open models safer—and more open?

A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks. These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground. One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models.

Most of the safety tools used for closed models, such as filters and monitoring, aren’t applicable to open models, but there are other possibilities. Some researchers are interested in trying to train models that are never exposed to training data that teaches them about bad or otherwise undesirable behavior—an open model that never learns about hacking, for example. But purging training datasets of all references to misbehavior without harming model performance remains a challenge.

Other researchers are working to build models that are resistant to retraining, so that an open model’s safety training can’t be so easily removed. The theory behind these “tamper-resistant” models makes a lot of sense: If you repeatedly try to retrain a model to be unsafe and reinforce any resistance that the model shows to that retraining, eventually you’ll get a model that’s fortified against future retraining attempts. In practice, however, no current approaches to making models tamper-resistant hold up against all tampering attacks, according to a recent preprint.

But Saad Hossain, an engineer at the AI medical imaging company Deep Breathe and the paper’s lead author, hopes that future techniques will prove more effective. “My reason for optimism is that it’s a very active area of research, and a lot of people are trying to come up with new and better methods,” he says.

If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits. Publishing the internal structures, or weights, of models might not be enough to disrupt AI-mediated concentration of power. “I think there are very genuine benefits to open source in terms of deconcentrating power, but they’re not sufficient in themselves,” Hobbs says. Open weights are a bare minimum standard for open models: Researchers can learn much more about how models work if they have access to details about their training, including the data on which they were trained, but AI companies are typically reluctant to divulge this information.

Accessibility matters for open models too. Without computer chips that can run sophisticated models, you can’t actually use the model weights, even if you have them. Those chips have become prohibitively expensive as AI companies snap up more and more of them. “Openness is a floor, not a ceiling, for what we need to do to ensure that our technological futures benefit everyone,” Widder says.

Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course. If everyone has access to advanced AI hardware and advanced models to run on it, then anyone could potentially be a hacker. But there are strategies for mitigating these risks. Many experts advocate for some version of staged release, in which models start their life closed and gradually become more and more freely accessible as their safety is assured.

Figuring out exactly how to implement such strategies will require striking a careful balance between the risks and benefits of open models. But if open models are a necessary element of a positive AI future, as some experts believe, that effort will be well worth it.

Calabasas would be ripe territory for a certain kind of writer. The iconography is all there — the freeways and gas stations, the parched red hills teeming with rattlesnakes. You could easily imagine them taking notes, out there in the middle of nowhere but so close to somewhere, trying to discern how this particular hub of car dealerships and office parks became the new center of popular culture.

Kanye West saw it first (or maybe second, after Kris Jenner). A suburb of a suburb, Calabasas, population 22,000, with no heritage or identity (except that most of the houses were built in the 1980s and seem to be over 9,000 square feet), a place he could mold and shape and brand to his image. When Kim and Kanye began their $40 million renovation of a $20 million mansion, Kanye declared (in the title of an unreleased album he recorded with Drake), Calabasas Is the New Abu Dhabi, words which appeared on billboards in L.A. And there is something about its sudden rise that feels like other desert cities — Las Vegas or Dubai — that seemingly materialized overnight through the sheer power of money and ambition.

Kanye launched Adidas Calabasas, a collection of sweats and sneakers emblazoned with the town’s name, in March 2017, and as if on cue, Dior chose to stage its 2018 Cruise runway show in the nearby hills. Shortly after, Kanye rolled out his Yeezy Season 6 campaign, featuring faux paparazzi images of Kim running errands around town. They cut out the fashion press entirely, releasing the images via Kim’s social media. The campaign felt mundane, futuristic, dystopian, and yet somehow one of the more realistic portrayals of fashion in the modern era. Kim was photographed making a series of “runs” to 7-Eleven, McDonald’s, and a gas station, clad in a neutral palette of leggings, sports bras, and sweatpants. She was always on the move, coming or going, captured in the liminal space of the parking lot, the privacy and comfort of her ghost- gray Maybach never more than a few steps away. Styled by Carine Roitfeld, the images were testament to the power of Kim and Kanye’s celebrity at the peak of their creative partnership, creating an entirely new visual language for Kim and for Calabasas. It was a full-circle moment, one that began 20 years earlier with 16-year-old Kim working at Body, then folding clothes with her sisters at their boutique, Dash — just a family of shopgirls from the Valley.

When Kim and Kanye officially started dating in the spring of 2012, after they’d been circling each other for nearly ten years, Kim was still mostly reality-show famous — the face of Skechers shoes; that is, until she was dropped after her divorce from Kris Humphries, cut from the brand’s 2012 Super Bowl ads, and replaced by a French bulldog. She was hawking QuickTrim diet pills — the company settled a class-action lawsuit that year for $5 million. In 2012, Kim released her fourth and fifth fragrances; the latter, called Glam, was sold through Debenhams, the now-defunct Macy’s of Great Britain. Endorsement-wise, she had risen no higher than being the face of Midori, the (neon green, melon flavored) liqueur that hadn’t been popular since the 1980s. Her two-year contract included television and magazine ads and awkward public appearances, which required her to wear all green. The ad campaign’s tagline: “Midori is easy.”

Kanye, on the other hand, was the ultimate cultural alchemist — at the apogee of contemporary multidisciplinary success. In 2011, he headlined Coachella (in a blouse from Celine); he made his official debut as a designer, premiering his DW by Kanye West collection during Paris Fashion Week; and he commissioned Givenchy’s creative director, Riccardo Tisci, to design the cover art for Watch the Throne, the album he made with Jay-Z. On what would become the highest-grossing hip-hop tour of all time, Kanye was frequently spotted wearing the not-yet-available Nike Air Yeezy II sneakers, which became a massive hit and contributed to his rising status in the fashion world.

From his perch as the arbiter of cool, Kanye was captivated by Kim. “I realize that he loves, like, a project, right?” she told me. “I think he really fell in love with the idea of me, and the project behind it all. He loves things that maybe aren’t cool and ‘I’m going to make them cool.’ Whether it’s, like, ‘I’m going to stop rapping and do a whole singing album, like 808s.’ And everyone’s like, ‘How could you not rap? It’s blasphemy!’ And then it’s the best album. I think he’s like, ‘Let me be with a reality star. No one respects it. I’m going to show you how cool it is.’ He changed my life. He absolutely changed my life.” She leveled me with a look that I knew well. By then, we had spent seven years in each other’s company. I first met her in 2019 and started interviewing her about her life two years later. “Listen,” she said. Pause. “It’s a huge part of my story.”

The decade that passed between Kim Kardashian’s graduation from Marymount High School in 1998 and the premiere of Keeping Up With the Kardashians in 2007 represents the in-between, if not lost years for Kim and her family, an era spent exiled in the anonymous suburbs of the San Fernando Valley. While the Kardashian reality show would be presented as an aspirational, low-stakes sitcom, the years that preceded it have the darker cinematic feel of one of Paul Thomas Anderson’s melodramatic “Valley” films, a sprawling epic about a fractured family of strivers hustling their way back from the margins of the entertainment industry.

The period plays like a montage — late in the second act — in which time condenses, character develops, and story lines intersect: Robert Kardashian licking his wounds in the wake of the O.J. trial; Kris starting a new family with Caitlyn Jenner, then named Bruce, in Hidden Hills, planting the seeds of her television empire; and Kim, officially a Valley girl, living in Encino with her father, working at a boutique on Ventura Boulevard and attending community college — dabbling in eBay and ecstasy — a long way from fame and fortune. “I just remember we were in an archaeology class,” she told me, “and I knew I didn’t want to be an archaeologist.”

When I pressed Kim on whether this period ever felt directionless, she responded, as usual, with a compulsory positive spin: “That time in my life was so, so much fun. And so special. It was, like, the normal years, the calm before the storm. I was just experimenting and finding myself.” Robert was also beginning to find himself again. He had met a widowed former beauty queen named Jan Ashley, and after dating for six months the couple was married on November 25, 1998. The marriage would be short-lived, lasting all of one month, but the fallout would alter the direction of Kim’s life. As she put it to me one day, “As soon as they got married, she wanted all the kids out of the house. She’s like, ‘Robert, get her an apartment.’ So I was out.” Kim had just turned 18.

Kris, of course, dropped everything and took Kim to Bed Bath & Beyond to set her up at a new place. “And then I found out where she was living: Northridge,” she wrote ominously in her memoir, Kris Jenner … and All Things Kardashian. Northridge is an unglamorous neighborhood (even for the Valley) famous for being the epicenter of the 1994 earthquake. “Why would you want to live in Northridge?” Kris asked. “Oh, I just like it over there,” Kim answered with one of the least convincing lies imaginable (no one “just likes it over there” in Northridge). And then things got weirder, Kris wrote: “Another day, she pulled up to my house out of the blue in a brand-new Jaguar. How did she buy herself a brand-new car, and a Jaguar no less, without my help?’”

Damon Thomas first laid eyes on Kim when she was 13 years old at Michael Jackson’s Neverland Ranch, where TJ Jackson, whom she was dating at the time, once threw her a birthday party. Thomas, 23, had already made a name for himself by 1992 — for getting his jaw broken by Dr. Dre, who was sentenced to 90 days in jail for the assault — and in the years that followed became a legitimate songwriter and producer, working with the likes of Babyface, Tupac, and Justin Timberlake. Kim remembers, “I first met [Damon] through TJ and all those people in the music business. But then he was a customer at Body, so I really met him there.”

The apartment in Northridge was little more than a front to fool her parents. Still 18, Kim almost immediately moved into Damon’s enormous home, which came complete with a recording studio, a Ferrari in the driveway, and a 4-year-old child from a previous relationship. Kim’s friends from Marymount were confused. As Simone Harouche remembers, “We were all very young, and we were going out all the time and partying, and all of a sudden … she was staying home and watching the daughter. She got really domestic really fast.”

Even more confusing was that on January 22, 2000, Kim married Damon at the Little White Chapel in Las Vegas. “Nobody knew!” Kourtney told me. When I asked her if she thought marrying Damon was out of character for Kim, she posited a theory: “This could be a reach, but when I went away to college, I feel like maybe Kim felt like she wanted her own thing — something for her. Like, where’s her place? What does she do with her life? So she fell into this unhealthy relationship.” Kim’s friend Zoe Winkler reminded me that Kim is the daughter of Kris, a woman who couldn’t wait to get busy having six children. “Kim’s always been in serious relationships,” Winkler said. “She wanted to have a family and be a mom. And I think there was a part of her that maybe got into the fairy tale of it all. And you have to remember who Damon was at the time. We were like, ‘Oh, he’s a music producer.’ I think we thought he was this older cool guy, and then we realized he wasn’t.”

Kim and Damon were living like Y2K royalty: “He would show up in the Ferrari, and all my friends thought he was the coolest guy. ‘Come on, girls, let’s all go to this Justin Timberlake session.’ We went skydiving with Damon and Justin. ‘Let’s go to Britney’s studio.’ And I’m the biggest Britney fan. It was that vibe,” Kim told me. The couple’s sprawling house was filled with whatever musicians Thomas was recording with at the moment. Kim remembered, “He had these backup singers who would record with him all the time — from the South — and they would stay with him, and they would teach me how to cook and we would make sweet potatoes and mac and cheese and fried chicken. The first time I ever tried to make Damon some chicken, it wasn’t even fully cooked. And these backup singers were like, ‘Oh, no, girl, you need to learn how to make chicken!’”

Considering the court documents from Kim and Damon’s 2003 divorce filing, Kim’s cooking lessons take on a darker tone. The declarations to the court, which are public documents,are unadjudicated allegations, including many that were contested. Though these were sworn affidavits, they were never presented in court with evidence or witnesses because it didn’t go to trial. However, the hundreds of pages of declarations about money — they owed $466,030 in unpaid taxes and penalties — and physical abuse paint a disturbing picture.

In the filings, Kim — described simply as a “19-year-old salesgirl with a high school education” — details the control Damon exerted over her life: “In March 2000, Damon told me to quit my job. He said that he did not want me to have contact with my old boyfriends who would be able to reach me at the clothing store. He said that he wanted to know where I was at all times. Therefore, I quit my job … He often arrived home at 4:30 a.m. and expected me to prepare a meal for him at that hour … Damon told me not to leave the house unless I first told him when and where I was going. Sometimes he would not allow me to leave … When Damon told me that he was unhappy about my going to college and wanted me to stop attending classes, I quit … He told me that my mother and sister were evil and had bad intentions towards me.”

And then, in one of the most shocking details: “My father called me outraged,” Kim alleged in court documents, “to tell me that Damon had brought nude pictures of my sister to his office, showed him the photos and said, ‘Your daughters are whores and I have the pictures to prove it.’ He then made packages and sent the pictures gift-wrapped to my best friend’s place of employment in Encino to scare us.”

At the time, Kim found a confidante in Brandy Norwood, whose younger brother, Ray J, would become Kim’s boyfriend and sex-tape co-star. (Kanye first met Kim while recording a song with Brandy.) Thomas had played piano and keyboards on her first album, in 1994, contributing songs and production. Brandy and Kim were about the same age. The two women became close, likely drawn together by the fact that they were often the youngest people in the room. “I opened up about my life to her,” said Kim, “and I think she saw that I was in a really unhappy situation. She was like my sister. ‘Why are you wasting your days? You have one life. This isn’t what your life should be like.’ And I was like, ‘You know what? You’re right.’” It would take Kim multiple attempts to extricate herself from her relationship with Damon, but on April 13, 2003, she snuck into the house while he was gone, packed as many of her belongings as she could fit in her Mercedes, and left for good.

One afternoon in March 2022, Kim and I were hanging out at her offices, and I said to her that the only period of the show when she seemed a little lost was around her 30th birthday. She talked about it so much during season five that Kourtney finally said to the camera, “Kim thinks by the time the clock strikes midnight on her 30th birthday, she’s gonna turn into a little old troll in a cave.” Kim agreed with my assessment that she was low-key depressed and said, “That’s why I married Kris Humphries. Out of, Oh my God, holy shit, I’m not married. Why are all my friends married? Why am I not married? And I think I just pushed myself into that, because I was like, This is where you’re supposed to be in this phase of your life.”

Kim and Kris Humphries were a mismatch from the start: He is six-foot-nine and she is five-two. He was crude and immature, treating Kim like a rag doll, tripping her, or throwing her into various bodies of water in a way that made her family, not to mention the viewers, uncomfortable. Like Robert Kardashian, Humphries wanted a traditional marriage and could not fathom a world where his wife would want anything more than to stay at home and have his babies. He was controlling financially, despite Kim having her own money. After insisting they move back to his home state of Minnesota, he said to her, “By the time you have kids … no one will probably care about you, let’s be honest.” The perfect metaphor for Kim’s feelings of suffocation was finding herself surrounded by her fiancé’s size 17 shoes, which were “lined up around my whole room. I literally got claustrophobic.”

Kim’s sex tape, which had come out eight years earlier, and the Kris Humphries wedding are inextricably linked as instances in which Kim felt pressured — by Ray J; by producers of the show — to make her most intimate moments public and monetize them. Both would be viewed as cash grabs, which is the root cause of much of the “Kim hate” and the narrative of unearned success that has dogged her throughout her career. In our conversations, she has referred to these two events separately as the biggest mistakes (and regrets) of her life. When I asked her when she knew her marriage to Humphries was over, she said, “I knew it before we were married in my soul. I just thought, Well, it’s cold feet. But your gut, your soul, is always right. And then I thought, Well, they’re filming for a show, and if I bail now, they’re going to call me ‘the runaway bride’ and it will be an even bigger thing. But I should have just not gotten married.”

But Farnaz Farjam, one of the show’s long-time producers, told me, “Kim didn’t have the confidence to back out.” Farjam suggested that surviving the backlash from the Humphries wedding fiasco, combined with meeting Kanye in the midst of the fallout, was the very thing that helped her grow an ever-thicker skin. “In early seasons,” said Farjam, “Kim was this hopeless romantic. She would get shy; she could get vulnerable; she wore her emotions on her sleeve. She liked being sexy and having all that attention, but she wasn’t confident. I think she had to go through some hardships — recognizing that it’s not the end of the world — to build that up.”

Kim told me that it was her grandmother, MJ, who finally got through to her and gave her some perspective. “My grandmom was like, ‘Listen. My parents saved up all their money so I could have a big wedding because I thought I was in love. About a month or two in, I realized I’d made a terrible decision and I was so embarrassed. It was in the town paper! I just wasted everyone’s time and money and I was mortified. I knew I had to get a divorce, and I just did it. I thought my parents would never speak to me again.’” Kim laughed. “And she said to me, ‘You have to be happy. You have to be.’” And although MJ hadn’t wasted $10 million getting married in front of 10 million people, the sentiment was somehow the same. Like her grandmother and her mother before her, Kim blew up the traditional fairy tale — literally, Kim’s Fairytale Wedding — for something else, something unknown.

Not long after the split, Kim and Kanye were on the phone. She was at a low point; he was trying to cheer her up: “Why don’t you fly to Paris and come to my show?” Kim got on a plane, sat in the front row at Kanye’s fashion debut, and that, she said, “is when we really got together.” She once said that Kanye “jokes that he put on this whole fashion show just to get a date with me.” The show was attended by Anna Wintour and every major fashion critic, not to mention several designers, including Azzedine Alaïa, who did not come to a fashion show for just anybody; his presence in the front row signaled that fashion was, at the very least, prepared to take Kanye seriously.

That night, Kim stayed with Kanye in his apartment in Paris; they were up all night. “And from that point on, I was like, Oh! Okay!” On a KUWTK anniversary special, she says, “I swear from the moment I landed, I fell madly in love with him, and I thought, Oh my God, why didn’t I do this sooner? Like, this is what real life is like — love and fun and real support.” Kim being Kim, she was comforted by the idea that she “had to go through” the debacle of marrying a man she didn’t love on television “to get there.” Kanye, she once said to me, “was so much fun. He was so wild. But I think I was probably a bit infatuated.

“And then seven months into dating Kanye, I got pregnant,” she said. “We hadn’t even had a first real fight until I was pregnant.” Needless to say, this was not planned. Kim had stopped taking birth control after going to a fertility clinic with Khloé, who was trying to conceive with basketball player Lamar Odom at the time. “And I was like, ‘Don’t worry, I’ll get all my blood tests with you so it won’t be scary.’ And we did it together. And then the results came back: ‘Khloé, you’re fine. But Kim? You have some problems.’” The fertility experts explained to her that she had very few eggs left, so she should stop taking the Pill to clean out her system, as getting pregnant was going to be difficult for her. “I never had a pregnancy scare or anything in my life,” Kim told me, “so I just went to Miami without birth control and got pregnant that first month. I was like, Fuck. I literally thought my life was over.”

When she called Kanye to tell him, she was hysterical. “I was crying so hard I couldn’t get it out. He thought a family member of mine had died. I was hhh-ahh, hhh-ahh, hhh-ahhh … He was like, ‘What’s happening?’ And I was just like, ‘Oh my God, I’m pregnant.’ It came so out of left field for me; I was shocked. I don’t know why I was so shocked. Come on. But when the doctors tell you, ‘I don’t think you’ll ever get pregnant, you have the uterus of a 50-year-old, you’re going to have to do all this IVF.’” Even Kim’s gynecologist — who had been Kris’s doctor and who delivered Kim — said to her, “Hey, I think this was a fluke.” Kim realized the decision of whether to keep the child was one she needed to make alone and told Kanye, “I need a week. I don’t want to talk to anyone. I don’t want to talk to you. I need some time to think.” And that’s what she did. At the end of the week, she’d made up her mind. “Okay, let’s move forward and let’s have a baby.”

I asked Kim about those early days of dating Kanye and the way he completely changed her look. “Fairly new into the relationship,” she said, “Kanye was like, ‘Can I give you a fashion makeover?’ and I didn’t even know what that meant. But I was open: ‘Sure! Dress me up!’ A team of stylists came in. I was in my first house on Abington, and I thought I had the best shoes — I thought I had it all. He put me in this black Givenchy leather dress and a pair of Tom Ford snakeskin shoes and took me to a Lakers game. I came home and there were shoes piled up almost to the ceiling that had been taken out of my closet, and I only had two pairs left — that Kanye’s team kept. I almost started to cry. I spent years collecting them! And then there were racks and racks of new clothes, designers I’d never heard of before, like Lanvin.”

Though among her friends, Kim was considered to have the best taste, her early-aughts style tended more toward Kitson — or sexy, like the Hervé Léger bandage dress. “I just didn’t know anything about high fashion. There were all these fashion books piled up. It was time to get to work and learn.” She was now enrolled in Kanye School. And if there is one thing Kim has emphasized more than any other about what she got from Ye, even long after their divorce, it is this: “He gave me so much confidence.”

In 2012, Kanye had tried, unsuccessfully, to procure for his new girlfriend an invitation to the Met Gala. I was in meetings at the 4 Times Square offices of Vogue when Anna Wintour’s eyes rolled nearly all the way up into the back of her head at the mere mention of the Kardashians. She refused to let Kim anywhere near the Met Ball. The following year, though, Kanye performed at the gala, and while Kim was not officially invited, Anna granted her plus-one status. Kim walked the red carpet that night, eight months pregnant in a skintight Givenchy floral-print dress with matching gloves and shoes — “upholstered like a sofa,” as one critic pointed out. She caused a sensation, generating more press hits and social-media attention than anyone in the Met Gala’s history.

While the laypeople of social media saw the dress as a faux pas — another opportunity to mock Kim — many fashion people were smitten with the bravery of pulling off something so risky: a look that amounted to a modern, perverse take on a dowdy ensemble Queen Elizabeth might have worn. Indeed, Carine Roitfeld — the ne plus ultra of fashion people — approached Kim that very night and asked if she would fly to Paris the next week to be photographed by Karl Lagerfeld, creative director of Chanel, for the cover of CR Fashion Book, Carine’s fashion magazine. And let’s not be coy: People like Carine and Anna were also responding to the fact that Kim’s massive social-media following seemed to grow exponentially by the minute. There was symbiosis: Fashion and media were evolving at light speed; they needed Kim as much as she needed them. As Kim’s friend Tracy Romulus pointed out, “The fashion world didn’t accept her until she went to the Met Ball with him. Kanye called Wintour, that was all him, because he saw the version of her that we see. He believed in her. He saw the beauty, he saw the elegance … where he was just, like, ‘No. She’s not just a reality-TV star. She’s beautiful, she’s amazing, she’s relevant; every designer should be dressing her.’ He fought for Kim’s place there.”

Kim gave birth to her first child, North West, on June 15, 2013, after eight difficult months of pregnancy. “I had a rough time from the start and a few scares,” she told me. “I thought I miscarried. I was bleeding a lot. At about six months, I thought I was going into labor, and then I ended up giving birth about five and a half weeks early.” It was a traumatic delivery. Kim had preeclampsia and placenta accreta, which makes for a really painful post-birth experience. “I think when you’re in it, you just kind of roll with it,” Kim said, putting her usual spin on life’s most difficult moments. “And, you know, it was obviously the best thing I ever did.”

The couple got married in May 2014 and every over-the-top detail was curated by Kanye, including multiple private jets to take 200 guests from their rehearsal dinner at the Palace of Versailles to their wedding venue in a 16th-century fort in Florence. Meanwhile, Kanye had been lobbying Wintour for months to convince her that his girlfriend deserved a Vogue cover, telling her over lunch at the Beverly Hills Hotel that Kim was a bigger fashion influence than First Lady Michelle Obama. After the wedding, they finally appeared on the cover of Vogue together, with the headline “#WORLDSMOSTTALKEDABOUTCOUPLE.” Kim wore her custom Givenchy wedding dress in a multipage Annie Leibovitz spread that outraged the fashion world (myself included, as the cover story I’d been working on for months got bumped) and that Anna has had to defend ever since.

The same year, Kim would return to the Valley, buying the house in Hidden Hills on Long Valley Road that was built on Lisa Marie Presley’s former property. The real-estate listing called it a “French Country pièce de résistance” with “groin vaulted” ceilings, eight fireplaces, two swimming pools, and a vineyard. Kris had walked by the suburban colossus many times and encouraged Kim and Kanye to go take a look at it, even leaving a flyer with pictures of the house on their bed. Meanwhile, people were astonished that Kanye agreed to live in a McMansion five minutes from his mother-in-law. When Kim took Kanye to see it, “He said, ‘I like it. It’s okay,’” said Kim. “In anyone else’s world, that means ‘I love it.’” (“That’s my specialty,” Kanye once said, “not liking stuff.”) Kanye said he would only agree to buying the house if they hired Sandy Gallin to redesign it.

Gallin had been the manager of superstars like Michael Jackson, Cher, and Barbra Streisand. But he had a surprising second act as an interior designer to the Hollywood elite. When asked once where he took his inspiration, he mentioned the staircase at Tara in Gone With the Wind and the palatial estates on Dynasty — a far cry from minimalism, to say nothing of Kanye’s preference for the primal rawness of primitive futurism. It was left to Kim to convince Sandy to reimagine their faux French Normandy–ish McMansion on Long Valley Road. “So my mom and I flew to the Hamptons to talk him into it,” Kim told me. “And Sandy said, ‘I will only do your home if you give me the keys and don’t come back until I’m done. You can’t have any input.’” I can’t believe anyone thought this was a good idea. “Kanye and I walked in when he was done and Kanye walked right out. He said, ‘I won’t come back until it’s fully redone.’ And then he said, ‘I’m going to fly to Belgium to see Axel Vervoordt and get him to do the house.’ And he did. And he came back with Axel. And we moved out again and moved back in with my mother.”

It is quite a leap from the Sandy Gallin aesthetic to the somber, colorless world of Axel Vervoordt, but that is how quickly Kanye’s tastes were evolving during those peak creative years. Testing “the limits of remodeling,” as New Yorker writer Ian Parker put it, they ripped out millions of dollars’ worth of sumptuousness and fell into collaboration with Vervoordt to create what Kanye himself described as a “futuristic Belgian monastery.” In a cover story in Architectural Digest, Vervoordt said, “Kanye and Kim wanted something totally new. We didn’t talk about decoration but a kind of philosophy about how we live now and how we will live in the future. We changed the house by purifying it, and we kept pushing to make it purer and purer.” In December 2017, three and a half years and two renovations later, they finally moved in. Kanye’s makeover was complete. And as Kim said, “It worked.”

Four years after they moved into the house, on February 19, 2021, Kim filed for divorce. There had been bumpy moments throughout their marriage, but the wheels finally came off in 2020. Kanye caught a severe case of COVID-19 at the outset of the pandemic in February. Kim nursed him through it while sleeping in her kids’ bedrooms for weeks. When he recovered, he took off, holing up at his ranch in Cody, Wyoming, with friends and employees for months. (“I got him out of my bed!” she once joked with me. “He never came back!”) On July 4, Kanye, who had never once bothered to vote, announced on Twitter that he was running for president — news to Kim, whose “like” of his tweet was her only public comment. The campaign lasted only 11 days but created a ruinous wake. During his one and only rally in Charleston, South Carolina, he melted down in front of the cameras, crying over the fact that he’d wanted Kim to have an abortion when she was pregnant with North. It was an unimaginable breach of Kim’s privacy — what tiny shred remained.

Then came an episode of KUWTK on October 28, 2020, Caitlyn’s birthday. “The relationship with Caitlyn and the rest of the family had been dinged,” said Farjam, “and everybody is trying to come back together and be supportive. And Kanye came to Caitlyn’s house with Kim, and he just started ripping into Kris and the family and questioning them about not voting for him. He just made it all about himself. That whole 30-minute battle was very telling, but we had to edit it out.” In the final episode, just one clip from that day made it onto the show: Kim sitting in a room with Kourtney, Kendall, and Kylie, bawling. “I just honestly can’t do this anymore,” she says in the segment. “I feel like a fucking failure and it’s, like, a third fucking marriage … Yeah, I feel like a fucking loser.” She talked about feeling “stuck,” but she was also resolute: She refused to relocate to Wyoming. Her home, her life, was in Hidden Hills with her children and family. “He should have a wife that supports his every move and travels with him and does everything I can’t.”

Kim chose her family, but she also chose herself. She had filed for divorce just a few months shy of their seventh wedding anniversary, citing “irreconcilable differences.” She requested joint physical and legal custody of their four children, a distinction that suggested that Kim, ever the optimist, was looking forward to one day amicably co-parenting with Kanye, just like her mother and father had done and just as her sisters were doing with their exes. And from there, Kim began her long ascent out of the murk of the Kanye years. Two months after she filed for divorce, she was included on the Forbes “World’s Billionaires List” for the first time — her company, Skims, was by then valued at nearly $4 billion. It was the ultimate shopgirl flex after a divorce: becoming a billionaire retailer in her own right, indeed surpassing Kanye’s success with Yeezy.
