In 1990, then–District of Columbia mayor Marion Barry was the target of a D.C. Metropolitan Police Department and FBI sting operation in which he was lured to a hotel room by an ex-girlfriend, Rasheeda Moore, and recorded smoking crack cocaine. As a result, Barry served six months in prison, and though he was later reelected as mayor, his drug use left an irremediable stain on his reputation and raised larger questions about misgovernance and corruption. In her Guggenheim exhibition, “Father Country I Do Love You,” American artist Taryn Simon, 51, comes at this historical event — and others — from an oblique angle, focusing not on the man at the foreground of the controversy but on those operating behind the scenes, shaping world history while staying out of view. This is a novelistic body of work from the perspective of a federal agent telling the story of his professional life in a series of fact-filled vignettes that are at once enigmatic and revealing of the inner workings of the U.S. government as well as the far-reaching consequences of individual actions. It takes up the entirety of the Guggenheim’s rotunda and is the first monographic photography exhibition to do so, suggesting — along with it being timed to the 250th anniversary of the United States — that the museum has chosen Simon to present work of historical significance at an unprecedented scale.

Drawn from nearly a decade’s worth of Simon’s conversations with an actual but anonymized retired FBI agent, these encyclopedic artworks appear to revel in the research that underpins them. Simon takes a hyperreferential and maximalist approach to the transmission of history. At times, the photographs have the glossy, didactic quality of the figures in a textbook. Simon refers to the conversational biographical sketches that accompany her images as “chapters,” and the one concerned with Barry is titled A squad agent informed me I’d be babysitting. In this scene, the agent describes being tasked with looking after Moore’s young children in a Hilton hotel room while she went out on her covert mission. The text concludes with the line “People said the mom and kids would probably go into witness protection because of all the death threats.” It’s a characteristic entry in that it relays, in an offhand way, the precarity and danger the agent came close to, recounted with the unflappability and detachment of a seasoned professional whose position kept him safe. The entry is paired with a suite of portraits of a number of Black men and women wearing MooreWraps, versatile multi-wear garments created by Moore’s sister with proceeds donated to victims of domestic violence and incarceration. Simon took the campy photographs in the same Hilton hotel where Moore’s children awaited their mother, and the images make up what the wall text calls a MooreWrap cruise-collection look book.

This sort of puzzling connection between text and image is repeated throughout the exhibition. Whether you take pleasure in learning about these factoids depends on your appetite for esoteric trivia. In our conspiratorial age, the idea that there are fine, obscure relationships between seemingly disparate things is a thought seductive on the surface but oftentimes shallow underneath. A more charitable way to think about these digressions is to see them as akin to the tangents in a novel, in which minor details accumulate in service of immersing the reader in a narrative that will prove cohesive in the end. The 42 intricate episodes lining the walls of the Guggenheim’s rotunda follow the iconic winding path of the museum’s white spiral — a path not unlike the circuitous course of a life or a nation’s history. But by the end, it’s difficult to know what the narrative amounts to, apart from an accrual of memories that gestures at the sociohistorical only to flesh out the self-mythology of the show’s government-worker protagonist, a nationalistic Everyman whose journey we follow through more than five decades.

The title of the show, “Father Country I Do Love You,” points to the source of the exhibition’s pathos: a filial devotion best expressed by the extensive and impressive research that went into its creation. Each photograph’s staging is meticulous, and there is an almost exhaustive attempt to interweave the agent’s narratives with the visual language of each image. No symbol is wasted, and no connection feels too tenuous to pursue. When we learn that the protagonist of the exhibition is a stand-in for Simon’s father, who worked for the U.S. government and was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s in 2020, this attentiveness feels all the more resonant, reading like an attempt to salvage the lost or obscure details of the biography of a parent losing their memory. The exhibition’s wall text is set against a wood-paneled backdrop meant to conjure a replica of the Bangkok living room of an intelligence officer who once worked with her father. The warm faux teak making up the room evokes a copy of a copy, and Simon describes building out this childhood living room alongside her father with fondness, as though it was a formative early experience of art-making. She presents it as a task that doesn’t only display a father bringing his global professional context down to the understanding of his child but demonstrates the work of world-making Simon would go on to pursue.

Later in the text, Simon mentions that her father ate his Life Cereal each morning with Diet Coke in lieu of milk, which is to say he did not adhere to convention, and that despite the gravity of his work, he maintained a childlike and whimsical side. That quality is also evident in Simon’s use of bright lighting, stately primary colors that bring to mind early life to mind, and the show’s invocation of a world teeming with curiosities, such as a sun-soaked family film shot on Super 8. Quoting her father, Simon writes, “America … was the best story on earth, if you could find someone to tell it.” It’s clear that Simon luxuriates in the process of storytelling from an offbeat vantage, but the instability of genre and the kind of story she is telling is never quite resolved.

The tension between the artist’s documentarian and novelistic impulses is one viewers come up against repeatedly throughout the exhibition. It’s a series of true stories that use the emotional manipulations of fiction to engage an audience, and because we know the project is at least partly — if not primarily — the excavation of buried family history, the viewer is placed in the role Simon occupies, that of the introspective child speculating about the lionized but imperfect father. In a way, that makes this show an apt allegory for the propagandized American citizen, uninformed, hopeful in spite of themselves, eager to preserve their innocence and yet slowly learning how the sausage is made.

The narrative tone of certain chapters is conspiratorial while demystifying state secrets as if guiding an audience through insider baseball. In How democracy started, we learn of the FBI’s covert presence in Greece and the bureau’s response to the Greek Marxist-Leninist group 17N, who used lethal violence to advance their anti-imperialist goals. The text reads, “I was in Athens to make sure they knew that in America, that gets you prison for life. Punishment is an important part of preserving democracy.” In the final paragraph of this chapter, the agent describes going on a tour of ruins in the country designed to teach tourists about the democracy’s origins. “Made me feel pretty motivated,” he says in closing.

The coupling of violence with law and order is ever present in the agent’s recollections, but tonally, the show feels light. Simon comes across as less of a polemicist and more of a stylist. There is something instructive in the agent concluding a diatribe on quelling revolutionary violence with a note about feeling inspired. This chapter is accompanied by somewhat twee images of an owl doll, a bottle of designer perfume, a high heel, and a golden microphone positioned against various ancient Greek ruins, including the Parthenon and the Monument of the Eponymous Heroes. The photographs represent the props tour guides use with visitors at these landmarks. One interpretation of the image-text pairing is that these epic historical sites are now places of leisure for potentially self-infantilized audiences who are as dislocated from the past as they are from the democratic ideals these locations represent. But the critiques throughout are issued mildly, and I cannot imagine anyone coming away feeling very wounded by this exhibition.

“Father Country I Do Love You” benefits from opening during America’s semiquincentennial, as the occasion suggests a broader appeal than this very subtle, conceptual body of work might otherwise offer even the most savvy and curious museumgoers. Simon is an artist’s artist, and arguably a writer’s writer, drawn to minutiae even as she demonstrates ambition in terms of theme and scope. Her interest seems to be the whole world, or at least the way her nation’s tentacles spread into it. Throughout her career, Simon has deftly taken on fraught historical or political baggage but always in a way that prioritizes the emotional core of the material. That’s precisely what she did in The Innocents (2000–2003), which is comprises portraits of the wrongfully convicted taken at the charged sites of misidentification or arrest. It’s a prescient project in that it anticipates how sophisticated and ubiquitous surveillance technologies would go on to become in our age of Flock cameras and Meta glasses. Almost a decade later, in the impressive An Occupation of Loss (2016), Simon recruited professional mourners to reenact their bereavement customs in a sonic performance. This was the result of seven years of research conducted with mourners and anthropologists. As part of orchestrating this project, Simon was also involved in securing visas for the various international performers, encountering in the process the uneven access to travel for cultural workers across classes, nationalities, and milieus. This work evidences both a moral courage and brash authority on Simon’s part and speaks to the deep ethical complexity of her concerns and strategies as an artist. Rather than circumventing the confines placed on herself and her subjects by bureaucracy or borders, she integrates these limitations into the work itself.

In “Father Country I Do Love You,” she attempts to transcend yet more constraints, creating a mammoth body of work that is the first of its kind in this iconic Manhattan institution. There are over 1,000 objects in the exhibition. It is a massive undertaking, and one stands in awe at how Simon managed to conduct so much painstaking archival work while producing this volume of images, videos, and installations that seem to come from a wholly original place that is neither obvious nor derivative. You get the sense that the demands Simon placed on herself as an artist are demands she is content to share with her viewers, trusting them with the material’s complexity. It’s an exhausting show to get through, and like a piece of experimental fiction, part of its reward is piecing together something formally innovative, of making sense of a text that subverts expectations. On one hand, it is a relief to see an exhibition explicitly about imperialism, patriotism, machismo, and memory that is not didactic or anxious about its “aboutness.”

On the other hand, I did occasionally long for Simon to give us a moment of reprieve and offer something simple and straightforward. Mercifully, at the top of the spiral, she does. A video of Simon’s father tapping an assortment of Kodachrome slides with his hand is projected on a large screen. The slides feature images of the far-flung destinations he traveled to. The vestiges of his fading memory flash by with a haunting plainness, the melancholy of all this Americana and the sadness of a mind ravaged by time strike the viewer plainly at the end of this maximalist piece of life-writing. But it is a somewhat deflated conclusion for an exhibition that insists so much upon chronology and duration, that claims a considerable amount of time and attention from its viewers, only to deposit them in the same terrain where they began and withhold a conclusion that might meet the lofty narrative promises made.

At the apex of the rotunda, I thought of a line from the opening of Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man: “Beware of those who speak of the spiral of history; they are preparing a boomerang.” Simon’s historic exhibition takes place in a bright architectural spiral that suggests the possibility of never-ending upward motion, but it does not seem able to move beyond its premise or starting point, flinging its viewers back into the past and stagnating there. “Father Country I Do Love You‘“s inertia may very well be a critique of America’s relationship to its history. Still, it’s unclear whether Simon has any desire to pull herself away from the rich, granular details she has stockpiled and commit to something as overarching and final as a criticism of the nation that fascinates her — though is that what art is even for?

The Justice Department is virtually certain to try to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, a former Trump White House aide and a key January 6 witness. And if Donald Trump’s prosecutors do attempt to abuse the legal process to pursue this particular political vendetta — one of many in this DoJ’s “Lock her up!” era of criminal enforcement — they’ll ultimately fail in the courts. Again.

The most fundamental problem with a potential perjury indictment of Hutchinson is that prosecutors almost certainly can’t carry their burden of proof. The gist of the Justice Department’s grand-jury probe (first reported by Punchbowl News) is Hutchinson’s June 2022 testimony to Congress that a Secret Service agent, Tony Ornato, told her about a January 6, 2021, incident in which Donald Trump demanded that the Secret Service drive him to the U.S. Capitol Building and physically lunged at the driver or the steering wheel of his armored car when the Secret Service refused. Trump has furiously denied that any such thing ever happened.

Here’s the key point: Hutchinson did not claim that she witnessed this event. She testified only that Ornato told her about it. The question, then, is not whether the scrum inside the armored car actually happened. The question is whether Ornato told the story to Hutchinson. Hutchinson claims he did; Ornato, a fierce Trump loyalist who broke ordinary Secret Service protocol by serving as a White House security official, has denied Hutchinson’s account.

It’s a literal “she said, he said.” And there’s essentially no way prosecutors can prove that Hutchinson lied — in other words, that Ornato never told her the story about the armored car — beyond a reasonable doubt. Even if prosecutors could somehow establish that Ornato was a more believable witness than Hutchinson, and that she probably lied, that’s still not even close to a prosecutable case.

If anything, the available indicators suggest Hutchinson told the truth and Ornato is the one who’s fudging. After hearing testimony from dozens of witnesses, including Hutchinson and Ornato, members of the January 6 Select Committee from both sides of the aisle concluded that Ornato had serious credibility problems.

And Ornato has a history of gossiping with his White House colleagues and then denying it in public. In a separate incident, former Trump White House staffer Alyssa Farah Griffin posted on social media in 2022 that Ornato had lied to the press about a conversation she’d had with Ornato and Mark Meadows inside the White House. (Disclosure: Griffin is a CNN colleague and friend of mine.) Another former Trump White House staffer, Keith Kellogg, claimed Ornato told him that the Secret Service was planning to move then–Vice-President Mike Pence to Joint Base Andrews on January 6. Ornato later denied publicly that he had said any such thing to Kellogg. (Sound familiar?) So either three of Ornato’s colleagues independently fabricated stories they claimed he’d told them for no apparent reason — or Ornato is an inveterate office busybody who denies his behind-the-scenes statements when they become public.

It’s not certain that prosecutors will be able to clear even the low bar posed by a grand jury, which technically requires a showing of “probable cause” to obtain an indictment (though Justice Department policy has long counseled that prosecutors should not seek an indictment unless they believe the evidence will probably be sufficient to secure and sustain a conviction beyond a reasonable doubt). And Trump’s Justice Department has largely forfeited its credibility in the nation’s capital. D.C. grand juries have recently rejected a string of proposed indictments, including one against Senator Mark Kelly and other Democratic lawmakers who posted an online video reminding soldiers that they have the right to refuse illegal orders. And trial juries have returned not-guilty verdicts in politically charged cases, including the trial of the D.C. protester who chucked a Subway sandwich at a federal agent. Don’t be shocked if a grand jury declines to charge Hutchinson. And if it does indict, there’s next to zero chance that a trial jury will unanimously find her guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

That’s assuming a hypothetical Hutchinson indictment even reaches trial, which seems doubtful. Her legal team will have a textbook motion to dismiss based on vindictive prosecution — when a person is charged criminally after and in retaliation for exercising some legal right or process. Here, Hutchinson testified against Trump and now faces reactionary prosecution for it.

And the president has provided Hutchinson’s defense with stark evidence of his personal animus toward her. He has publicly expressed disdain for Hutchinson (a “total phony and ‘leaker,’” among other put-downs). And just in case there was any doubt, Trump explicitly called for Hutchinson’s prosecution in 2024: “Has she now changed her testimony? Will she be prosecuted for what she did and said? What about the Unselect J6 Committee. They destroyed almost everything, including real evidence and findings. What’s going to happen with them — Serious crimes have been committed?” (Joe Biden, seemingly wary of Trump’s threat, preemptively pardoned all the committee members — but not witnesses like Hutchinson — on his last day in office.)

If there’s any doubt about what DoJ leadership might do, consider the recent reporting from Sarah Fitzpatrick at The Atlantic that Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director Kash Patel of the FBI are feeling the heat because Trump wants more scalps. One former official told Fitzpatrick, “The president wants indictments. He wants people in handcuffs … no matter how thin” the supporting evidence might be. Far be it from Blanche and Patel, both of whom have risen to the heights of law enforcement by indulging the president’s worst retributive instincts, to take a principled stand.

The story is nothing new. Trump issues a call to prosecute his political enemies; Blanche and Patel spring to attention and cobble together some preposterously flawed criminal investigation or charge, which promptly collapses once tested by a grand jury or in a court: Letitia James (three times), James Comey (twice), Kelly and his Democratic colleagues, Don Lemon, Jerome Powell, Kilmar Ábrego Garcia. None of these cases have resulted in a conviction, and none will.
A Hutchinson prosecution might produce a fleeting retributive endorphin rush for Trump and his enablers. But in the end, it’ll wind up on the same scrap heap as all the others.
One of the core challenges in diabetes is controlling your blood sugar after eating, particularly when carbohydrates are involved.
But new findings give further evidence that it's not just what you eat that matters when it comes to controlling blood glucose – when you eat is also an important factor.
In a study published in Diabetes, researchers found that mice fed olive oil before consuming glucose saw a reduced increase in blood sugar afterward.

"Our findings suggest that the order in which nutrients reach the gut can engage a coordinated hormone-nerve response that changes how quickly the stomach delivers glucose to the intestine," says endocrinologist Daisuke Yabe from Kyoto University.
While the new findings have only been demonstrated in mice for now, it's not the first time we've seen evidence that the order foods are eaten can affect how blood sugar levels respond after a meal.

Meal-sequencing is an emerging dietary approach to help treat and manage diabetes and obesity, with evidence showing that eating vegetables or foods rich in protein or in fat prior to eating carbohydrates helps to keep people's blood sugar lower.

It's thought that this could be due to certain nutrients slowing the process of gastric emptying, which means food moves more slowly into the small intestine, delaying the absorption of glucose into the bloodstream.

Another possibility is that eating some foods before carbs may induce the secretion of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) – the appetite-suppressing and insulin-boosting hormone mimicked by drugs like Ozempic.
To explore these mechanisms further, Yabe's team conducted an experiment with mice, evaluating three separate conditions after an overnight fast.

In one test, mice were given olive oil 15 minutes before being given glucose. Another group received glucose first, then olive oil. A third group of mice served as controls, consuming water followed by glucose.

Blood tests after the feeding experiment showed that mice fed olive oil before the glucose had significantly lower blood glucose immediately after the meal, with marked reductions at the 15- and 30-minute marks compared to the other mice, although the effects appeared to diminish by 60 minutes.

The mice fed olive oil first also showed slower gastric emptying and had higher levels of the hormones glucagon, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), and GLP-1 in their blood – suggesting a range of hormonal responses that may help slow gastric emptying and limit blood sugar spikes.

The researchers tested other fats in addition to olive oil, including flaxseed oil, lard, coconut oil, and fish oil. Olive oil generally performed the best in terms of controlling blood sugar, although flaxseed oil and lard produced similar results in some measures.

In separate experiments using mouse models of diabetes, pre-loaded olive oil offered similar benefits to blood sugar and gastric emptying, suggesting the mechanism operates even when the body's ability to produce insulin is substantially reduced.

In other tests using drugs and genetically engineered mice, the researchers blocked the animals' glucagon and GLP-1 signaling. They found that if one of these pathways was disrupted, olive oil still had beneficial effects, but if both pathways were blocked, the blood sugar reduction was weakened or lost, and the effects to slow gastric emptying vanished.

Similarly, in a final experiment, the researchers found that if they surgically disrupted vagus nerve signaling in mice, olive oil's ability to mitigate blood sugar increases and slow gastric emptying was weakened or no longer detectable, even though the animals' hormonal responses remained intact.
Taken together, it looks like olive oil's benefits to control blood sugar involve both hormones and neural pathways, the team thinks.
"The effect appears to involve an integrated endocrine-neural response rather than a single hormone," the researchers write.
"These observations suggest that early nutrient sensing activates coordinated endocrine responses that contribute to slowing gastric emptying and limiting glucose excursions."
Given that olive oil doesn't show the same benefits if it's consumed after glucose, the order of the nutrients is a controlling factor, the study authors say.

It's possible that if glucose is eaten first, its rapid absorption into the bloodstream may suppress the responsiveness of pancreatic alpha cells, impairing their ability to release glucagon in response to fatty acids. By contrast, consuming olive oil first may activate fatty acid-sensing mechanisms before blood glucose levels rise substantially.

There's still a lot we don't fully know about this mechanism, and it's worth reiterating that these olive oil effects have so far only been shown in mice, with no guarantee we'd see the same benefits in human patients.

But the findings highlight a common ingredient that researchers might easily be able to test in people in future studies, and give us some new clues toward a better understanding of the ways meal sequencing may work.
"Our group has long been interested in practical dietary approaches that people can continue in everyday life," Yabe says.
"Meal-sequencing is appealing because it merely changes how a meal is eaten rather than requiring people to avoid entire food groups."

Catholics serving in the U.S. Army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent U.S. archbishop said on Monday.

In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the U.S. armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.

Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan’s victims, and lamented the shooting. But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the U.S. wanted to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries.”
“I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Broglio said.
U.S. Army regulations do allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations, and the Army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad.
Questions about the effect on young viewers

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and international observers. U.S. President Donald Trump approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the livestreaming to proceed.

The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the U.S. military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest.

Hegseth said last week he wants U.S. soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and location of Hasan’s shooting spree. Hegseth has argued that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent.

Broglio questioned whether the effect of a livestreamed execution on young viewers had been considered. He said the U.S. military had a good reputation and asked if there was “really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world.”

Broglio’s statement was issued shortly after he met on Monday in Rome with Pope Leo, who has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war. Leo on Saturday condemned the death penalty, without mentioning the Hasan case specifically.
Vice President JD Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get livestreamed, he would not watch it.

ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot has arrived back in Europe, landing in Cologne, Germany, following her return to Earth with Crew-12 after 237 days, nearly eight months, aboard the International Space Station for her εpsilon mission.

Sophie, together with NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrei Fedyaev, undocked on 7 October at 12:05 GMT/14:05 CEST, beginning a 27 hours and 29 minutes return journey back to Earth.

After splashdown on 8 October at 15:34 GMT/17:34 CEST and initial medical checks aboard the recovery vessel, Sophie and her crewmates travelled to shore by helicopter before boarding a NASA plane at the nearest airport. They were flown together to Ellington Field in Houston for initial post-flight activities.

On 9 October Sophie boarded a French Air and Space Force Airbus A330 MRTT Phénix bound for ESA’s European Astronaut Centre (EAC) in Cologne, Germany. She landed at 04:21 GMT / 06:21 CEST on 10 October and was warmly welcomed on the apron by family, friends, colleagues, journalists and representatives from ESA Member States.

“We are delighted to welcome back our ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot who embodied our values through her successful mission,” says Josef Aschbacher, ESA’s Director General. “The inspiration that Sophie has provided with her mission matters a great deal as we enter into such a decisive moment for Europe. Human spaceflight and exploration remain at the centre of our attention as we prepare for the Intermediate Ministerial Council Meeting in Rome in December. Our ambition is clear: Europe must secure a role in exploration commensurate with its political and economic weight.”

Sophie will spend the next two to three weeks adjusting to Earth’s gravity and undergoing data collections at :envihab, a German Aerospace Center (DLR) facility located next to EAC. DLR teams work closely with ESA, providing operational, medical and scientific expertise to support astronauts’ return, recovery and readaptation to life on Earth. Sophie will then continue her rehabilitation and follow-up activities with the EAC training team.

Sophie spent a total of 237 days, 5 hours and 18 minutes in space after being launched on 13 February 2026 from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, USA. The εpsilon mission set a new European record for the longest single spaceflight, exceeding by more than 35 days the previous record held by ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano for his Beyond mission. Crew-12 is also the longest SpaceX Dragon mission to date, surpassing the previous record of 235 days set by Crew-8.

Sophie is the second European woman, after ESA astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti, and the first French woman to conduct an Extra Vehicular Activity (EVA), or spacewalk. Sophie completed three spacewalks in 14 days, spending a total of 19 hours and 42 minutes working outside the Station. Throughout εpsilon, Sophie carried out a wide range of European experiments spanning fields from health research to materials science, biology, fluid physics, radiation physics and fundamental science.

Alongside this broad research programme, Sophie also helped to test technologies for future exploration missions, including the new European exercise device E4D and in-orbit metal 3D printing, and supported commercial research payloads.

Over the course of Expedition 74 and 75, Sophie worked on experiments and payloads for International Space Station partners, contributing to the international research programme carried out aboard the orbiting laboratory.

Sophie also spent around 218 hours working on 35 European payloads, and about 25 hours on ESA systems maintenance or upgrades in Columbus, Europe’s microgravity research facility in orbit. She completed all the εpsilon-specific experiments proposed by the French space agency CNES, and all ESA experiments that were assigned to her.

“Sophie was the first of her class to be assigned to a mission, embarking on a fast-track journey she brilliantly completed. Her return now marks the successful completion of an outstanding mission aboard the International Space Station, says Daniel Neuenschwander, ESA Director of Human and Robotic Exploration. “During εpsilon, she has contributed to an ambitious programme of science, technology and exploration, while representing Europe in an international endeavour that depends on the commitment of thousands of people. Missions like εpsilon help build the knowledge, experience and inspiration we need as Europe pursues its ambitions for exploration and discovery. We are immensely proud to welcome her back to Europe and grateful to all the teams and partners who supported her throughout this journey.”

During her free time, Sophie took more than 1,1 million social media followers along on the εpsilon adventure, sharing insights into the science experiments she worked on and life aboard the Station, as well as views of Earth from orbit and her Sunday Morning Science series, which took advantage of microgravity to demonstrate scientific concepts. Sophie’s social media content during εpsilon generated more than 403 million views.

Sophie also reached and inspired more than 290 000 students through the CNES educational experiment Chloriss conducted in about 4000 schools, ESA’s AstroPi challenge, the International Space Station’s amateur radio programme ARISS, and a poetry contest. She also took part in more than 40 live events with schools, museums, institutions and journalists around the world.

True to the meaning behind εpsilon, Sophie’s contribution was one of many that came together to make the mission possible. Behind εpsilon’s achievements was a collective effort involving ESA teams and centres across Europe, including EAC, the Columbus Control Centre (Col-CC) and the network of User Support and Operations Centres (USOCs), alongside national space agencies such as CNES and many partners.
SpaceX and NASA are preparing to fly a resupply cargo flight to the International Space Station on Tuesday morning.
The pre-sunrise launch will be SpaceX’s 35th mission to the orbiting outpost as part of NASA’s Commercial Resupply Services (CRS) contract.

Liftoff of SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is scheduled for 6:33 a.m. EDT (1033 UTC). The rocket will fly on a northeasterly trajectory upon leaving the pad.

If all goes well, the Cargo Dragon spacecraft, tail number C211, will dock with the zenith port of the Harmony module on Oct. 15 around 11 a.m. EDT (1500 UTC). The space-facing docking port was recently vacated by the Crew Dragon Freedom, which safely delivered the four members of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission back to Earth with a splashdown on Oct. 8.
Spaceflight Now will have live coverage beginning about an hour prior to liftoff.

SpaceX will launch the mission using the Falcon 9 first stage booster B1096. This will be its eighth launch after previously flying NASA’s IMAP, CRS-34, NROL-77, NROL-95, GPS-III 9, Kuiper Falcon 01, and Starlink 6-87.
It is the fourth flight for Dragon C211. It’s previous cargo runs included CRS-26, -29, and -33. The spacecraft will remain docked to the ISS for about a month following docking.

Stowed in the unpressurized trunk of Dragon C211 is the final pair of ISS Roll-Out Solar Arrays (iROSAs), which will help to augment the power generation of the aging space station. The spacecraft also contains a clamshell apparatus that will house the failed Canadarm2 joint that was removed during the June 30 spacewalk.

“Additional equipment we’re launching includes a dose pump for our toilet, some pre-treat quality sensors, a robot microcontical tool used for space station maintenance and utilization tasks with external replacement units and impairments,” said Bill Spetch, the deputy manager of Commercial for NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program.

“We also have a wealth of science experiments on board, including studies to manufacture artificial retinas, understand how microgravity affects the growth of 3D heart tissue models, study how glass forms when made with non-traditional elements, and better understand how inflammation is linked to neurodegenerative diseases.”

When NASA’s Perseverance rover reached the inner edge of Mars’ Jezero Crater in September 2023, mission scientists were surprised by what they found. Called the “Margin Unit,” the geologic area stretches along the shoreline of an ancient Martian lake, so they expected sedimentary rocks, which would have formed as layers of sand piled on top of each other over millennia. Composed of clay and silt, sedimentary rocks on Earth are good at preserving past microbial life. The scientists were especially intrigued by strong signals of carbonate minerals detected by Mars orbiters. On Earth, carbonates frequently form in shallow ocean and lake environments capable of supporting life.

Instead, the rover team found igneous rock, which can form deep underground from magma or from volcanic activity at the surface. Igneous rocks are excellent record-keepers, particularly because mineral crystals within them preserve details about the precise moment they formed. In this case, they preserved an astonishingly complex record of water activity on early Mars. In fact, these rocks showed signs of having interacted with water on at least three separate occasions, with each encounter further altering their chemistry and appearance. The findings were published Monday in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

The instrument behind the findings is SuperCam, which perches on the rover’s mast and determines the mineralogy of geologic features based on the light they reflect. When the science team spots an intriguing rock, they can send commands for SuperCam to fire its laser up to 21 feet (6.5 meters) away. The spectrum of the resulting plasma reveals the target’s chemistry. Perseverance has analyzed more than 185 bedrock targets across the unit this way.

“Before we arrived at the Margin Unit, the main hypothesis — derived from orbital observations — was that the carbonate seen from orbit formed from interaction with the lake that existed in Jezero Crater,” said Candice Bedford, a research scientist at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana, and the study’s lead author. “But now we know that this location became a sort of crossroads for aqueous systems. The Margin Unit findings are important because Jezero Crater sits inside one of the largest exposures of carbonate on Mars, so what we learn here reaches well beyond this crater.”

Perseverance explored the Margin Unit across approximately 870 feet (265 meters) of elevation. At higher elevations, it found rock that was coarse-grained and crystalline — hallmarks of the mineral olivine — with almost no sign that water had ever touched it. Made of magnesium and iron, the area’s olivine unit formed in a body of magma deep underground, cooling slowly enough for its grains to grow large, and reached the surface only after the ground above it eroded away. Lower in the unit, on the lakebed, the rock looks transformed, as the olivine grains were fractured with silica between them.

Carbonate and silica minerals are an important signpost in the search for ancient life. When water interacts with olivine on Earth, the reaction can release hydrogen, which can be a food source for some microbes, and it leaves behind carbonate and silica, two minerals that lock in traces of the past existence of those microbes.

The Perseverance team can determine the sequence of the Margin Unit’s interactions with water, but not their age. On the first occasion water reached the rocks of the Margin Unit, carbon-dioxide-rich groundwater reacted with olivine, resulting in ridges of carbonate that run through the fractures in bedrock at low elevations. Today, these carbonate-filled fractures are left standing as the softer rock around them wears away.
The second time water reached the rocks may have been related to the lake that once existed in the crater.

“Some of the Margin Unit rocks also contain silica,” said Eleni Ravanis, a planetary scientist at the University of Hawaii at Manoa and a coauthor of the study. “Turning olivine into carbonate can leave silica behind, and we see more of that silica in rocks that sat below the water line.”

Last came a water event that generated mineral veins at one location in the eastern part of the Margin Unit, about 10 inches (25 centimeters) thick, creating minerals like calcium sulfate and fluorite. Finding fluorite is an important clue because it typically forms when hot water circulates through volcanic rocks, revealing that this area experienced a later, heated underground-water event.

“If there is one thing I have learned after 10 years working with Mars rovers, it is that Mars constantly throws surprises at you,” said Bedford. “It is very rare that things are as we expect them to be from orbital data. I hope this work helps reshape how scientists view the history of water in Jezero Crater and across Mars. Ultimately, I hope it helps planetary scientists reconstruct the changing climate and habitability of early Mars.”

A key objective of Perseverance’s mission on Mars is astrobiology, including the search for signs of ancient microbial life. The rover characterizes the planet’s geology and past climate and collects and stores Martian rock and regolith.

Managed for NASA by Caltech, Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California built and manages operations of the Perseverance rover on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate as part of NASA’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio. SuperCam is co-led by Purdue University in Indiana, Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico, and IRAP (Research Institute in Astrophysics and Planetology) and CNES (Centre National d'Etudes Spatiales) in Toulouse, France.

NASA’s SpaceX 35th commercial resupply mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT Tuesday aboard a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, carrying more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and hardware, bound for the International Space Station. Following its successful launch, the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft will carry new scientific experiments, cargo, and the final pair of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays to the orbiting laboratory.

Dragon is scheduled to autonomously dock at 11 a.m., Thursday, Oct. 15, to the space-facing port of the space station’s Harmony module. NASA will stream rendezvous and docking coverage beginning at 9:15 a.m., through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online:

The final pair of solar arrays will complete the space station’s power system augmentation, boosting available electricity for research, operations, and the station’s safe, controlled deorbit. Astronauts will install the arrays during a series of spacewalks planned for later this fall.

Dragon also is delivering several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture artificial retinas in microgravity that could help restore vision for patients on Earth and 3D heart tissue models to advance large-scale drug testing on future space missions. Dragon also will carry materials to study how a new type of glass is formed in microgravity, and brain organoids that could uncover potential treatment targets for neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis.

These are just a sample of the hundreds of investigations conducted aboard the orbiting laboratory in the areas of biology and biotechnology, physical sciences, and Earth and space science. Research and technology investigations taking place aboard the space station benefit people on Earth and lay the groundwork for other agency deep space missions. As part of NASA’s Artemis program, the agency will send astronauts to the Moon to prepare for future human exploration of Mars, inspiring the world through discovery in a new Golden Age of innovation and exploration.

The Dragon spacecraft is scheduled to remain at the space station until mid-November when it will depart and return to Earth with time-critical research and cargo, splashing down off the coast of California.

The company that previously operated as Elbit Systems’ American subsidiary made its AUSA expo debut this week as Twenty-Six Defense.

Under the new brand, the Texas-based defense firm debuted Primex, a lightweight wearable meant to provide soldiers with night-vision capabilities and augmented reality so they can “maintain awareness without distraction or cognitive overload.”
For the design, Twenty-Six Defense said it engineered Primex for sustained operational use by equipping it with “the lightest head-borne load and near-neutral center of gravity.”

The company explained Primex uses low-light sensors, thermal imagery, and real-time processing to produce an ultra-low-latency digital perception that enables operators to better interpret the surrounding area even amid challenging environmental conditions.

What separates Primex from other advanced lightweight heads-up display units for operators, according to Twenty-Six Defense, is that its design was built on mature technologies that have already been fielded.
The company said it already produces AN/PSQ-44 Enhanced Night Vision Goggles, which contain features that allow for rapid target acquisition and augment reality to enhance visual clarity.

In August, Ernie Basic, Twenty-Six Defense’s senior director of research and development, explained how his company was developing equipment for the Soldier Borne Mission Command, a project to deliver augmented reality wearables to soldiers.
He said the technology combines fighter-pilot displays with night-vision systems, so soldiers get “the full operational picture.”

“You are not only seeing what is in front of you. You can leverage a feed coming from a drone or from other assets,” he said. “You can start seeing what is going on behind a house or another structure, cue a squad to a different location, and continuously update them.”
In addition to Primex, Twenty-Six Defense showcased defensive weapons and equipment like the XM1168 mobile 120mm mortar system, Autonomous Relocatable Surveillance Tower and SkyStriker Block 4E.

It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in and out of wakefulness myself, I take hold of my phone. With scarcely a thought, I switch from one app to another, scrolling through images and opinions and adverts for no discernible reason beyond habit.

Later, I head for my office and open my laptop to a slew of half-completed documents and an inbox brimming with emails. My stress levels begin to nudge upwards. I have vague memories of what my professional life felt like before smartphones and video calls. I used to do my writing by hand. And I could concentrate for hours at a time, getting little upticks of arousal from lifting my head from the page, letting the hold on my pen loosen, and gazing at the life beyond my window, the light softening on my skin and eyes like snowfall on warm tarmac.

Nowadays, my productive bursts come from caffeine and sugary or salty snacks, even if I try to pick the healthier ones, and from checking my emails or picking up my phone to update my inbox. By the end of the day, the sheer volume of work I expect myself to do, now that digital tools make so much possible, has kept me nailed to my seat. Another day has passed and the hope I’d had that I might have time for a run or a hike outside has been dashed again. I wish I could say that this is atypical. Yet, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I went from hours spent in nature and on physical activities to a passive, phone-addicted individual, meeting people first and sometimes only online. I am not alone.

We have fallen into habits that are steadily deskilling the human body, eroding capacities honed by evolution to support our wellbeing as we move through the world. Some of these capacities are weakening through disuse: we have come to rely on our phones, for example, and now, increasingly, on AI, to rapidly do work that would once have required something more physical – like looking around, or asking someone, or going to find and consult a book. Reliance on GPS may weaken both our spatial attention and the fluency of our wayfinding. In surrendering to a quick technological fix, we are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. Other capacities are being retrained by machines and algorithms to work against us: for instance, smartphones and chatbots can train us to keep reaching for them even when we no longer enjoy using them, turning a conscious choice into an automatic habit and a colossal waste of time. The body that results is less able to assess its own condition, improvise and regulate itself. The crucial distinction is between technologies that strengthen our capacities and those that repeatedly substitute for the actions through which those capacities are formed.
Algorithms that regurgitate patterns and recommendations can release us from the effort of exploration and disrupt the play and curiosity from which preferences are formed and understood.

This is a strange turn of events for an animal whose success comes mostly from the extraordinary ability to learn through experience. It would be easy to blame our deskilled bodies on the machines themselves. But, for centuries, modern human societies have been sold the lie that we are machines.

Long before the digital revolution, René Descartes described the body as a machine governed by physical laws, declaring that animals such as ‘worms and flies and caterpillars move mechanically’. But he treated rational thought as a separate and uniquely human power. The body might behave like a machine, but the thinking mind stood apart from it. Build something correctly, and its function follows.

By the middle of the 20th century, the comparison between organisms and machines had been recast in the language of information. During the cybernetics revolution of the 1950s, the US computer scientist Norbert Wiener envisaged a future in which ‘messages between man and machines, between machines and man, and between machine and machine, are destined to play an ever-increasing part’. Writing in The Human Use of Human Beings (1950), he warned against wholesale automation, while also noting that ‘we are not stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves’. A person could be imagined as a pattern of information surviving in another form.
If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Mechanical language also persisted in the study of living behaviour. In The Foundations of Ethology (1981), the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz wrote that animal behaviour was as rigidly programmed as a sequence of movements in a clock. Transhumanist thinkers then carried the machine comparison further, imagining technologies that could transfer a mind to a computer.

Machines now promised more than control. They offered a glimpse of immortality: the organism might be repaired, remade and ultimately replaced. The somewhat embarrassing body, with its impulses and eventual frailty, might then be cast aside. If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Today, we can see this fear writ large in the technological quest for a bodiless life. If a person is ultimately a pattern of information, that pattern might be restored or even uploaded. AI is only the latest iteration of this ancient impulse to escape the vulnerability of the body.

After all, the brain is itself a physical organ, continually shaped by what the body does and encounters. Once we decide that the mind is the real human and the rest of the body only hardware, it becomes easier to disregard the physical work, including the neurocognitive work of a biological brain, through which we move, find our way, put thoughts into words, and recognise our own needs. A machine may do some of that work faster, but each act it takes over is one that the body no longer performs and that the body, including the brain, no longer learns through. The irony is that a project motivated by the desire to overcome bodily fragility is helping to produce more fragile bodies.

On top of all this, we have little evidence that either thought or intelligence actually work like machines, and almost no indication that life is an abstract system that might emerge in silicon or mathematics. Instead, a substantial body of work, especially in systems biology, points to a quite different conclusion: that life and intelligence emerge from the unique qualities and organisation of our self-maintaining bodies, rather than from abstract models of information and algorithms.

For the past six years, I have been researching the latest science on what life is and how it works. As best as we can tell, the intelligent actions of organisms derive from the imperatives of a living body that must regulate and preserve its own conditions for existence. When cybernetics was ascendant, the molecular structure of DNA had only recently been discovered, and the emerging view of genes as information encouraged an oversimplified picture of the body as running on a program that could be made more efficient. Yet such confidence has since waned among biologists. While genes carry some of the information that shapes our bodies, many changes in how a cell or a body functions arise from the system as a whole. Genes cannot be understood apart from the living bodies in which they act.

First and foremost, life persists through physical plasticity. Consider how our bodies keep together. Living bodies do something unusual in the Universe: they perform work to preserve their own organisation. Life-forms use energy to remain discontinuous with the environment. In simple terms, organisms resist disintegrating into the background. While machines execute tasks, living beings pursue ends. Machines push energy around and produce things. They are, in this sense, allopoietic: they make something other than themselves. Organisms are autopoietic: they work to maintain and remake themselves. Living bodies take up and transform energy for this self-maintenance, and this is achieved by the body as a whole. Moment by moment, our bodies adapt to the environment and their current state in end-directed, physical transformations. It’s not so much that we think and therefore act but rather that we embody and therefore amend.
The same qualities that make life-forms so causally special can undermine us when trained by harmful environments

The boundary of the body also creates a distinct inner environment, one that is physically and chemically different from the surrounding world. Through this difference, the body acts as a translator, turning external changes into useful internal physical responses. This allows a life-form to carry out specific reactions in controlled conditions that support their survival and flourishing. Internal regulation also gives organisms a unique logic of their own. They can then act according to the current state of their bodies and the world as they find it. Our bodies detect changes that have consequence for us, evaluate them against our needs, and reorganise into useful action. Thus, living beings might be understood as a remarkable kind of organisation of matter: a bounded, metabolically open, self-maintaining form that gives rise to purposeful, intelligent action. This is key to understanding both the skills of our flesh, and why we can think of ourselves as being ‘deskilled’ today. When we recognise that our bodies are intrinsically intelligent in their organisation, we don’t need a conscious agent beyond the flesh. The body is the agent from which intelligence emerges and also, in the fullest sense, who we are.

Consider what happens if you’re thirsty. The process starts before you consciously decide to have a drink. Rather, the osmoreceptor neurons in the hypothalamus shrink slightly as water leaves them. That physical change opens ion channels, letting sodium enter cells. This altered electrical state then opens calcium channels, and calcium flows in. Calcium triggers tiny sacs to release neurotransmitters into the space between cells, passing the signal to other neurons until the state of being thirsty turns to action. The movements through which we quench our thirst arise from minute physical changes in interconnected parts of our bodies. These signals help guide us towards water and make us aware of our thirst.

The physical organisation of an organism is inherently evaluative. It is from this embodied evaluation that agency emerges. Yet the same unique qualities that make life-forms so causally special and intelligent can undermine us when repeatedly trained by harmful environments. Instead, we can acquire patterns or lose pathways that progressively weaken our intrinsic intelligence, which we need to flourish. For example, one study found that only a single week’s worth of leg immobilisation can reduce thigh-muscle volume by about 5 per cent. A separate study found that, by 15 days of non-use, the firing behaviour of the cells controlling the leg muscle begins to diminish.

Ordinarily, as we walk, optic flow – the shifting images on our retinas as we move through our surroundings – enables our bodies to sense our movement relative to the world. Receptors in our muscles, tendons and joints detect the movement of our limbs. Signals from the inner ear add information about location and orientation. Together with landmarks and memories of past journeys, these signals help us work out where we are and how to reach our destination. It’s a vast, coordinated sensorium that takes us across the landscapes of our world.

So, what happens if you rely on an app to find your way? GPS can make navigation easier and less energetically costly. Yet studies of large-scale navigation have also demonstrated that physically moving through an environment produces better spatial knowledge than viewing the same journey on a 2D source. When we routinely follow GPS directions, an external source supplies information we would otherwise work out through our own sensing and movement. One longitudinal study that followed 13 GPS users over three years found that those users had a steeper subsequent decline in their spatial memory as mediated by the hippocampus, compared with control groups who didn’t use GPS. This suggests that, when we practise wayfinding less often, our ability to notice where we are and readjust may dwindle.

Something similar may be at work in our increasing reliance on tools like ChatGPT. Like finding our way, articulating our thoughts is a dynamic, embodied act, whether writing or speaking. Learning a new speech movement, for instance, changes how we perceive speech sounds, as well as how we generate them. We develop these abilities by repeatedly finding a word, uttering it, listening to it, and correcting it as necessary – tasks that draw on multiple regions within our bodies. This is just as relevant for writing. But when an AI writing app automatically provides structure, it also diminishes the skills of selection and self-correction from our repertoire. In one study, passively copying AI-generated writing, unlike drafting first and then using AI for revision, was found to lessen an individual’s confidence in subsequently performing the task unaided. It is execution – physically doing it – that builds our embodied skills. That is why using AI to revise a draft we have written is fundamentally different from asking it to produce the draft for us. It’s not that computational tools are inherently bad or unhelpful – far from it – but rather that when they replace the physical effort of our bodies, our own agency and skill take a hit.
Our thoughts emerge as much from bodily intelligence and awareness of the world as from symbols on a screen

This is something I feel increasingly keenly. Sometimes, when I know I’ve spent yet another day indoors at my desk, I get myself outside and walk the road uphill to where I can look at the view across the dale. It is often hard to release my mind. It feels as if, from concentrating all day and neglecting the rest of my body, I have become a clenched fist somewhere inside my skull. Yet once the light and the breeze and the sounds of birds reach me, the grip eases, a sensation of pleasure passes over me, and ideas begin to free up too.

The expansive thoughts and sensations that come as I step outside are enabled by the physical changes that accompany my movement. My heart rate has increased, sweeping nutrients and oxygen through my tissues and into my brain. My muscles begin contracting, clearing sugars and fats from my bloodstream, immediately working to counteract some of the effects of sitting for so long. Each step is a bodily integration of balance, senses and muscular force, allowing me to predict what will happen next, and the more I do this, the more I can calibrate my actions in the environment. The thoughts that come from this physical enactment are hopeful and generous, and often unexpected. Yet this shouldn’t surprise. When we move in the world, we draw on physical capabilities that are relatively underused when we remain indoors and seated. From balance to sensing what is happening inside us, our bodies are continuously perceiving and, crucially, remembering in the flesh. Our thoughts can emerge as much from bodily intelligence and our awareness of the wider world as from abstract symbols on a screen.

It is only when we imagine that our ability to act has nothing to do with the body that we end up taking seriously the idea that we can live contentedly as machines. Far from upskilling us, a technology that shuts us off from embodied learning risks diminishing the intelligence it seeks to enhance.

The technologies with which we are increasingly interconnected lack the complex interiority required for real intelligence to arise. There’s no body, no independently formed interests, no being. There’s no metabolism or organisation or persistence.

And yet we turn to them because they have been designed either to ease the friction of the hard work our bodies must put in to develop skills or because they promise to make us more productive. More insidiously, they do so by modelling the appearance or behaviours of living beings. A recent analysis by the psychologist Clara Colombatto, the philosopher Jonathan Birch and the neuroscientist Stephen Fleming found that exposure to these systems leads to an increase in attributions of mental capacities to them. Another study, by the behaviour scientist Yaoxi Shi and others, found that regular five-minute conversations with an AI on personal issues resulted in a small but meaningful decrease in preference for seeking human support.

The danger is that the systems now coordinating us don’t answer to biological needs. They don’t get tired or hungry or lonely. Yet they increasingly regulate the behaviour of beings who do. In short, we are losing our own agency to parasites: systems that simulate agency while feeding on ours. They can be designed to direct us without ever needing to understand what a human body is and what an individual needs for their betterment.

Of course, human beings have always outsourced some agency into shared structures, be they laws, public health systems or institutions. This has largely been to our benefit. But today our technologies capture attention, predict behaviour, automate choice and monetise our impulses, while keeping our bodies anchored to the machines on which we increasingly rely. These coordinating systems are often extractive and indifferent to our flourishing. We might imagine we’re escaping the body, but the technologies that make this seem possible depend on mines and cheap labour and come at a planetary cost. And if our technologies weaken the feedback loop between our bodies and the world, they may weaken it in both directions. At its worst, we become less sensitive not only to what the world is doing to us, but to what our own actions are doing to the world.
The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day

We have engineered novel digital and commercial environments that can habituate harmful impulses in our bodies. As our bodies refit themselves in response to the unhealthy architectures we’ve engineered, we can find ourselves in a spiral of self-harm.

Recent work by the neuroscientist Kent Berridge and colleagues has shown how the brain systems that tell us we enjoy something and the systems that drive us to pursue this can drift apart. In other words, what we find ourselves craving and what we enjoy can end up at odds. When these systems become disrupted, the body’s learned patterns fall out of alignment with the satisfaction that once justified them.

Influential models of drug addiction describe a progressive shift from prefrontal control to the striatum, a deep part of the brain involved in actions that become automatic over time. As such, addiction is a change from thoughtful self-command to more habit-driven control. Nowadays, addictions might not come only in the form of obvious candidates like alcohol and nicotine, but also smartphones and chatbots. The bodily gifts that allow us to learn can train us into patterns that diminish our freedom to act otherwise.

I have come to believe that our bodily deskilling is, in many ways, a loss of faith in what it is to be alive. A life of physical effort and friction is not only unavoidable if we want to be as resilient and capable as possible, but it is, in a nontrivial sense, the source of our intelligence.

Our intelligence is sustained through communication between the body and the world as we sense, assess and learn from what we encounter. Such gifts are shared with other life-forms too. Unlike the human kind of phenomenal consciousness, embodied intelligence is found wherever there is a living body. Even a lowly bacterium can sense chemical differences across time, retain a short molecular memory of what it has encountered, and alter its movements. The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day, modifying their growth and defences based on prior experiences. Many of us view them as lesser agents than the computer programs we’ve invented, if we consider them at all. But this is not based on the available evidence.
If you can no longer navigate the world and recall in flesh how to act, then you will not be liberated by technology, but ruled by it.

James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
Webb has revealed a massive, dark matter-packed galaxy cluster that formed surprisingly early, challenging scientistsâ understanding of how the universe evolved.

- NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging theories about how the universe developed. The discovery also uncovered a surprising connection between scattered starlight and invisible dark matter that could transform how astronomers study the early cosmos.

A massive galaxy cluster dating back to an era when such enormous structures were only beginning to take shape is challenging scientists' understanding of how the universe evolved. New observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) reveal that the cluster contains an unusually dense concentration of matter, suggesting that some cosmic structures may have developed much faster than current models predict.

The galaxy cluster, known as XLSSC 122, has become the focus of three recent studies led by researchers at IPAC, Caltech's science and data center for astrophysics and planetary science. Their findings establish XLSSC 122 as the most distant galaxy cluster known to exhibit strong gravitational lensing, a phenomenon that allows astronomers to measure the mass of otherwise invisible matter. The research was presented at a press conference on June 17, 2026, during the 248th meeting of the American Astronomical Society.

Located approximately 10.4 billion light-years from Earth, XLSSC 122 stood out to astronomers because of its surprising maturity. Although it existed during a period when galaxy clusters were still assembling, it already displayed the size and organized structure typically associated with clusters in the modern universe.

Webb has now uncovered another remarkable feature. XLSSC 122 happens to lie directly in front of one or more galaxies that are even farther away. The cluster's powerful gravity bends and distorts the light traveling from those background galaxies, creating a rare effect called strong gravitational lensing. This fortunate alignment has given scientists an exceptionally precise way to measure how mass is distributed throughout the cluster.

"When we got those first images back from JWST, we said, 'wow, look at this, there's strong lensing coming from this cluster!'" said Kyle Finner, a staff scientist at IPAC and lead author of the first paper examining the cluster. "XLSSC 122 has now set the record for the most distant galaxy cluster displaying strong lensing, which is a valuable tool for astronomers."
An Ancient Galaxy Cluster Challenges Cosmic Predictions

The newly detected gravitational lensing has allowed researchers to examine the distribution of mass in an ancient galaxy cluster in greater detail than ever before. XLSSC 122 dates to a period known as "cosmic noon," roughly 10 billion years ago, when the universe was experiencing its most intense era of star formation.

During this time, galaxies were producing stars at rates up to 100 times higher than those observed in the present-day universe. Galaxy clusters were also becoming increasingly common as smaller systems gradually combined into larger structures.

Yet XLSSC 122 appears to have developed in an unexpected way. The new measurements show that a remarkably large amount of its mass is packed into its central region. According to standard cosmological models, the growth of massive structures should have been more gradual, making such a concentrated cluster particularly surprising at this early stage of cosmic history.
"XLSSC 122 is one of the first clusters we know of that formed in the universe, and it has a mass concentration that doesn't agree with our cosmological model predictions," said Finner.

To investigate the mystery further, Finner and his collaborators conducted two additional JWST studies, first authored by Zachary Scofield and Hyungjin Joo at Yonsei University. Together, the three papers provide a much more complete picture of this unusual cluster and offer new insights into galaxy cluster formation during cosmic noon.

Astronomers originally identified XLSSC 122 in 2014 through an X-ray survey carried out by the European Space Agency's XMM-Newton spacecraft. Later observations with the Hubble Space Telescope helped establish its distance of approximately 10.4 billion light-years and confirmed that the cluster appeared unusually developed for its age.

However, Hubble did not reveal clear evidence of strong gravitational lensing. That changed when JWST captured distinctive curved arcs of light surrounding the cluster's center, providing the first definitive signs of this phenomenon in XLSSC 122.
"Before JWST, we couldn't do this level of science in the early, distant universe," said Finner.
The gravitational distortions are caused primarily by something astronomers cannot directly observe: dark matter.

Although XLSSC 122 contains visible stars and glowing gas, these familiar forms of matter account for only a small fraction of the gravitational lensing effect. Most of the distortion comes from dark matter, an invisible substance that has not been directly detected through light but whose gravitational influence is supported by extensive astronomical evidence.

Scientists estimate that dark matter is approximately five times more abundant than ordinary matter, which makes up stars, planets, and everything around us. Its gravity helps hold galaxies together and shapes the universe's enormous network of galaxy groups, clusters, and filaments.

Because dark matter plays such an important role in cosmic structure, determining how it was distributed billions of years ago offers a powerful way to test theories describing the universe's development since the Big Bang approximately 13.8 billion years ago.
"Strong lensing is a way to measure the dark matter without actually seeing the dark matter," said Finner. "It gives us a sensitive probe of our cosmological models."
A Wider View Reveals a Galaxy Cluster Merger
In their second paper, the researchers investigated XLSSC 122 using another form of gravitational lensing known as weak lensing.

Strong gravitational lensing produces obvious distortions, including the striking arcs captured by JWST. Weak lensing, by comparison, causes much smaller changes in the apparent shapes of distant galaxies. These subtle effects are difficult to identify individually, so astronomers rely on statistical methods to detect them.

The two techniques provide complementary information. Strong lensing is especially useful for measuring the mass concentrated near a cluster's center, while weak lensing can reveal how matter is distributed across its outer regions.
"Weak gravitational lensing can constrain mass much further out, so you can get a better picture of the surrounding cluster area," said Finner.

By combining these measurements with X-ray and radio observations from other telescopes, the scientists determined that XLSSC 122 is still undergoing a merger. Its galaxies are continuing to come together as the larger cluster takes shape.
The broader analysis also reinforced the earlier finding that an unusually large amount of mass is concentrated near the cluster's center.
Ancient Starlight Offers New Clues to Dark Matter
The team's third and most recent paper revealed another important feature of XLSSC 122: faint light produced by stars that are no longer bound to individual galaxies.

Known as intracluster light, this diffuse glow comes from stars scattered into the spaces between galaxies. Webb's observations represent the earliest known detection of intracluster light, providing another way to examine the development of galaxy clusters in the distant universe.

The widespread distribution of this light supports the conclusion that XLSSC 122 is undergoing a merger. As galaxies interact and collide, some stars are pulled away from their original galaxies and spread throughout the cluster. In XLSSC 122, many of these displaced stars appear not to have settled into its dense central region.
The researchers also uncovered an intriguing connection between these wandering stars and dark matter.

Near the cluster's center, the shape of the intracluster light closely matches the distribution of dark matter inferred from strong gravitational lensing. This suggests that the faint glow of stars between galaxies could potentially serve as a visible indicator of where invisible dark matter is concentrated.

If astronomers observe the same relationship in other clusters, particularly those from the early universe, intracluster light could become a valuable new tool for mapping dark matter across cosmic history.
"In this cluster, the intracluster light essentially traces the dark matter," said Finner. "That light tells us that the cluster is in a merging state."
Could More Ancient Galaxy Clusters Challenge Cosmology?
The next goal for Finner and his colleagues is to identify and investigate dozens of additional galaxy clusters from similarly early periods in the universe's history.

Finding these distant objects requires a different approach from studying them in detail. Although JWST is exceptionally powerful, its relatively narrow field of view makes it better suited to examining selected targets than searching enormous areas of the sky.
Instead, astronomers must first identify promising candidates through wide-area X-ray and radio surveys, similar to the observations that originally revealed XLSSC 122.

One promising technique relies on the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, which occurs when energetic particles inside galaxy clusters scatter radiation from the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.

This interaction can create distinctive regions that appear as "holes" in observations of the cosmic microwave background. By searching for these signatures, astronomers can locate galaxy clusters that might otherwise be difficult to detect.

Finding more objects like XLSSC 122 could have major implications for cosmology. If other ancient clusters also contain unexpectedly concentrated dark matter and display unusually advanced development, scientists may need to revise some of their basic assumptions about how quickly large cosmic structures formed.

For now, XLSSC 122 provides an important test of existing models, but a larger sample will be necessary to determine whether its unusual properties are rare or part of a broader pattern in the early universe.

"It's still early in the JWST era," said Finner, "and if we can start to get data on tens or hundreds of these types of objects at this stage in the universe, then we can really start putting our cosmological models to the test."
