One way to protect coral reefs? Bring back seabirds

The remote Pacific Ocean has some of the most pristine coral reefs in the world. The corals themselves are bigger than cars, their delicate arms creating a dense underwater maze. Above them, the skies are filled with seabirds like red-footed boobies and white terns, searching for fish.

These species, separated by land and sea, are far more intertwined than once thought. Their relationship is the backbone of an entire ecosystem — a hidden connection that's changing the way scientists think about conservation.

That connection: bird poop. Coral reefs near seabird colonies are generally healthier, thanks to the nutrients that birds deposit in their guano. It's one reason tropical islands and atolls are biodiversity hot spots in the vast Pacific Ocean.

On some islands, this close-knit partnership has broken down. Seabird colonies have declined because of habitat loss and invasive species like rats. With fewer birds, fewer nutrients reach the ocean ecosystem.

Now, as coral restoration projects work to bring back reefs, they're also focusing on bringing back seabird colonies, reestablishing a connection that helps both species. Coral reefs are increasingly vulnerable to rising ocean temperatures, and biologists say they need every advantage in a hotter world.

"If we can figure out ways to just stop the local threats to ecosystems, they will, in a lot of cases, find ways to repair themselves," says Alex Wegmann, lead scientist for The Nature Conservancy's island resilience strategy. "They can reestablish their natural functions that will then allow them to adapt to the climate impacts that are coming."

More than a thousand miles south of Hawaii, there's a tiny group of islands known as Palmyra Atoll. In the rainforest there, a tiny chick the size of a fuzzy, white golf ball perches on a tree limb. The parents hover nearby, chattering rhythmically.

"That's a white tern chick, and a young one at that," Paige Mino, manager of the Palmyra Atoll National Wildlife Refuge with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, says as she looks up at the birds. "I think that their call sounds like an electric rubber band snapping," she adds with a smile.

The forest echoes with the calls of seabirds, like red-footed boobies, large birds with bright blue beaks and signature red feet. Almost all of the birds on Palmyra Atoll rely on the ocean, flying out to sea daily to feed on fish or squid, bringing some back for their young.

The abundance is thanks in large part to Palmyra Atoll's remote location. While it was likely visited by Polynesians who crossed the Pacific on seafaring voyages, the atoll wasn't permanently inhabited. In the 1800s, coconut plantations were developed. The U.S. military turned the atoll into a logistical station during World War II, building bunkers and roads.

In 2000, The Nature Conservancy bought Palmyra Atoll from private owners and transferred the majority of it to the federal government. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service manages it as a national wildlife refuge.

"There's no human impact of pollution or overcapacity, so I think it really gives the wildlife and vegetation the space to thrive," Mino says. "It gives the wildlife a chance to do what they naturally do."
Palmyra Atoll's thriving ecosystem has given scientists a window into the hidden processes that make it work, including some mysteries.

More than a decade ago, a team of scientists noticed something at Palmyra Atoll: Manta rays were more commonly seen in waters near seabird colonies. The massive mantas, some with a 9-foot wingspan, slowly glide through the water as they feed on tiny plankton.
That led them to uncover an efficient system of nutrient recycling that starts with the birds.

When seabirds return to land after eating fish at sea, they roost in the trees. There, they deposit a lot of nutrients in their guano. One study of almost 200 atolls estimated that seabirds brought more than 100,000 pounds of nitrogen back to land. That acts as a fertilizer, nourishing the trees and plants.

Those nutrients spread with Palmyra Atoll's frequent, heavy rains. They get washed into the ocean, where they help the entire marine food web. Tiny, microscopic plankton grow, feeding larger plankton that are eaten by many species, including fish and manta rays. Though it's not their primary food source, even corals eat plankton.

"Studies show that those marine nutrients from seabird guano are really valuable and important for the whole reef ecosystem," says Katie Franklin, who works on Palmyra Atoll conservation strategy for The Nature Conservancy. "Guano will help nourish the ecosystem from the rainforest to the reef, so we really just want to bring on more guano."
Scientists figured out the seabirds' role because there are places on Palmyra Atoll where birds are hard to find. Some forests are eerily quiet.

"We're standing in a dense monoculture of coconut palms," Franklin says, pushing past large palm fronds. "It is literally just coconut palms growing. There are way fewer birds in this type of forest."
The palm trunks are densely packed together, letting in very little sunlight. The trees are the legacy of coconut plantations established more than a century ago.

"None of these attempts at farming coconut palms ended up being very successful or profitable and were all abandoned," Franklin says. "But the impact that these coconut palm plantations made has lasted."

In 2000, almost half of Palmyra Atoll was covered in coconut palms, where few seabirds nest. It's why the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and The Nature Conservancy have started a decade-long project to bring the native forest back.

In blazing midday tropical heat, Katie Baur saws the trunk of a young coconut palm. The beach is covered in coconuts, all sprouting young trees. She's a conservation science volunteer with The Nature Conservancy who lives on the atoll for six months.
"It's hard — it's definitely not glamorous," she says with a laugh.
Since the project started in 2019, more than a million coconut palm trees and sprouts have been removed. Baur says once the palms are gone, the native forest returns rapidly.

"I get to go around the atoll and see places where new native flora is starting to reestablish," Baur says. "So it's exciting for me because I know that the work I'm doing now, in six months, in a year, is going to look like those places."
Even as native forest has returned to Palmyra Atoll, the ecosystem's recovery has also depended on tackling another tricky invader: rats.
Rats were likely brought to Palmyra during World War II accidentally, but they quickly made themselves at home.

"They probably thought they had gone to heaven," says Wegmann of The Nature Conservancy's island resilience strategy. "Palmyra is so productive as an ecosystem. There are invertebrates everywhere, land crabs, insects, cockroaches, lots of yummy things for them to eat, and there are no predators."

With unlimited food and warm weather year-round, rat populations boomed, topping an estimated 30,000 rats. As a result, seabird populations declined, particularly birds that build their nests on the ground. It's a pattern that's been seen on hundreds of other islands. One study found that 41% of highly threatened mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians are found on islands, where invasive species have been a major driver of extinctions.

In 2011, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, along with nonprofit partners, led a campaign to eradicate rats from Palmyra Atoll. Wegmann says when the rats were successfully removed, the ecosystem rebounded quickly.

"Land crab populations exploded and the forest exploded," Wegmann says. "We saw new crab species emerge. We saw more and more seabirds nesting in trees throughout the entire atoll. And we started to see the native forest trees that had not been reproducing with rats here start to reproduce."

Researchers are now hoping to see the return of other seabirds that seem to have disappeared from Palmyra Atoll. Eight species are thought to have once nested there, but are no longer found. One, the gray-backed tern, recently reappeared and has nested on the atoll for four consecutive years.

Even with its remote Pacific location, Palmyra Atoll is still threatened by global changes. In 2013, a marine heat wave elevated ocean temperatures for months, causing the corals to bleach and turn white. Many of the atoll's reefs have since recovered, but some didn't bounce back as readily.

As the climate gets hotter, the future for coral reefs globally is dire. Studies show that if humans continue burning fossil fuels, the planet will heat up more than 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), compared to preindustrial temperatures. At that level, between 70%-90% of coral reefs worldwide won't survive, according to a report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
With marine heat waves getting more frequent and intense, research shows it's vital that reefs recover as quickly as possible between bleaching events.

"We want to give them the best chance possible to do that," Wegmann says. "And we believe that by creating the habitat for the seabirds and maximizing that seabird nutrient benefit, we will give the reef its best chance of enduring whatever climate future comes."
Wegmann says the conservation lessons learned at Palmyra are being applied at other islands and atolls, like the Chagos Archipelago in the Indian Ocean.

Coconut palms have taken over half of the forested land at more than 200 atolls around the Pacific. Roughly a quarter of all tropical seabirds in the world also rely on atolls for nesting. While atolls seem small, the linkages between land and sea mean they play an outsized role in global biodiversity.

"They create this halo of influence on the ocean around them," Wegmann says. "If you add up all of the area of ocean for all the atolls just in the Pacific, it's about the same size as South America. So, protecting atolls is important for the individual atoll, but also for a huge amount of ocean surrounding it."

After the extended international break, the Champions League is back and gearing up for a rapid run of games. Just over three weeks from now, the league phase will be at its halfway mark, a clearer sense of the European hierarchy having emerged. Then again, we might get a bit of a sense on Tuesday night with several of the big hitters in action. Both Bayern Munich and Barcelona have games that fall into the tough places to go category. For the former, it's a journey north to Stavanger and the champions of Norway, while Hansi Flick's side will put their winning run to the test at Galatasaray, where the likes of Liverpool and Juventus lost last season.
Before we get to them, however, it's time to talk about last season's beaten finalists and their star player. After all, Bukayo Saka's season seems kinda weird.

Weird in that on paper the output looks really rather impressive, particularly in front of goal. Seven games into his campaign and Saka has three goals, one of them a penalty against Sunderland. For a player who only just scraped into double figures in each of the last two seasons, this should be an encouraging start. And yet it does not feel like Saka has set the Premier League or indeed Europe alight so far, and his performance Saturday against Leeds in the Premier League was the subject of widespread criticism with Arsenal legend David O'Leary saying that the No.7 is "not the player he was," nor the player that earned the £350,000-a-week contract.

It's not hard to see where that sentiment is coming from. As the game was winding down Arsenal's star winger was through one-on-one with Leeds keeper James Trafford. Saka seemed to get the ball stuck under his feet and bent an effort too close to the goalkeeper, whose save at least ensured Leeds only lost by a score of 2-1. As an isolated incident, no harm, no foul. It's just that Saka keeps missing these chances. Even discounting the penalty he scored, Arsenal's starboy has had a big chance -- a subjective tag applied by Opta to high-value shots -- in every game he has played this season. He has missed the last five of them.

A better hook from close range might have saved Arsenal from a heavy defeat to Brighton before the interational break, while his ballooning of a 0.7 expected goals (xG) chance against Napoli on Matchday 1 of the Champions League league phase came straight off a rugby pitch. These are infuriating misses for supporters and doubtless for Saka too, but in analytical terms they come with a positive: at least he is getting in position to miss those chances. You should worry a lot more if those shots aren't coming your way.

Good shots are coming Saka's way. The sample size of 581 minutes across seven league and European games is still small enough that we have to be a bit wary about drawing conclusions, but by this point we can at least point out some trends. Those might include Saka getting far better quality shots this season than anyone else. Going from the three shots per 90 he has hovered at in the last four seasons to 3.6 this season has delivered a doubling on non-penalty xG to 0.61. Saka's 0.177 xG per shot (again discounting the penalty) in the Premier League this season is the best by any non-striker with over 10 shots to their name.

Saka still likes to cut in from the right flank and try to bend one in from range. Now, however, he is supplementing those with a lot of poacher's chances. That they aren't going in yet has brought questions, but really there is no reason to think that won't change. For his Premier League career as a whole Saka is as close as you'll get to a goals = xG scorer, 62 of the former, 62.21 of the latter. And, anyway, it is not as if anyone has had any cause to doubt his technique over recent years.

If this early season trend does keep up, then it might be a valuable addition to a game where there are questions about what else might have been lost. Since the day Saka underwent surgery to address a severe tear on his right hamstring in December 2024, there have been questions as to whether he might have lost or be able to get back the burst of youth.

The tracking evidence we have suggests that there has been no obvious change in the speeds he hits. The season where Saka's average max speed per game was at its highest, according to Gradient Sports data provided for CBS Sports, was 2021-22, when he was at 31.28 km/h. Last season he was at 30.25 km/h, this season, 30.03 km/h. The vast majority of that difference between five years ago and today can be explained by the fact that this season's Arsenal do not get to run in behind anywhere near as often as they used to, the burden of being one of the best teams in the world, etc., etc. A fair bit more might reflect the niggling injuries since that hamstring tear that have robbed Saka of physical momentum.

That aside, there is no meaningful change in the distance Saka sprints or covers at high speeds per 90. His accelerations and decelerations are largely unchanged too. With nearly 400 games for club and country in the rearview, he could be forgiven for not having the vim of youth, but it was only back in August that Saka was saying he is "on top of my body" after an injury-addled World Cup.

Even if Saka has lost that yard of pace -- and he has always been a player who found space with his brain first and then his feet -- well then at least he is adapting in the right way. Every player slows down eventually; the best find themselves different ways to make an impact. It might be that Saka already has.

Saturday brought history for Barcelona, a 3-0 win over Getafe, making it nine wins from nine in all competitions, the first time in the illustrious history of this club that they have achieved that. Right now there is no more ferocious an attack in Europe than Hansi Flick's, averaging a staggering 3.85 goals per game without even that much overperformance on shooting. As you can see on the team profile below, the defense is not looking too shabby either.

Most encouraging at the weekend was how these numbers held up in spite of the absence of Raphinha, who did not travel to Istanbul as he nurses a thigh issue. The Brazilian is inarguably the player of the season so far with 14 goals and three assists in eight games. His replacement, Gabriel Jesus, barely missed a beat, however, and is averaging a goal every 41 minutes.

Like so many others from this summer, he looks a shrewd addition. Jesus and Adeyemi rounded out the supporting cast behind Lamine Yamal and Raphinha at relatively low cost. Much more was spent on Anthony Gordon and Rodri but both are excelling, the latter proving crucial in protecting a defense that still has not added that much-vaunted elite center back to partner Pau Cubarsi. This looks a significantly improved iteration of last season's Barcelona, one that has done all it can so far to prove itself capable of going multiple steps further in the Champions League.

The first question is what they have actually been able to prove. The Champions League routinely proves that, after its big three, La Liga does not have the depth of five or more years ago and it is not as if Barcelona have been taking on the best the division has to offer. Their 34 goals have been scored against teams ranked 15th, 12th, eighth, ninth, 16th, 13th and seventh in last season's table as well as promoted Racing Santander. Feyenoord at home was hardly the trickiest of Champions League openers.

Do Galatasaray offer a greater test? Well, maybe. When the mood takes Rams Park and the Gala players lift their game, plenty of Barcelona's contemporaries can attest that this is a nightmare fixture. Victor Osimhen at his best is a one-man counterattack who will love bursting into the space that Flick's defense so willingly leaves. Equally, Galatasaray could very simply play to their collective talent level and find themselves blown away, another side who don't really have the quality to match Europe's form team. It might be a while yet before we see a team who really can.

- The U.S. men’s team opened its new World Cup cycle with four straight wins, a first, while 13 of 28 players made their senior debuts.
- Teenagers accounted for more than half of the team’s 12 goals, with Cavan Sullivan, Julian Hall and Justin Ellis among the young standouts.
- Pochettino says the results matter less than the team’s commitment and potential ahead of the 2028 Olympics and next World Cup.
The U.S. men’s national team has opened a World Cup cycle with four consecutive victories for the first time since ... well, since ever.

What Mauricio Pochettino did with the U.S. team in the opening camp of the new World Cup quadrennium never had been done before. And Pochettino did it while using 28 players, including 13 who earned their first caps with the senior national team.

The kids were all right, as it turned out, with more than half of the 12 U.S. goals in the four games coming from teenagers who were playing with the team for the first time. So when the coach calls up his regulars next month for a two-leg Nations League quarterfinal with Haiti — the first competitive matches of the new cycle — expect some of those new players to receive invitations too.

“They are so smart. They have talent,” Pochettino said. “With more experience with these young talented players, plus the senior players that we have, we have a very good mix. I hope that we can guide this group of players to reach our best level and compete in our best way to try to be with the big national teams in the future.”

Others players who are age-eligible will join Steve Cherundolo’s U23 national team and begin preparations for the 2028 L.A. Olympics. The U.S. may be beginning the push for the next World Cup and Olympics with the deepest and most talented player pool in its history.

“So happy. So, so happy,” Pochettino gushed after last Tuesday’s 1-0 win over Canada. “Not because of the results but because of the performance and the commitment that the players showed. That is the way that we want to be in the future.”
Yes, this all could be a mirage. It wouldn’t be the first time we’ve been fooled.

Remember the 2006 cycle? After reaching the quarterfinals in 2002, a U.S. team that featured Landon Donovan, Clint Dempsey, Tim Howard, Kasey Keller and Brian McBride lost just 10 of 62 games over the next four years and was ranked No. 4 in the world before the World Cup in Germany.
Should U.S. men’s coach Mauricio Pochettino continue to build on the roster he has or should he try to start over as much as possible before the 2030 World Cup?

Or how about this past summer? A golden generation of Weston McKennie, Christian Pulisic, Tyler Adams and Timothy Weah had been groomed for years for this one tournament. Pochettino openly talked about reaching the final.
Instead, the U.S. went out in the round of 16 for the fourth time in as many World Cups.

So while history insists it’s wise to greet any success by the U.S. with a generous amount of skepticism, the early returns suggest this cycle could be different. The U.S. played quality teams in this international window — Mexico and Canada also reached the final 16 of this summer’s World Cup and are ranked among the top 30 in the world by FIFA, Mexico at 10 and Canada at 27.
With the next World Cup still four years away, however, Pochettino is looking beyond the results toward building something enduring.

“Not talking only about the results, talking about the way that we competed and the way that we came together, I think it was amazing,” he said. “That is a starting point to keep going with the basis and the principle that we were talking about. To develop and evolve in this way.
“The effort was massive. To play always with the same effort, the same commitment and the same passion, that is a thing that we need to keep.”
An inefficient youth pipeline, competition from other sports and an inability to develop a superstar are some of the reasons why the U.S. keeps losing in the World Cup.
Assuring that happens, Pochettino said, is a job for the coaching staff.

“How are we going to evolve with them?” he said. “How we are going to protect, how are we are going to guide, how are we are going to make them understand that now they have more responsibility? That is a mentality that we are trying to apply.”

Some players already proved they have the talent. Winger Cavan Sullivan, who will leave the Philadelphia Union for Manchester City next year, made three appearances, starting twice, in the fall window and became the youngest scorer in U.S. Soccer history with his goal against Mexico five days after his 17th birthday.

That broke a record teammate Mathias Albert, also 17, had set less than a week earlier against Chile. Last April, Albert, a month shy of his 17th birthday, became the youngest American to play in the German Bundesliga when he came off the bench for Dortmund.

Striker Julian Hall scored in each of his first three senior national team appearances, against Peru, Chile and Mexico. Just 18, he’s already made more than 60 appearances and scored 14 goals for the New York Red Bulls in MLS. Orlando City forward Justin Ellis, 19, had two goals in his first three international games, including the game-winner against Canada.

Then there’s goalkeeper Diego Kochen, 20, who has made 37 appearances for Barcelona’s B team. He played 135 minutes against Peru and Mexico and did not give up a goal. No position on the U.S. team is as wide open as goalkeeper, and Kochen has shown he deserves to be in the conversation.

All four very well could be called up for the Nations League matches, but they certainly will form the foundation of Cherundolo’s Olympic team in two years. And there could be more young players coming, Pochettino said.

“It’s a big pool,” he said. “In this window, certain players made their debut. But there are plenty of other young players who are on our radar and we are assessing them. Here in the USA but also outside the USA.
“We are watching different young kids that maybe, in the future, will have the opportunity.”
Four games into the new World Cup cycle, that future may be brighter — and closer — than ever.
Man stabs at least 8 people in South Korean mall
Police and fire officials in the South Korean city of Incheon say a man stabbed at least eight people at a shopping mall

SEOUL, South Korea -- A 59-year-old man stabbed at least eight people Tuesday at a shopping mall in the South Korean city of Incheon, police and fire officials said. One victim was in life-threatening condition and received surgery at a nearby hospital.
The suspect attacked shoppers as he moved through the mall before business owners and bystanders subdued him, according to Incheon’s Namdong District Police Station and witnesses.

The man has a history of violent offenses and mental illness and was required to wear an electronic monitoring anklet, according to South Korea’s Justice Ministry. The man’s name was not released, in keeping with South Korean practice for most criminal suspects.
Witnesses told South Korean media that the attacker appeared to have knives tied to both hands and stabbed people in different parts of the mall while moving up and down the floors on an escalator.

Nah Hyun-joon, who helped subdue the attacker using chairs with several other people, said he saw the man attack about four people in the second-floor food court before moving up to the third floor, where he stabbed at least one woman.

Nah said the attacker then headed toward a multiplex movie theater on the fourth floor but was blocked by several people holding chairs at the top of the escalator. Nah said he and others trapped the man from below and eventually subdued him near the escalator’s third-floor entrance, pushing him down with chairs and removing his knives, before police arrived.
“He just went around stabbing people,” Nah told OBS television. “He didn’t even say anything. He just stabbed whoever he saw."

The injured were taken to nearby hospitals, including one woman in her 20s who underwent surgery after arriving in cardiac arrest, Incheon’s fire department said. The department didn’t provide details on the severity of the other injuries.

The suspect was sentenced to four years in prison for attempted murder in 2015, according to South Korea’s Yonhap news agency. He was placed under electronic monitoring in 2019 and had committed no repeat offenses while under supervision, the Justice Ministry said.

The suspect was booked last month on suspicion of carrying a weapon after using a kitchen knife to puncture a protest sign outside a hospital where he had a dispute, and was receiving treatment for alcohol dependence and unspecified mental illnesses, according to the ministry.

Earlier on the day of the attack, the suspect attended a counseling session from 10 to 11 a.m. and then met his probation officer from 11:20 to 11:55 a.m., the ministry said. The attack began at 1:40 p.m.
The officer confirmed that the suspect had taken his medication and had lunch with him until 12:30 p.m. Authorities detected no attempts to destroy his monitoring device, the ministry said.

“We sincerely apologize over the great public concern caused by the knife attack by an individual under electronic monitoring,” the ministry said in a statement, adding that it would review both the supervision of the suspect and broader electronic monitoring procedures.
Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets in a cyberattack that reportedly caused refrigerators and freezers to overheat, spoiling food and sparking fires.

Fridges at French supermarket chains Carrefour, Monoprix, the Les Mousquetaires-owned Intermarché, and Coopérative U, among others, all saw fridges heat up to as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, Reuters reported on Monday.
Coopérative U's CEO Dominique Schelcher confirmed that cyberattacks had affected "refrigeration production facilities of several stores."

"Attacking equipment that is essential to the preservation of fresh products and the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and unprecedented. It is unacceptable," Schelcher said in a LinkedIn post.
CNBC has reached out to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché, Coopérative U, and E Leclerc for comment but did not immediately hear back.

Felix Aime, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said the attack affected several European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium, according to the Reuters article.
"I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at @intermarche @CooperativeU @Leclerc," European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said in a post on X on Monday.
"Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality."

The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles resurgence in decades. More than 3,600 confirmed cases and two deaths have been reported as of late September. Outbreaks in several states and exposures in public places like bars, sports stadiums and public transit have raised concerns about travel safety. Almost all U.S. measles cases involve unvaccinated individuals, and as the outbreaks grow in some states, the risk of exposure is getting higher. Here's what to know before traveling by plane or train.
- ✈️ People who've had two doses of the MMR vaccine are considered protected against measles.
- ✈️ The disease is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, breathes or sneezes. That airspace can remain contaminated for up to two hours.
- ✈️ Check with your healthcare provider about your vaccination status. They may recommend a booster based on your medical history and health.
- ✈️ Immunocompromised individuals may be unable to receive vaccination and often rely on herd immunity for protection. For measles, the vaccination threshold for herd immunity is 95%.
- ✈️ Measles can be hard to track because symptoms — such as fever, cough, and rash — typically appear seven to 14 days after exposure and can sometimes take long as 21 days to surface.

Oct. 13 (UPI) -- Hurricane Simon weakened to a Category 1 storm late Monday, as it moved slowly northwest along Mexico's west coast, lashing the region with heavy rain and flooding, forecasters said.

The storm was located about 90 miles west of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico, and 190 miles south of Mazatlan, Mexico, the NHC said in its 11 p.m. MST update. The storm had maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, a drop of 10 mph in three hours.
It was moving northwest at a 3 mph crawl.

A hurricane warning was in effect for Las Islas Marias, while a hurricane watch was in effect for north of Escuinapa to Bahia Tempehuaya. A tropical storm watch was also in effect for Cabo Corrientes to Escuinapa.
"Simon is expected to continue moving slowly northwestward during the next day or so, followed by a turn toward the north on Wednesday," the NHC said.
"Some additional weakening is forecast over the next day or so, but Simon is forecast to remain a hurricane through midweek and could re-intensify by Wednesday."
Simon was likely to produce rainfall totals of 5 to 10 inches across coastal west-central Mexico. Isolated maximum amounts of 15 inches were possible over Sinaloa by Thursday.
Storm surge was possible along the immediate coast near Las Islas Marias, the NHC said. Near the coast, the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves.
